sum: UDP's bare datagrams and when they beat TCP, the problems you inherit (loss, pacing, NAT, spoofing), and how QUIC rebuilds reliable, encrypted, multiplexed transport on top of UDP for HTTP/3.
prereq: net4
TCP's handshake, sequence numbers and ACKs, retransmission, congestion control, and head-of-line blocking when one lost segment stalls every later byte.
net2
A cold HTTPS visit spends one round trip on the TCP handshake and one on TLS 1.3 before the request; 0-RTT resumption is replayable.
net3
NAT devices keep a mapping per flow and expire it when idle; many hosts share one public address.
why:
In net4 you saw how much work TCP does: a handshake before any data, numbering every byte, retransmitting losses, and delivering everything strictly in order. For a file download or a database query that is exactly what you want. But imagine you are on a video call. A packet carrying 20 milliseconds of your friend's voice goes missing. TCP would stop delivering everything that came after it until the lost packet is retransmitted and arrives, perhaps 150 ms later. By then that sound is useless: the conversation has moved on, and you have heard a freeze instead of a tiny glitch. For the call, skipping the lost packet is better than waiting for it.

That is the case for UDP, the User Datagram Protocol: the transport that does almost nothing, and so lets the application decide what to do about loss and timing. DNS lookups, voice and video, online games and telemetry all use it.

There is a second, bigger reason to learn UDP today. TCP's design has limits that became painful on the modern web: it needs a handshake round trip before encryption can even start; a single lost packet stalls every request sharing a connection; a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data breaks every connection; and TCP lives inside operating-system kernels and is inspected by countless middleboxes, so improving it takes a decade. Engineers at Google, and then the IETF, responded by building a new transport, QUIC, on top of UDP. It is now what HTTP/3 runs on, carrying a large share of all web traffic from browsers to the big CDNs and platforms.

So this lesson has two halves. First UDP itself: what it provides, where it is the right tool, and the problems you take on when you use it, including why it is the favourite tool of denial-of-service attackers. Then QUIC: how it rebuilds reliability, encryption and multiplexing in user space on UDP, how its handshake saves round trips, how its independent streams remove head-of-line blocking, how connections survive network changes, and what it costs to run in production.
primer:
UDP: a postcard, not a phone call

TCP is like a phone call: you connect first, then talk in a continuous stream, and the line takes care of making sure every word arrives in order. UDP is like sending postcards. Each one is a self-contained datagram with an address on it. There is no setup, you can send one immediately, and each arrives whole or not at all. But some may be lost, some may arrive in a different order from the one you sent them in, occasionally one arrives twice, and the post office will not tell you about any of it.

That is almost literally the whole protocol. UDP's header is 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum. Compared with TCP's 20-plus bytes and its state machine, UDP adds only one thing to IP: ports, so the datagram reaches the right program. Everything else, if you need it, is your job.

Two properties make UDP genuinely useful rather than just primitive. It preserves message boundaries: one send is one datagram is one receive, so no framing is needed. And nothing ever waits: a lost datagram does not delay the ones after it, because there is no ordering to preserve.

QUIC: reliability rebuilt on postcards

Because UDP does so little, you can build a whole new transport on top of it without asking operating systems or network equipment for permission. QUIC does exactly that: it numbers its packets, acknowledges them, retransmits what is lost and controls congestion, like TCP, but it runs as a library inside the application, has TLS 1.3 encryption built in, and carries many independent streams in one connection.

The payoffs, each explained in the body: a new connection with encryption in one round trip instead of two (and zero on repeat visits), a lost packet only delays the stream it belongs to, connections survive changing networks, and the protocol can be improved by shipping a new library rather than new operating systems.

Where you meet them today

Every DNS lookup your laptop makes is almost certainly a UDP datagram. Every video call in a browser or app sends its audio and video over UDP. When you load a page from Google, YouTube, Meta or a site behind a large CDN in a modern browser, the requests very likely travel over QUIC. And the database connections, internal APIs and SSH sessions you work with daily are still TCP. All three coexist, and a single page load can use all of them.

How to choose, in one sentence each

Use TCP when you need a reliable byte stream and the standard tools, which is most of the time. Use QUIC (usually via HTTP/3) when latency on real-world networks matters, especially mobile and long-distance. Use raw UDP when late data is worthless, you need multicast, or you are building a transport yourself, and then accept that you own loss, pacing and security.
body:
1. The UDP datagram, and what "no guarantees" means

A UDP datagram is an 8-byte header plus payload, inside one IP packet:

FieldSizeMeaning
Source port16 bitswhere replies should go (optional in theory)
Destination port16 bitswhich program receives it, e.g. 53 for DNS
Length16 bitsheader plus payload, in bytes
Checksum16 bitsdetects corruption; optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6

A program opens a UDP socket, and every sendto() call produces exactly one datagram; every recvfrom() returns exactly one datagram, whole, together with the sender's address and port. There is no connection: the same socket can talk to many peers, and a server simply answers whoever sent the last datagram.

What can go wrong, concretely, is everything IP allows. A datagram can be lost (a full router queue drops it, or the receiver's socket buffer is full and the kernel drops it on arrival), reordered (two datagrams take different paths), duplicated (rare, from misbehaving equipment), or corrupted (and then dropped by the checksum). The sender is told about none of it.

2. When UDP is the right tool

  • Tiny request/response exchanges. A DNS query and its answer each fit in one datagram. Over TCP, a lookup would cost a handshake plus the exchange, and servers would hold state for billions of short connections. Over UDP it is one round trip, and if the answer does not come back, the client simply asks again after a timeout.
  • Real-time media. Voice and video calls send small packets every 10 to 20 ms, usually in the RTP format, which adds timestamps and sequence numbers. The receiver uses a jitter buffer (a small delay, perhaps 30 to 100 ms, that smooths out variation in arrival times), plays packets in order, and conceals any that are missing. Retransmitting would arrive too late to play.
  • Games and state updates. A player's position is sent 20 to 60 times per second; each update replaces the previous one, so a lost update is best forgotten.
  • Telemetry and discovery. Metrics agents (StatsD) fire-and-forget counters where occasional loss is acceptable; local service discovery uses broadcast or multicast (one datagram to a group of listeners), which only UDP supports.
  • Building a new transport. QUIC, the WireGuard VPN and media protocols like WebRTC's data channels use UDP as a thin, universally allowed wrapper, and do their own reliability and congestion control on top.

3. The problems you inherit

Choosing UDP means taking on, yourself, the jobs TCP was doing:

  • Loss, reordering and duplicates. Put a sequence number in every message so the receiver can detect gaps, discard duplicates and stale data, and decide whether to request a resend.
  • Congestion control and pacing. Nothing stops a UDP sender from transmitting faster than the path can carry. If it does, routers drop the excess, including other people's TCP packets, whose senders politely back off while yours keeps going. Well-behaved UDP applications measure loss and delay and adjust their rate, and send at a steady pace rather than in bursts.
  • Size. Keep datagrams below the path MTU. The header allows about 64 KB, but a datagram bigger than the link's MTU is split into IP fragments; losing any fragment loses the whole datagram, and many firewalls drop fragments entirely. Safe sizes are about 1,200 bytes: QUIC requires paths to carry at least 1,200-byte datagrams, and DNS now recommends a 1,232-byte limit.
  • NAT and firewalls. A NAT (net3) creates a mapping when you send, but because there is no FIN to say a UDP "conversation" is over, it expires mappings after inactivity, often within 30 seconds to a few minutes. Long-lived UDP flows send keepalives more often than that.
  • Receive buffer overflows. If the application does not read fast enough, the kernel drops arriving datagrams when the socket buffer is full, and counts them (netstat -su shows "receive buffer errors"). With TCP the sender would have been slowed by flow control; with UDP data just disappears.

4. Spoofing and amplification

TCP's handshake proves the client can receive packets at its claimed address; a forged source address never sees the SYN-ACK, so the connection cannot proceed. UDP has no such proof. Anyone can send a datagram with a spoofed source address, and the server will send its reply to whoever owns that address. Combine that with a service whose reply is much bigger than the request, and you get a reflection and amplification attack:

In February 2018 GitHub was hit by 1.35 Tbit/s of traffic reflected from misconfigured memcached servers on UDP port 11211; the production section tells that story. Any protocol you design on UDP must avoid being an amplifier, typically by never sending more to an unverified address than it received from it. QUIC builds that rule in.

5. QUIC's building blocks

QUIC was developed at Google from 2012 and standardised by the IETF in 2021 as RFC 9000 (the transport), RFC 9001 (how TLS secures it), RFC 9002 (loss detection and congestion control) and RFC 9114 (HTTP/3). Its vocabulary:

  • A connection is between a client and a server, identified by connection IDs chosen by each side, not by IP addresses and ports.
  • Each UDP datagram carries one or more QUIC packets, each with a packet number that only ever increases.
  • Each packet carries frames: STREAM frames with application data, ACK frames acknowledging received packet numbers, CRYPTO frames carrying the TLS handshake, and control frames for flow control and connection management.
  • A stream is an independent, ordered byte sequence within the connection, like a lightweight TCP connection. Either side can open many; HTTP/3 uses one per request.

Almost everything after the first few bytes of each packet is encrypted, including the packet number and all frames. An observer on the network sees UDP ports, a few flag bits and the connection ID, and nothing else.

6. The handshake: one round trip, sometimes zero

With TCP and TLS 1.3 (net2), the client waits one round trip for the TCP handshake and another for the TLS handshake before it can send its request, so the response arrives after three round trips. QUIC carries the TLS 1.3 handshake messages inside its own first packets, so connection setup and key agreement happen together:

In detail: the client's first datagram contains an Initial packet carrying the TLS ClientHello, padded to at least 1,200 bytes (which, as we will see, is an anti-amplification measure). The server replies with its own Initial and Handshake packets carrying the ServerHello, certificate and Finished, and can already send application data. The client finishes the handshake and sends its request in the same flight. For a returning client, TLS 1.3 session resumption lets it derive keys for 0-RTT data and include the request in its very first flight. As with TLS 0-RTT over TCP, that early data can be replayed by an attacker, so it is only safe for idempotent requests (net2).

7. Streams without head-of-line blocking

Recall from net4 that TCP delivers one ordered byte stream per connection, so when HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over TCP, one lost packet blocks all of them. QUIC keeps order per stream. Each STREAM frame says which stream it belongs to and at which byte offset, so the receiver reassembles each stream independently:

This mattered enough that HTTP/3 also needed a new header compression scheme. HTTP/2's HPACK relies on all header blocks arriving in order across the connection; HTTP/3's QPACK is designed so that a stream's headers can usually be decoded without waiting for other streams.

8. Reliability and congestion control, rebuilt

QUIC acknowledges packets, not bytes. ACK frames list ranges of received packet numbers (like TCP's SACK, but with many more ranges) and report how long the receiver delayed the ACK, so RTT is measured accurately. Because packet numbers never repeat, when data is lost its frames are placed into a new packet with a new number. That removes a long-standing TCP ambiguity, where an ACK for a retransmitted segment could refer to either the original or the retransmission, confusing RTT measurement. Loss is detected when a later packet has been acknowledged and either enough packets or enough time have passed, similar to Linux TCP's RACK method (net4). Congestion control follows the same principles as TCP, starting cautiously and backing off on loss, and implementations ship CUBIC or BBR; because it is a library, changing algorithm is a software update. Flow control exists at two levels, per stream and per connection, so one greedy stream cannot use all the receiver's buffer.

9. Connection migration

A TCP connection is its 4-tuple; if the client's address changes, the server sees packets from an unknown tuple and the connection is dead. When a phone walks out of Wi-Fi range onto mobile data, every TCP connection breaks and every app reconnects, paying the handshakes again. QUIC packets carry a connection ID, so a server receiving packets from a new address with a known connection ID recognises the connection. It validates the new path (sending a challenge that the client must echo, so an attacker cannot redirect traffic to a victim) and continues. Clients switch to fresh connection IDs when migrating so observers cannot link the old and new paths.

10. TCP, UDP and QUIC side by side

TCPUDPQUIC
Unitbyte streamdatagrammany streams (+ optional datagrams)
Setup before data1 RTT (+1 for TLS)none1 RTT with TLS; 0 on resumption
Reliability and orderyes, one order per connectionnoneyes, one order per stream
Congestion controlkernelnone (your job)library
Encryptionseparate (TLS)nonebuilt in, headers too
Survives address changenon/ayes (connection IDs)
Where it runsOS kernelOS kernelapplication or library
Typical useAPIs, databases, SSHDNS, media, gamesHTTP/3, mobile apps

Read the table as a set of trade-offs rather than a ranking. TCP is the dependable default with the best tooling and the cheapest CPU. UDP is a blank canvas that gives full control and full responsibility. QUIC packages the best current ideas about transport into a library, at the cost of running more code in your process and needing UDP to be allowed.

11. Discovering and falling back

A browser cannot know in advance whether a site speaks HTTP/3 or whether the network lets UDP through. Usually the first visit uses HTTP/2 over TCP, and the response carries an Alt-Svc header such as h3=":443"; ma=86400, meaning "HTTP/3 is available on UDP port 443, remember this for a day". Newer sites also publish an HTTPS DNS record that advertises HTTP/3 before the first connection. Browsers then try QUIC, often racing it against TCP, and fall back silently if UDP is blocked, as it is on some corporate networks. Any service offering HTTP/3 must therefore keep offering HTTP/2 over TCP.
deep:
Anti-amplification and address validation

A QUIC server receiving a first packet cannot yet know whether the source address is genuine, so it could be used as a reflector. RFC 9000 therefore limits a server to sending at most three times the number of bytes it has received from an address until that address is validated, which happens when the client proves it received the server's packets. The client's first datagram must be padded to at least 1,200 bytes, which both gives the server a budget for its certificate-heavy reply and ensures the path supports QUIC's minimum datagram size. Under attack, a server can go further and send a Retry packet containing a token the client must echo, proving its address before the server does any expensive cryptography, the same idea as TCP SYN cookies.

Load balancing QUIC

Layer-4 load balancers traditionally hash the 4-tuple to pick a backend. With migration, the tuple changes mid-connection, so a tuple hash would send the migrated connection to the wrong server, which knows nothing about it. The solution is to route on the connection ID: servers issue connection IDs that encode which backend they belong to (optionally encrypted so outsiders cannot learn the mapping), and the balancer decodes it. The IETF's QUIC-LB work standardises such schemes. Stateless balancers that cannot do this simply lose migration; stateful ones must track connection IDs. Either way, UDP port 443 must be open through every firewall and security group on the path.

The CPU cost and how it is being closed

Kernel TCP benefits from decades of optimisation and hardware offloads: the network card segments large sends and coalesces received packets, and encryption can be offloaded too. A user-space QUIC stack originally made one system call per packet and encrypted each packet in software, costing noticeably more CPU per byte. The gap is being closed by UDP GSO and GRO, which let one system call send or receive a batch of datagrams that the kernel or card splits and merges; by sendmmsg/recvmmsg for batching; by pacing in the kernel; and by careful memory handling. For most services the remaining overhead is acceptable; for bulk transfer inside data centres, kernel TCP usually remains cheaper.

Visibility: the price of encryption

Operators used to debug TCP performance from passive captures: sequence numbers, retransmissions and RTT are all visible in the headers. QUIC hides packet numbers and ACKs, deliberately. What remains visible is the UDP header, the connection ID, and one optional spin bit that flips once per round trip so on-path observers can estimate RTT if the endpoints choose to allow it. Debugging therefore moves to the endpoints, which can emit qlog event logs (packets sent, lost, acknowledged, congestion window changes) to be viewed in tools such as qvis, or export TLS keys so Wireshark can decrypt a capture on a test machine.

Unreliable data inside QUIC, and WebTransport

Some applications want QUIC's encryption, congestion control and NAT friendliness but also want to send some data unreliably, such as game state or media frames. RFC 9221 adds a DATAGRAM frame: unreliable, unordered messages carried inside the encrypted, congestion-controlled connection. Browsers expose this, together with multiple streams, through the WebTransport API over HTTP/3, giving web apps a UDP-like option for the first time, alongside WebRTC (net11).

Versions, GREASE and keeping the protocol flexible

QUIC's designers expected middleboxes to try to parse whatever was left visible, so they defended even those few bits. Every packet with a long header carries a version number, and a client and server can negotiate versions; QUIC version 2 (RFC 9369) exists largely to prove that negotiation keeps working in practice. Endpoints also grease the protocol: they send random values in reserved fields and occasionally use reserved version numbers, so any middlebox that assumed those values were fixed breaks immediately in testing rather than years later in production. It is the same lesson as TCP's ossification, applied pre-emptively: a field that never varies will eventually be treated as a constant by someone.

Why not just fix TCP?

Many of QUIC's ideas were tried in TCP: Fast Open for faster handshakes, multipath TCP for migration, bigger initial windows. Each was slowed by two facts. TCP lives in operating-system kernels, so improvements reach users only as fast as phones and servers upgrade their OS, which takes years. And middleboxes that parse TCP headers drop or mangle unfamiliar options, so new features fail on some fraction of paths. Running over UDP in user space, with encrypted headers, makes QUIC deployable by updating an app or a library, and keeps middleboxes from freezing it. It is an architectural lesson: put the parts you want to evolve where you control them.
prod:
Failure modes you will meet

  • UDP blocked or throttled. Some enterprise firewalls block UDP 443 or rate-limit UDP generally. Clients fall back to TCP, so nothing breaks outright, but you lose the latency benefits for those users, and connection attempts that race QUIC and TCP waste a little work. Track the share of requests on HTTP/3 versus HTTP/2 by network to see it.
  • Missing firewall rules for QUIC. A team enables HTTP/3 on its load balancer but the security group or network ACL only allows TCP 443. Clients try QUIC, time out and fall back, adding delay to the first connection. The fix is simple once noticed: allow UDP 443 end to end.
  • Silent UDP drops at the receiver. A metrics collector or DNS server under load drops datagrams because its socket receive buffer is full. Nothing errors; data just goes missing. Watch RcvbufErrors in netstat -su or nstat, raise net.core.rmem_max and the socket buffer, and add more reader threads.
  • NAT timeouts on UDP flows. VoIP calls lose audio in one direction after a pause, or a game client stops receiving updates, because a NAT mapping expired. Send keepalives every 15 to 25 seconds on long-lived UDP flows.
  • Fragmentation. Large DNS responses (for example with DNSSEC signatures) fragment, fragments are dropped by a firewall, and lookups time out for some domains only. DNS Flag Day 2020 moved the ecosystem to a 1,232-byte default EDNS buffer, with truncation and fallback to TCP for anything bigger.
  • CPU increase after enabling HTTP/3. Edge servers use more CPU per request than with TCP; capacity plans must account for it until GSO/GRO and batching are enabled.

War story: 1.35 Tbit/s from memcached

On 28 February 2018 at 17:21 UTC, GitHub was hit by one of the largest DDoS attacks recorded at the time: 1.35 Tbit/s and about 127 million packets per second. The traffic came from memcached servers, a caching system that some operators had left listening on UDP port 11211 on the public internet. Attackers sent them small requests with GitHub's addresses as the spoofed source, and memcached replied with responses up to 51,000 times larger. GitHub's site was fully unavailable for about five minutes and intermittently for four more. It recovered by withdrawing its BGP announcements from its transit providers and routing through its DDoS mitigation provider, which filtered the UDP 11211 traffic at the edge of its network. The lessons were aimed at the whole ecosystem: never expose UDP services that answer unauthenticated requests with large replies, networks should drop packets with forged source addresses, and critical sites need a mitigation provider on standby.

Observability and tools

For UDP: ss -uan lists UDP sockets and their queues; netstat -su and nstat give datagram and error counters; tcpdump shows datagrams in full because UDP itself is not encrypted. For QUIC: browser DevTools show the protocol per request (h3); Chrome's chrome://net-export captures detailed connection logs; servers and libraries can write qlog; Wireshark can decode QUIC if you give it the TLS keys through the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable. At the load balancer, watch HTTP/3 request share, handshake failures and fallback rates.

Knobs

Socket receive and send buffer sizes (net.core.rmem_max, SO_RCVBUF) for high-rate UDP; UDP GSO/GRO enablement in the QUIC library; congestion control choice in the QUIC stack; the Alt-Svc max-age (how long clients remember HTTP/3 support); QUIC idle timeout and keepalive intervals relative to NAT timeouts; and whether to accept 0-RTT, and for which request types.
myths: UDP is faster than TCP.

UDP has no handshake and no retransmission, so it avoids waiting, but it does not move bits faster. For bulk transfer, a naive UDP sender either floods the network and loses data or must reinvent TCP's congestion control. UDP wins when late data is useless or when a protocol like QUIC builds a better transport on top of it.
UDP means unreliable, so anything built on it is unreliable.

UDP just leaves reliability to the layer above. QUIC, built on UDP, is as reliable as TCP, with numbered packets, acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control, and it is what HTTP/3 uses to carry web pages and API calls.
QUIC is HTTP/3.

QUIC is a general-purpose transport; HTTP/3 is the mapping of HTTP onto it. Other protocols run on QUIC too, such as DNS over QUIC and WebTransport, and QUIC also offers an unreliable datagram extension for media.
QUIC is always faster than TCP.

QUIC saves a handshake round trip and avoids cross-stream head-of-line blocking, which helps most on long, lossy mobile paths. Inside a data centre with sub-millisecond RTT and almost no loss, the gains are tiny, and QUIC's user-space processing costs more CPU than kernel TCP with hardware offload.
UDP datagrams can be as large as you like, up to 64 KB.

The header allows about 64 KB, but anything larger than the path MTU (usually about 1,500 bytes, less in tunnels) gets fragmented into IP fragments, and losing any fragment loses the whole datagram; many firewalls drop fragments entirely. Real protocols keep datagrams around 1,200 to 1,400 bytes; QUIC and modern DNS use 1,200 and 1,232 bytes as safe sizes.
Encrypting QUIC headers is just about privacy.

It is mainly about keeping the protocol changeable. Middleboxes that could read TCP headers came to depend on them and broke new TCP features. QUIC encrypts almost everything except a few fields needed for routing, so networks cannot build assumptions into their equipment and the protocol can keep evolving.
lab:
Twenty minutes. You will see that UDP keeps message boundaries and loses data silently, capture DNS over UDP, and check which sites speak HTTP/3. Linux, macOS or WSL; the loss step needs Linux or WSL.

  1. A UDP echo pair in Python. Save as udp.py and run it: 
    import socket, threading
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9999))
got = []
def serve():
    while True:
        data, addr = srv.recvfrom(65535)
        if data == b"END": break
        got.append(int(data.split(b":")[0]))
threading.Thread(target=serve).start()
c = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
for i in range(1000):
    c.sendto(f"{i}:hello".encode(), ("127.0.0.1", 9999))
c.sendto(b"END", ("127.0.0.1", 9999))
import time; time.sleep(0.5)
print("received", len(got), "of 1000; out of order:", sum(a > b for a, b in zip(got, got[1:])))
    Look for: each datagram arrives as exactly one recvfrom, with its number intact: boundaries are preserved. On loopback you will usually get all 1,000 in order.
  2. Add loss. On Linux/WSL, inject 10% loss on loopback: sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 10%, rerun the script, then remove it with sudo tc qdisc del dev lo root. Look for: roughly 900 received and no error anywhere: the sender never finds out. (If the END marker itself is lost, the server thread hangs; press Ctrl+C and rerun.) Compare with net4's byte-stream lab, where TCP would have retransmitted silently.
  3. Watch DNS over UDP. Run sudo tcpdump -i any -nn udp port 53 in one terminal and dig example.com in another. Look for: exactly two datagrams, one query and one response, with no handshake. Then run dig +tcp example.com and see the TCP handshake appear before the same query.
  4. Find HTTP/3 advertisements. curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc and the same for https://www.google.com. Look for: h3=":443", the site telling clients "HTTP/3 is available on UDP 443". If your curl was built with HTTP/3 support (curl -V lists HTTP3), try curl --http3 -sI https://www.cloudflare.com and note HTTP/3 200.
  5. See it in the browser. Open DevTools, Network tab, enable the Protocol column, and load a big site twice. Look for: h2 on the very first request and h3 on later ones: the Alt-Svc discovery in action.
  6. Look at QUIC on the wire. Capture with Wireshark using the filter quic while loading that site. Look for: Initial packets with long headers, visible connection IDs, and then packets whose contents Wireshark shows only as "Protected Payload". Compare with a TCP capture where sequence numbers and ACKs are plainly visible.
recap: UDP adds only ports, a length and a checksum to IP: independent datagrams with preserved boundaries, and no connection, ordering, retransmission, flow control or congestion control.
UDP suits cases where late data is worthless or the application wants control: DNS lookups, voice, video, games, telemetry, and as a base for new transports.
Using UDP means handling loss, reordering and duplicates, pacing your sending rate, keeping datagrams below the MTU, and refreshing NAT mappings that expire quickly.
Because UDP has no handshake, source addresses can be spoofed, enabling reflection and amplification attacks via open DNS, NTP or memcached servers.
QUIC is a reliable, encrypted, multiplexed transport running in user space over UDP, standardised in RFC 9000 in 2021, and HTTP/3 runs on it.
QUIC combines its transport handshake with TLS 1.3, so a new connection needs one round trip and a resumed one can send data immediately with 0-RTT.
QUIC streams are independent, so a lost packet only delays the streams whose data it carried, removing TCP's cross-stream head-of-line blocking.
QUIC identifies connections by connection IDs rather than the address 4-tuple, so connections survive a phone switching networks.
QUIC's costs are higher CPU use, networks that block UDP (so clients must fall back to TCP), load balancers that must route by connection ID, and less visibility for passive monitoring.
glossary: 0-RTT
Sending application data in the very first flight of a resumed connection, using keys from a previous session; saves a round trip but can be replayed.
ACK frame
QUIC's acknowledgement, which lists ranges of received packet numbers, similar to TCP's SACK.
Alt-Svc
An HTTP response header advertising that the same site is available over another protocol, e.g. h3 (HTTP/3) on UDP port 443.
Amplification factor
How many times larger a reflected response is than the request that triggered it.
Connection ID
An identifier carried in QUIC packets that names the connection independently of IP addresses and ports.
Connection migration
A QUIC connection continuing after the client's IP address or port changes, e.g. moving from Wi-Fi to mobile data.
CUBIC and BBR
Congestion control algorithms: CUBIC reacts to loss, BBR paces to a measured bandwidth and RTT (net4). QUIC libraries offer both.
Datagram
One self-contained UDP message, delivered whole or not at all.
DDoS (distributed denial of service)
Overwhelming a target with traffic from many sources so legitimate users cannot reach it. Covered in net14.
DNS (Domain Name System)
The name-to-address directory; most queries are single UDP datagrams. Covered in net6.
DNSSEC
Cryptographic signatures on DNS records; the signatures make responses larger, which is why DNS size limits matter. Covered in net6.
EDNS(0)
An extension letting DNS clients advertise that they accept UDP responses larger than the original 512-byte limit.
Fragmentation
Splitting an IP packet that is larger than a link's MTU into pieces; losing any piece loses the whole packet.
GREASE
Deliberately sending random values in reserved fields so that middleboxes cannot assume those fields are fixed, keeping them usable for future versions.
GSO / GRO (generic segmentation / receive offload)
Kernel and network-card features that process many packets as one large batch, cutting per-packet CPU cost; now available for UDP.
Head-of-line blocking
One missing piece of data holding up delivery of everything queued behind it.
HPACK / QPACK
Header compression for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 respectively; QPACK is designed so streams can decode headers without waiting on each other.
HTTP/3
HTTP mapped onto QUIC streams. Compared with HTTP/2 in net8.
HTTPS DNS record
A DNS record type (RFC 9460) that can tell clients a site supports HTTP/3 before they connect.
IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)
The open standards body that publishes internet protocols as RFCs, including QUIC and HTTP/3.
Jitter
Variation in packet delay; real-time media uses a jitter buffer to smooth it out.
MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)
The largest packet a link carries, usually 1,500 bytes on Ethernet (net1).
Multicast
Sending one datagram to a group of receivers; only possible over UDP.
NAT (Network Address Translation)
Rewriting addresses at a router; UDP mappings are kept only while traffic flows (net3).
NIC (network interface card)
The network hardware in a machine; modern NICs offload work such as segmentation and checksums from the CPU.
NTP (Network Time Protocol)
The UDP protocol computers use to synchronise clocks; open NTP servers have been abused for amplification.
Pacing
Spreading packets evenly over time instead of sending them in bursts, to avoid overflowing router queues.
Packet number
QUIC's per-packet counter; it is never reused, so a retransmission is always a new packet with a new number.
qlog
A standard logging format for QUIC endpoints, used with visualisers because encrypted traffic is hard to inspect on the wire.
QUIC
A transport protocol over UDP providing reliable, encrypted, multiplexed streams with TLS 1.3 built in (RFC 9000).
Reflection attack
Sending requests with the victim's address as the spoofed source, so servers send their replies to the victim.
RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol)
The standard UDP-based format for carrying audio and video, with timestamps and sequence numbers.
Spoofing
Forging the source address of a packet; easy with UDP because there is no handshake to prove the address.
Stream
An independent, ordered byte sequence inside a QUIC connection; many streams share one connection.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
The kernel's reliable, ordered byte-stream transport (net4).
TLS (Transport Layer Security)
The encryption and authentication protocol; QUIC carries its TLS 1.3 handshake inside its own packets. Covered in net9.
UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
The minimal transport: an 8-byte header with ports, length and checksum over IP.
User space
Code running as a normal application or library, as opposed to inside the operating-system kernel.
WebTransport
A browser API over HTTP/3 offering multiple streams and unreliable datagrams to web applications.
WireGuard
A modern VPN protocol that runs over UDP.
drill:
Choose and justify

Pick TCP, UDP or QUIC for each and justify: (a) a multiplayer game's position updates at 30 Hz; (b) the same game's in-game purchases; (c) a mobile app's API, used heavily on flaky cellular networks; (d) a service-mesh call between pods in one data centre; (e) bulk nightly backup transfer of 2 TB between regions.

Answer
  • (a) UDP, with a light custom protocol: each update supersedes the previous one, so retransmitting a stale position only adds delay. Add sequence numbers to drop out-of-order packets, interpolate over losses, pace sending and send NAT keepalives.
  • (b) Reliable delivery: TCP (HTTPS) or a reliable QUIC stream. Purchases must arrive exactly once and be confirmed by the server; use idempotency keys so a retried request does not charge twice.
  • (c) QUIC / HTTP/3: fewer handshake round trips, 0-RTT resumption for idempotent calls, no head-of-line blocking under loss, and connection migration when the phone changes network all matter on mobile. Keep HTTP/2 over TCP as the fallback for networks that block UDP.
  • (d) TCP (HTTP/2 or gRPC): RTT and loss inside a data centre are tiny, so QUIC's advantages are small, while kernel TCP is cheaper on CPU and well supported by meshes, proxies and tooling.
  • (e) TCP, tuned: large windows or several parallel streams to fill a high bandwidth-delay path (net4), BBR on long lossy paths, or a purpose-built transfer tool. UDP-based bulk tools exist, but they must implement their own congestion control to avoid harming other traffic.
Diagnose: missing metrics

Your team sends application metrics as UDP datagrams (StatsD style) to a collector. During traffic peaks, dashboards show counts dropping by 20% even though request logs show traffic rising. No errors are logged anywhere. What is happening, how do you confirm it, and what would you change?

Answer

At peak, datagrams arrive faster than the collector reads them, its socket receive buffer fills, and the kernel drops the excess on arrival. UDP has no flow control, so senders are never told, and no application logs an error. Confirm on the collector host with netstat -su or nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors: the counter rises during peaks. Also check for loss on the path if the collector is remote (NIC and switch drop counters). Fixes, in order: increase the socket receive buffer (SO_RCVBUF, capped by net.core.rmem_max) to absorb bursts; add reader threads or processes with SO_REUSEPORT so reading keeps up; reduce datagram count by aggregating on the sender (a local agent that pre-aggregates per host is the standard pattern); and for metrics that must not be lost, such as billing counters, switch to a reliable transport or a push to a queue. Accept that UDP metrics are "best effort" and label dashboards accordingly.
qa: E
What does UDP not provide that TCP does?

Connection setup, reliable delivery, ordering, duplicate suppression, flow control and congestion control. UDP only adds ports, a length and a checksum to IP, delivering independent datagrams with their boundaries preserved.
Follow-up: What does UDP give you that TCP does not? — Message boundaries, no handshake delay, no head-of-line blocking, multicast, and full control over timing and retransmission.
E
Give three applications that use UDP and explain why.

DNS, because a query and answer each fit in one datagram, so a handshake would triple the cost. Voice and video calls, because a packet that arrives late is useless and should be skipped rather than retransmitted. Online games, because each position update replaces the last. QUIC and VPNs like WireGuard also use UDP as a base on which to build their own transport.

Follow-up: What does a video call do about lost packets then? — It conceals them: forward error correction or interpolation fills small gaps, and the codec asks for a fresh key frame if too much is lost.
E
What is QUIC in one paragraph?

QUIC is a transport protocol, standardised in RFC 9000 in 2021, that runs in user space on top of UDP and provides what TCP plus TLS provide: reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled, encrypted delivery. It adds independent streams, a combined one-round-trip handshake, 0-RTT resumption and connection migration. HTTP/3 is HTTP running on QUIC.
Follow-up: Why build it on UDP rather than as a new IP protocol? — Firewalls and NATs pass UDP but block unknown protocols, so a new protocol number would not be deployable on the real internet.
M
What problems with TCP does QUIC solve?

It merges the transport and TLS handshakes for 1-RTT setup and 0-RTT resumption, removes head-of-line blocking between multiplexed streams, supports connection migration across IP changes using connection IDs, and evolves in user space rather than the kernel. It also encrypts its headers so middleboxes cannot ossify it.
Follow-up: What does it not solve? — Congestion control still starts slowly, head-of-line blocking still exists within one stream, and the speed of light is unchanged.
M
Why are UDP services commonly abused for DDoS amplification?

Without a handshake, attackers can spoof the victim's source address; a small request to an open UDP service such as DNS, NTP or memcached triggers a much larger response sent to the victim, multiplying the attacker's bandwidth. CISA lists DNS at 28 to 54 times and memcached at up to 51,000 times.

Follow-up: How does QUIC avoid being an amplifier? — Before a client's address is validated, a QUIC server may send at most three times as many bytes as it received, and clients must pad their first packet to at least 1,200 bytes.
M
How does QUIC avoid head-of-line blocking between streams?

Each QUIC stream has its own ordering. Packets carry frames tagged with stream IDs and offsets, and the receiver reassembles each stream separately, so if a packet carrying data for stream 4 is lost, streams 0 and 8 keep delivering while only stream 4 waits for the retransmission. TCP has one byte order for the whole connection, so everything waits.

Follow-up: Why did HTTP/3 need a new header compression scheme? — HTTP/2's HPACK assumes headers arrive in order across streams; QPACK lets streams decode headers independently so compression does not reintroduce blocking.
M
How does a browser know it can use HTTP/3 for a site?

Usually the first connection uses HTTP/2 over TCP, and the response includes an Alt-Svc header such as h3=":443", telling the browser the site also speaks HTTP/3 on UDP port 443; later connections try QUIC. Alternatively, an HTTPS DNS record can advertise HTTP/3 support before the first connection. Browsers race or fall back to TCP if UDP is blocked.
Follow-up: Why must there always be a TCP fallback? — A few percent of networks block or throttle UDP 443, typically corporate firewalls, and clients there must still work.
M
How does QUIC connection migration work, and why does it matter?

TCP identifies a connection by the two IPs and ports, so when a phone moves from Wi-Fi to mobile data its address changes and every connection breaks. QUIC packets carry connection IDs, so the server recognises the connection from the new address, validates the new path, and continues. Users keep downloads and calls going across network changes without new handshakes.
Follow-up: What must a load balancer do to support it? — Route packets by connection ID rather than by address tuple, for example by encoding the backend's identity in the connection IDs it issues.
M
If you build a protocol directly on UDP, what must you handle yourself?

Loss detection and whatever recovery your application needs, reordering and duplicate detection (sequence numbers), congestion control and pacing so you do not flood the network, datagram sizes below the path MTU, keepalives to refresh NAT mappings, and protection against spoofing and amplification. Most teams should use QUIC or an existing media stack rather than reinvent these.

Follow-up: Why is congestion control a moral obligation, not just an optimisation? — A UDP sender that ignores loss keeps blasting while TCP flows back off, starving everyone else on the bottleneck and risking congestion collapse.
M
Why is DNS mostly UDP, and when does it use TCP?

A typical query and answer each fit in one datagram, so UDP avoids a handshake and server state for billions of tiny exchanges. When an answer is too large for the advertised UDP size, the server sets the truncation flag and the client retries over TCP; zone transfers and DNS over TLS use TCP too. Since DNS Flag Day 2020, 1,232 bytes is the recommended EDNS buffer size to avoid fragmentation.
Follow-up: Why avoid fragmented DNS responses? — Fragments are often dropped by firewalls, causing timeouts, and they have been used in cache-poisoning attacks.
H
What are the operational costs of moving a large service to HTTP/3?

CPU: QUIC runs in user space with per-packet encryption and fewer hardware offloads, so it costs more per byte than kernel TCP, though UDP GSO/GRO and batching narrow the gap. Networking: firewalls and security groups must allow UDP 443, and load balancers must support QUIC and route by connection ID for migration. Observability: encrypted headers mean passive tools see little, so you rely on endpoint logs like qlog. And you keep HTTP/2 over TCP for fallback, so you run both stacks.

Follow-up: How would you measure whether it helped? — Compare real-user latency percentiles by protocol and network type, watch fallback rates, and focus on mobile and long-distance users where gains appear.
H
How does QUIC's loss recovery differ from TCP's?

QUIC packet numbers increase monotonically and are never reused, so a retransmitted frame travels in a new packet with a new number and the sender always knows which transmission an ACK refers to, removing TCP's retransmission ambiguity and making RTT samples accurate. ACK frames carry many ranges and the exact ACK delay, and loss is detected by packet and time thresholds, much like TCP's RACK. Congestion control is pluggable, so implementations ship CUBIC or BBR as a library choice.

Follow-up: What is retransmitted, packets or data? — Data: lost frames are re-queued and may be sent in a different packet alongside other data, so there is no one-to-one mapping between original and retransmitted packets.
H
What is 0-RTT in QUIC, and how do you use it safely?

A client that has connected before can encrypt its first request with keys from the previous session and send it in the first flight, so the server can respond without waiting a round trip. But the server cannot distinguish that first flight from a copy captured and replayed by an attacker, so 0-RTT data must only carry idempotent requests such as a GET with no side effects. Servers and CDNs typically accept 0-RTT only for safe methods and can add replay caches, and applications can reject early data with a 425 Too Early status.
Follow-up: Is 0-RTT forward secret? — Not for the early data: it is encrypted with a key derived from the earlier session, so compromise of that ticket key exposes it.
H
Choose a transport for a real-time multiplayer game and justify it.

Use UDP for the fast state updates, with a small custom protocol: sequence numbers to discard stale or out-of-order updates, the latest full state or deltas against acknowledged snapshots, and interpolation to hide losses. Send important one-off events, such as a purchase or a chat message, reliably: either a reliable channel you build over UDP or a separate TCP or QUIC connection. Add pacing, a jitter buffer on the client and NAT keepalives.
Follow-up: Why not send everything over one TCP connection? — A single lost packet would stall all later updates behind it, so players would see freezes followed by bursts of stale positions.

why:
Every connection your code makes starts with a name: api.stripe.com, db.internal, my-service.default.svc.cluster.local. Before a single TCP packet can be sent, that name has to become an IP address. The system that does this, DNS, is so reliable most of the time that engineers forget it exists, which is exactly why it is behind so many outages. There is a well-worn joke among operations engineers, "it's always DNS", and a haiku that ends "it was DNS".

Consider three real situations. A team migrates its database to a new host, updates the DNS record, and half of its services keep talking to the old host for an hour, because the record had a long TTL and some clients never re-resolve. A company's DNS provider is hit by a denial-of-service attack, and its website becomes unreachable worldwide even though every one of its servers is perfectly healthy. A Kubernetes cluster's DNS pods are overloaded, and random requests across dozens of services stall for exactly five seconds. None of these is a bug in application code; each is a DNS mechanism behaving exactly as designed.

DNS is also a tool you actively use. It is how CDNs send each user to a nearby server, how multi-region services fail over, how you prove to a certificate authority or an email provider that you own a domain, how services find each other inside a cluster, and one of the first places a security reviewer looks.

net2 walked through a lookup once. This lesson goes inside it: how the namespace is organised into zones and delegated, what stub and recursive resolvers do, how caching and TTLs really work (including caching of "does not exist"), the record types you will meet, how DNS is used to steer traffic, what goes over the wire, how DNSSEC and encrypted DNS protect it, and how DNS behaves inside Kubernetes. The production section then catalogues how it fails.
primer:
The problem: names for people, numbers for routers

Routers forward by IP address, but people and configuration files use names, and addresses change: servers move, CDNs pick different edges for different users, failover switches regions. DNS (the Domain Name System) is the directory that turns a name into its current address, and into other kinds of information such as which servers accept a domain's email.

The analogy: a directory of directories

No single directory could hold every name on the internet and handle every lookup. So DNS works like asking for a phone number through a chain of receptionists. The main switchboard (the root) does not know your friend's number, but it knows who handles every country code. The ".com" desk does not know it either, but it knows who handles "example.com". Example.com's own receptionist (its authoritative server) finally gives the number. Your company has one assistant (the recursive resolver) who makes these calls for everyone and writes answers on a notepad, crossing them out after a set time (the TTL), so most questions are answered from the notepad without any calls.

Where the analogy breaks: the notepad is shared by millions of people, so a wrong entry, or a stale one, affects all of them until it expires; and the chain of receptionists is enormous but mostly idle, because the notepads answer nearly everything.

The tree of names

Why DNS is fast despite the tree

Walking root, TLD and authoritative servers for every lookup would be slow and would melt the root servers. It almost never happens. Your browser and operating system cache answers; your recursive resolver caches answers for everyone who uses it, including the referrals for com and other TLDs, which it needs to fetch only once a day or so. A popular name is usually answered from the resolver's memory in a millisecond or two. The tree is the source of truth; the caches do the work.

What a record looks like

Every piece of DNS data is a resource record with a name, a TTL in seconds, a type and a value. This is what dig prints:

api.example.com.   300   IN   A       203.0.113.10
www.example.com.   3600  IN   CNAME   example.cdn-provider.net.
example.com.       86400 IN   MX      10 mail.example.com.

Read the first line as: "the name api.example.com has an IPv4 address (A record) of 203.0.113.10, and you may cache this for 300 seconds". The IN means the internet class, which is the only one you will use. The second line is an alias (CNAME): "www is really that CDN name; look that up instead". The third names the mail server. Those three types, plus a handful more in the body, cover almost everything you will touch.

If you remember one operational fact from this lesson: a DNS change reaches a client only when every cache between them has let the old answer expire. Everything about DNS migrations follows from that.
body:
1. Zones and delegation

The namespace is one big tree, but it is managed in pieces called zones. The root zone contains, for each top-level domain (TLD) such as com or in, a set of NS records naming the servers responsible for it. The com zone, run by its registry, contains NS records for every registered .com domain. The example.com zone, run by whoever owns the domain (often through a DNS provider such as Route 53 or Cloudflare), contains the actual records for www, api and so on. Handing a subtree to other servers is called delegation, and it is always done by NS records in the parent zone.

One chicken-and-egg problem: if example.com's name servers are ns1.example.com and ns2.example.com, a resolver cannot look up their addresses without already asking them. So the parent zone also publishes their addresses, called glue records, alongside the delegation.

When you "register a domain", you pay a registrar, which tells the TLD registry which name servers to list in the parent zone for your domain. When you "move DNS to a new provider", you change those NS records at the registrar. Because the parent's NS records have long TTLs, often two days for .com, that particular change genuinely does take a day or two to reach every resolver, which is where the folklore about slow "propagation" comes from.

Every zone also has an SOA (Start of Authority) record at its top, the zone apex, carrying administrative data: a serial number that secondary servers use to notice changes, and the TTL for caching negative answers.

2. Resolvers: stub and recursive

Two kinds of client software take part in every lookup.

The stub resolver is a small piece of the operating system or C library. On Linux its configuration lives in /etc/resolv.conf: which recursive resolvers to ask (up to three nameserver lines), which search domains to try for short names, and options such as ndots, timeout (5 seconds by default) and attempts (2 by default). The stub sends one query and waits for one final answer. It does not walk the tree.

The recursive resolver does the real work for many clients: your ISP's resolver, your company's, your cloud provider's (such as the one at the VPC base address plus two in AWS), or a public one like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. On a cache miss it starts from the root (every resolver ships with a root hints list of the 13 root server names, a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net, each actually served from many sites worldwide by anycast), follows referrals down to the authoritative server, and caches everything it learns along the way: the final answer, the NS records and glue for com and example.com, for their TTLs. A busy resolver therefore rarely needs to talk to the root at all, and usually goes straight to the authoritative servers of the domain being asked about.

Between the application and the stub there may be further caches: the browser's DNS cache, a language runtime's own cache (the JVM, for example, has its own lookup cache), and a local caching daemon such as systemd-resolved. Each layer is another place an old answer can linger.

3. Caching and TTLs, precisely

When a resolver receives a record with TTL 300, it may answer from cache for up to 300 seconds, counting down; clients asking later get the remaining TTL, which is why dig run twice shows a decreasing number. After expiry the next query triggers a fresh lookup. That is the whole mechanism: DNS is pull, never push. Nobody tells caches that a record changed.

The consequence for changes is precise. If a record's TTL is T and you change it at time 0, a resolver that fetched it just before time 0 may keep serving the old value until almost time T. So the worst case for everyone to see the change is one old TTL, plus any client that ignores TTLs.

Resolvers also cache "no". If a name does not exist, the authoritative server answers NXDOMAIN and includes the zone's SOA record; the resolver caches the negative answer for the smaller of the SOA's own TTL and its "minimum" field (RFC 2308). This negative caching protects authoritative servers from floods of queries for missing names, but it means a record created shortly after someone asked for it may stay invisible to them for that period.

Choosing TTLs is a trade-off. Short TTLs (30 to 60 seconds) make failover and migration fast, but every cache miss costs a lookup (tens of milliseconds, sometimes more), authoritative servers get more queries, and if your DNS provider goes down, clients lose your records within a minute. Long TTLs (hours) are cheap and ride out short provider outages, but lock in mistakes. A common pattern: long TTLs on stable records (MX, NS, verification TXT records), 60 to 300 seconds on records you may need to move.

4. Record types you will actually use

TypeMapsTypical use and gotchas
A / AAAAname → IPv4 / IPv6several records = several addresses; clients choose
CNAMEname → another namepoint at a CDN or load balancer; no other records may exist at the same name, so not at the apex
ALIAS / ANAMEapex → another name (provider feature)provider resolves the target and serves its A/AAAA
NSzone → its name serversdelegation; long TTLs
SOAzone metadataserial number, negative-caching TTL

TXTname → textdomain verification, email policy (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)

HTTPS / SVCBservice → parametersadvertise HTTP/3 support, ports and hints (net5)
