PTRIP → namereverse DNS, e.g. 9.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa; used in logs and email reputation

The CNAME rule deserves a sentence of explanation because it trips everyone up. A CNAME says "this name is that other name, for every record type". If example.com were a CNAME, it could not also have the SOA and NS records every zone apex must have, so the combination is forbidden. That is why DNS providers invented ALIAS-style records: the provider's server resolves the target itself and answers with plain A and AAAA records at the apex.

CNAMEs also chain: www.shop.com can point to shop.cdn-provider.net, which the CDN's own DNS answers, often differently for different users:

5. On the wire

A DNS message is small and binary: a header with a 16-bit transaction ID and flags, then the question (name and type), then answer, authority and additional sections. Queries normally go over UDP port 53: one datagram out, one back, no handshake (net5). The client matches the reply to its question by the transaction ID and its own source port, retries after a timeout if nothing comes back, and moves on to the next configured resolver if that fails too.

Classic DNS limited UDP answers to 512 bytes. EDNS(0) lets the client advertise a bigger buffer, and since DNS Flag Day 2020 the recommended size is 1,232 bytes, chosen so answers fit in one packet without IP fragmentation on almost any path. If an answer is larger, the server sets the truncated (TC) flag and the client repeats the query over TCP port 53. Zone transfers between primary and secondary authoritative servers also use TCP.

Two response codes you must recognise: NXDOMAIN, "the name does not exist", and SERVFAIL, "I could not get a valid answer", which means something is broken upstream (unreachable or misconfigured authoritative servers, or a DNSSEC validation failure), not that the name is missing. A third outcome, an answer with no records of the requested type (NOERROR with an empty answer, sometimes called NODATA), means the name exists but has no, say, AAAA record.

6. Steering traffic with DNS

Because an authoritative server can answer each query however it likes, DNS is a powerful traffic control tool:

  • Round-robin: return several A records, possibly in rotating order. Clients spread out roughly. No health awareness.
  • Weighted: return endpoint A for 90% of queries and B for 10%, for gradual migrations or canary releases.
  • Latency- or geo-based: answer with the region or edge nearest to the querying resolver. The server only sees the resolver's address, so providers use the EDNS Client Subnet extension, where the resolver passes along a truncated form of the client's address, to pick better.
  • Health-checked failover: the DNS provider probes endpoints and stops returning unhealthy ones.

All of these are limited by caching: a decision stays in effect for a TTL, and a client that picked a dead address keeps trying it. So the standard architecture is DNS for coarse, global decisions (which region, which CDN edge), and load balancers for fine-grained, per-request decisions inside a region (net10).

7. Security: poisoning, DNSSEC and encrypted DNS

Classic DNS has no authentication: a resolver accepts the first reply whose transaction ID and port match its question. Cache poisoning exploits this. An attacker triggers a lookup and floods the resolver with forged replies guessing the ID; if one is accepted, the resolver caches the attacker's address and serves it to every user. In 2008 Dan Kaminsky showed how to make this fast: query random nonexistent names like x123.example.com so each attempt is a fresh cache miss, and include forged referrals that hijack the whole domain. The immediate defence was randomising the query's source port as well as its ID, multiplying the guessing space by tens of thousands.

The complete defence is DNSSEC. Each zone signs its records with its own key and publishes the signatures. The parent zone publishes a DS record, a hash of the child's key, and signs that; so a validating resolver can follow a chain of trust from the root's key, which it has built in, down to the answer, and reject anything forged. DNSSEC provides authenticity and integrity, not confidentiality, and it adds real operational risk: an expired signature, a key rotation mistake, or a DS record left at the parent after disabling signing makes the whole domain fail to resolve (SERVFAIL) for users of validating resolvers.

Privacy is a separate problem: classic DNS queries travel in plaintext, so anyone on the path, and the resolver operator, sees every name you look up. DNS over TLS (DoT, port 853), DNS over HTTPS (DoH, port 443) and DNS over QUIC (DoQ) encrypt the hop between the client and its resolver. Browsers and operating systems increasingly enable DoH by default. Note that they protect only that hop: the resolver still sees your queries, and resolvers talk to authoritative servers mostly in plaintext.

8. DNS inside Kubernetes

In a Kubernetes cluster, a DNS server (usually CoreDNS) answers names for Services, such as payments.prod.svc.cluster.local, and forwards everything else to upstream resolvers. Each pod gets a resolv.conf like this:

nameserver 10.96.0.10
search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

The ndots:5 option says: if a name has fewer than five dots, first try it with each search domain appended. That lets code say just payments or payments.prod. But it means a lookup of api.stripe.com (two dots) is tried as api.stripe.com.prod.svc.cluster.local, then api.stripe.com.svc.cluster.local, then api.stripe.com.cluster.local, and only then as itself, each failing with NXDOMAIN first, and each for both A and AAAA. One logical lookup becomes eight queries. At scale this multiplies CoreDNS load and adds latency to every external call. Fixes: write external names fully qualified with a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.), lower ndots in the pod's dnsConfig, and run a node-local DNS cache so repeated lookups never leave the node.
deep:
Why "it's always DNS": failure amplification

DNS sits at the start of every connection, so a DNS problem is instantly a problem for everything. Three properties amplify it. First, a lost UDP query is only retried after the stub's timeout, 5 seconds by default in glibc, so small packet loss turns into multi-second latency spikes that look like application slowness. Second, when a resolver is slow, clients retry and applications retry on top, multiplying load on an already struggling resolver. Third, caches hide problems until TTLs expire, so a broken change can appear fine for minutes and then fail everywhere at once, far from the moment of the change. Mature teams therefore treat DNS changes like code deploys: reviewed, staged, monitored from many locations, and easy to roll back.

The DNSSEC chain of trust and its sharp edges

A signed zone has a key-signing key (KSK), whose hash the parent publishes as a DS record, and a zone-signing key (ZSK) that signs the records, itself signed by the KSK. Validation follows DS → KSK → ZSK → signature → record, from the root down. The operational hazards come from the cached pieces you do not control. The DS record lives in the parent zone with the parent's TTL: Slack learned in September 2021 that the .com zone tells resolvers to cache DS records for 24 hours, so after they turned signing off, validating resolvers kept expecting signatures and returned SERVFAIL. Negative answers need signed proofs of non-existence (NSEC or NSEC3 records), and a provider bug in how those proofs described wildcard records made some resolvers cache "no A record" answers for Slack. The general lesson is that DNSSEC changes are a multi-day, multi-party procedure with a rollback plan that accounts for every TTL involved.

Resolver location, Client Subnet and privacy

Geo-steering assumes the resolver is near the user, which was true when everyone used their ISP's resolver. Public resolvers and encrypted DNS break that assumption: a user in Chennai using a resolver instance in Singapore may be sent to a Singapore edge. EDNS Client Subnet fixes steering by passing the first 24 bits of the client's IPv4 address to the authoritative server, but it leaks location information and fragments resolver caches (one cached answer per subnet instead of one per name). Some large public resolvers therefore send it only to providers that need it, and anycast-based CDNs sidestep the issue by routing on the client's own packets instead of DNS answers.

Client behaviour matters as much as TTLs

What actually determines failover speed is what clients do. Browsers re-resolve often. Many server-side HTTP clients keep connections in a pool for minutes or hours and never look up the name again while a connection stays open, so a DNS change affects only new connections. The JVM caches successful lookups for 30 seconds by default, but forever when a security manager is installed, and some older libraries cache for the process lifetime. Connection pools to databases behave similarly. For DNS-based failover to work, clients need bounded connection lifetimes (for example, recycle pooled connections every few minutes) and sane DNS caching, and failover procedures should expect a long tail of stragglers on the old address.

Split-horizon and private zones

Organisations often serve different answers inside and outside their network: api.example.com resolves to a private load balancer for employees and servers, and to a public edge for everyone else. Clouds implement this with private hosted zones attached to specific VPCs. It is convenient and reduces exposure, but it is a classic source of "works for me" confusion: the same name gives different answers depending on which resolver you ask, so debugging must always start by asking "which resolver did this client use, and what did it return?"

DNS as a data-exfiltration and command channel

Because DNS queries are allowed out of almost every network and are forwarded by resolvers to whichever authoritative server owns a domain, attackers encode data in query names (c2VjcmV0.attacker.example) to smuggle it out, or receive instructions in TXT answers. Defences are forcing all DNS through monitored resolvers, blocking direct outbound port 53 and unknown DoH endpoints, and looking for unusual query volumes and long random-looking labels. This is also why enterprises are wary of browsers doing DoH to external resolvers: it bypasses their monitoring.
prod:
How DNS takes production down

  • Provider outage or DDoS. On 21 October 2016, a botnet of hacked cameras and routers (Mirai) flooded Dyn, a major managed DNS provider, and sites whose domains used only Dyn, including Twitter, GitHub, Netflix and Reddit, became unreachable for parts of the day in waves, while their servers were fine. Users whose resolvers had cached records kept working until the TTLs ran out. The lesson most teams took: critical domains need a second authoritative provider.
  • Bad changes. A typo in a record, a deleted record, an accidental TTL of 0, or a zone file pushed with the wrong serial. Because of caching, the blast radius grows as TTLs expire, so the incident may start well after the change.
  • DNSSEC mistakes. Expired signatures or broken DS records produce SERVFAIL for users behind validating resolvers only, a confusing partial outage. Slack's September 2021 rollout caused about 24 hours of intermittent failures for under 1% of users, mostly behind corporate resolvers and Google Public DNS.
  • Expired domains and certificates. A forgotten domain renewal takes everything down at once; registrars' reminder emails go to a departed employee. Put expiry dates in monitoring.
  • Resolver overload and 5-second stalls. CoreDNS pods or a VPC resolver hitting limits (AWS's VPC resolver has a per-network-interface packet rate limit) drop queries; clients see exact 5-second delays from the stub's retry timeout. Node-local caches and lower ndots are the standard fixes.
  • Stale addresses after migrations. Clients keep connecting to an old IP for long after the TTL because of connection pools or runtime caches. Keep the old endpoint alive and watch its traffic.
  • Dangling records. CNAMEs left pointing at deleted cloud resources enable subdomain takeover; security teams scan for them.

A debugging order that works

When a name misbehaves, ask these in order. What does the authoritative server say right now (dig @ns1.provider.example api.example.com)? What does the resolver this client actually uses say, and with what remaining TTL? What does the client itself see, including any hosts-file entry, runtime cache or search-domain expansion (getent hosts api.example.com on Linux uses the same path as most programs)? And is the client even resolving, or reusing an old connection? The answer is almost always a difference between two of those four views.

Observability

Monitor resolution of your key names from many networks and regions (synthetic checks), and alert on SERVFAIL rates and latency. On resolvers and CoreDNS, track query rate, cache hit ratio, response codes, upstream latency and dropped queries. On clients, DNS lookup time is visible in HTTP client metrics and traces if you instrument it, and in browsers through the Navigation and Resource Timing APIs (net2). Keep zone changes in version control (for example Terraform or OctoDNS), with review and an audit trail, because "what changed?" is the first question in every DNS incident.

Knobs

TTLs per record; SOA negative-caching TTL; a second authoritative provider; health checks and routing policies on the DNS provider; ndots, search domains, timeout, attempts and single-request-reopen in resolv.conf or pod dnsConfig; node-local DNS caches in Kubernetes; runtime DNS cache settings (such as the JVM's networkaddress.cache.ttl); and maximum connection lifetimes in pools so clients eventually follow DNS changes.
myths: DNS changes take 24 to 48 hours to 'propagate'.

Nothing is pushed anywhere. Resolvers keep an old answer until its TTL expires and then ask again, so a change is visible everywhere within one TTL of the old record, plus whatever time a client that ignores TTLs keeps its copy. With a 60-second TTL, a change is effectively live in about a minute. The '48 hours' folklore comes from old default TTLs and from registrar-level changes to NS records, which do carry long TTLs.
Setting a short TTL right before a migration makes the switch fast.

Resolvers already holding the record keep it for the old TTL. If the TTL was one day, lowering it an hour before the change does nothing for caches filled earlier. Lower the TTL at least one old-TTL ahead of time, wait, then make the change.
DNS round-robin gives you load balancing and failover.

Returning several A records spreads clients roughly, but DNS does not know which servers are healthy, clients and resolvers pick differently, and caches keep dead addresses for a full TTL. It is coarse steering. Health-checked DNS failover helps, but fine-grained balancing and fast failure handling belong in load balancers.
DNSSEC encrypts my DNS queries.

DNSSEC adds signatures so a validating resolver can prove records are authentic and unmodified. It does nothing for privacy: queries and answers are still readable on the wire. Privacy comes from DNS over HTTPS, TLS or QUIC between you and your resolver.
My application follows DNS changes automatically.

Many runtimes and libraries resolve a name once and keep the address: connection pools reuse sockets indefinitely, some JVM configurations cache lookups forever, and some clients cache for their process lifetime. A DNS-based failover only helps clients that actually re-resolve and reconnect.
If a name does not exist yet, creating it makes it resolvable immediately.

Resolvers cache 'does not exist' answers too (negative caching), for a time set by the zone's SOA record, often minutes to an hour. If someone queried the name before you created it, they may keep getting NXDOMAIN until that negative entry expires.
lab:
Fifteen minutes with dig (Linux, macOS, WSL; on Windows PowerShell, Resolve-DnsName works for most steps). You will read a response, walk the tree, watch caching and negative caching, and do a lookup over HTTPS.

  1. Read a full response. dig www.wikipedia.org. Look for: the status: field in the header (NOERROR), the flags (rd ra mean recursion desired and available), the ANSWER section (probably a CNAME then A records), the TTL column, and at the bottom SERVER: (which resolver answered) and Query time:.
  2. Watch caching. Run dig +noall +answer www.wikipedia.org twice, ten seconds apart. Look for: the TTL counting down by about ten, and a much lower query time on the second run: the resolver answered from cache.
  3. Walk the tree yourself. dig +trace api.github.com. Look for: root servers answering first with NS records for com., then .com servers answering with GitHub's name servers, then GitHub's servers giving the answer. This is exactly what a recursive resolver does on a cache miss.
  4. Look at other record types. dig +short NS github.com, dig +short MX gmail.com, dig +short TXT google.com, dig +short CAA google.com, dig +short HTTPS cloudflare.com. Look for: delegation, mail servers with priorities, verification and SPF strings, the certificate authorities allowed to issue, and HTTP/3 advertised in DNS (alpn="h3,h2").
  5. See a negative answer. dig no-such-name-12345.example.com. Look for: status: NXDOMAIN and an SOA record in the AUTHORITY section: its last number and its TTL set how long resolvers will cache "does not exist".
  6. Reverse lookup. dig -x 8.8.8.8 +short. Look for: dns.google., served from a PTR record under 8.8.8.8.in-addr.arpa.
  7. Compare resolvers. dig @1.1.1.1 +short www.netflix.com and dig @8.8.8.8 +short www.netflix.com. Look for: possibly different addresses: the answer depends on who asks and from where.
  8. DNS over HTTPS with curl. curl -s -H 'accept: application/dns-json' 'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A'. Look for: a JSON answer with the same data, fetched over an encrypted HTTPS connection that an on-path observer cannot read.
  9. Your own stub configuration. cat /etc/resolv.conf (Linux/WSL) or scutil --dns (macOS) or Get-DnsClientServerAddress (Windows). Look for: which resolver your machine uses and any search domains; this is the first thing to check when "DNS works for me but not for them".
recap: DNS is a hierarchical, distributed, heavily cached database that maps names to records; the namespace is a tree rooted at '.', split into zones, each served by its own authoritative name servers.
A parent zone delegates a child zone with NS records (plus glue addresses when needed), which is how resolvers walk from the root to .com to example.com.
Stub resolvers on clients ask recursive resolvers, which do the walking and cache every answer, including referrals and 'does not exist' results, for their TTLs.

The key record types are A and AAAA for addresses, CNAME for aliases, NS and SOA for zone structure, MX for mail, TXT for verification and email policy, SRV and HTTPS for service details, CAA for certificate issuance and PTR for reverse lookups.
A TTL trades agility against load and resilience; lower it at least one old TTL before a planned change, and remember that some clients ignore TTLs.
Authoritative servers can return different answers by client location, weight or health, which is how CDNs and multi-region failover steer traffic, but DNS steering is coarse and slow to converge.
Queries are normally single UDP datagrams on port 53, falling back to TCP for large answers; DoH, DoT and DoQ encrypt the client-to-resolver hop.
DNSSEC signs records along a chain of trust from the root so resolvers can detect forged answers, but it adds operational risk and no privacy.
DNS failures are sudden and wide: resolver outages, provider DDoS, expired domains, bad changes, dangling records and Kubernetes search-path amplification are the usual causes.
glossary: A record
Maps a name to an IPv4 address.
AAAA record
Maps a name to an IPv6 address.
ALIAS / ANAME
A provider-specific record that behaves like a CNAME at the zone apex by resolving the target and serving its addresses as A/AAAA records.
Anycast
Announcing the same IP address from many locations so queries reach the nearest; used by root servers and large DNS providers.
Authoritative name server
A server that holds a zone's records and gives definitive answers for names in it.
CAA record
Lists which certificate authorities may issue certificates for a domain.
Cache poisoning
Tricking a resolver into caching a forged answer, so it sends users to an attacker's address.
CNAME record
Says a name is an alias for another name; the resolver continues the lookup at the target.
Delegation
A parent zone handing authority for a subdomain to other name servers, using NS records.
DNSSEC
DNS Security Extensions: signatures on records and a chain of keys from the root, letting resolvers verify answers are authentic.
DoH / DoT / DoQ
DNS over HTTPS, over TLS and over QUIC: ways to encrypt queries between a client and its resolver.
DS record
Delegation Signer: a hash of a child zone's key, published in the parent zone, linking the DNSSEC chain of trust.
ECS (EDNS Client Subnet)
An extension where a resolver passes part of the client's IP address to authoritative servers so they can pick a nearby answer.
EDNS(0)
Extension mechanism for DNS that lets clients advertise larger UDP response sizes and carry options.
FQDN (fully qualified domain name)
A complete name ending at the root, e.g. api.example.com. with the trailing dot; not subject to search-domain expansion.
Glue record
An address for a name server supplied by the parent zone, needed when the name server's name is inside the zone it serves.
JVM DNS cache
The Java runtime's own cache of lookups, controlled by networkaddress.cache.ttl: 30 seconds by default, forever when a security manager is installed.
KSK / ZSK (key-signing key / zone-signing key)
The two DNSSEC keys of a zone: the KSK, vouched for by the parent's DS record, signs the ZSK, which signs the zone's records.
MX record
Names the mail servers for a domain, with priorities.
ndots
A resolver setting: names with fewer dots than this are first tried with each search domain appended. Kubernetes pods use 5.
Negative caching
Caching the fact that a name or record does not exist, for a time set by the zone's SOA.
NOERROR / NODATA
NOERROR is the success response code; an answer that is NOERROR but empty (informally NODATA) means the name exists but has no record of the requested type.
NS record
Lists the authoritative name servers for a zone.
NSEC / NSEC3
DNSSEC records that prove a name or record type does not exist, so negative answers can be validated too.
NXDOMAIN
The response code meaning 'this name does not exist'.
PTR record
Maps an IP address back to a name (reverse DNS), stored under in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa.
Recursive resolver
The server that answers clients by walking the hierarchy and caching results, e.g. your ISP's resolver, 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8.
Registrar
The company through which you register a domain and set its NS records in the parent TLD zone.
Root zone
The top of the DNS tree, served by 13 named root server identities (a to m) replicated worldwide by anycast.
Search domain
A suffix the stub resolver appends to short names, e.g. turning 'db' into 'db.corp.example.com'.
SERVFAIL
The response code meaning the resolver could not get a valid answer, e.g. because authoritative servers failed or DNSSEC validation failed.
SOA record
Start of Authority: zone metadata including the serial number and the negative-caching TTL.
SPF, DKIM, DMARC
Email authentication published in TXT records: SPF lists servers allowed to send for a domain, DKIM publishes keys to verify message signatures, DMARC says what receivers should do when checks fail.
Split-horizon DNS
Serving different answers for the same name to internal and external clients.
SRV record
Gives the host and port for a named service, e.g. _sip._tcp.example.com.
Stub resolver
The minimal DNS client in the operating system or C library that forwards queries to a recursive resolver.
Subdomain takeover
An attacker claiming a deleted cloud resource that a leftover CNAME still points to, and so serving content on your subdomain.
SVCB / HTTPS record
Service binding records that advertise protocol support (such as HTTP/3), ports and addresses for a service.
TC (truncated) flag
A flag in a DNS response saying the answer did not fit in the UDP message; the client should retry over TCP.
TLD (top-level domain)
The last label of a name, such as com, org or in, each with its own registry and name servers.
Transaction ID
A 16-bit number the client puts in each query and the server copies into the reply, used to match replies to questions.
TTL (time to live)
In DNS, how many seconds a record may be cached; unrelated to the IP header's hop counter.
TXT record
Free-form text, used for domain verification and email policies such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)
A private cloud network (net3); cloud providers run a DNS resolver inside each VPC.
Zone
A part of the DNS tree managed as one unit and served by one set of authoritative servers.
Zone apex
The name at the top of a zone, e.g. example.com itself, which must carry SOA and NS records.
drill:
Plan a migration

You are moving api.example.com from an old load balancer (A record 203.0.113.10, TTL 86400) to a new one in another region, with no downtime. Internal Java services and external customers both call it. Write the plan.

Answer
  1. Two days ahead: lower the TTL on api.example.com from 86400 to 60. Wait at least 24 hours (the old TTL) so every cache has picked up the short TTL.
  2. Prepare: bring the new load balancer up and verify it end to end by testing with a hosts-file override or curl --resolve api.example.com:443:<new IP>, including TLS certificates for the name.
  3. Shift gradually if the provider supports it: weighted records sending 10%, then 50%, then 100% to the new endpoint, watching error rates and latency at each step. Otherwise switch the record in one change.
  4. Keep the old endpoint serving and watch its traffic. It will not drop to zero at 60 seconds: long-lived connection pools, JVM or library DNS caches and customers with odd resolvers keep using it. For internal Java services, check the DNS cache TTL setting and bound connection lifetimes, or restart them in a rolling fashion to pick up the change.
  5. Decommission only when old traffic has been near zero for a while (hours to days), then remove the old load balancer, and only then raise the TTL back to something like 300 to 3600.
  6. Rollback plan: during the window, switching the record back takes effect within about a minute, because the TTL is 60.
Diagnose: the five-second stalls

After a traffic increase, several services in a Kubernetes cluster show p99 latency spikes of almost exactly 5 seconds on calls to external APIs. Internal service-to-service calls are mostly fine. What is going on, and what do you check and change?

Answer

An exact 5 seconds is the fingerprint of the stub resolver's default timeout: some DNS queries get no answer and are retried after 5 s. External names are hit hardest because of ndots:5: each lookup of api.partner.com becomes up to eight queries through the search domains, multiplying the chance that one is dropped, and the load on CoreDNS grew with traffic.

Check CoreDNS pods' CPU, query rate and error metrics and whether they are being throttled; check the upstream resolver's limits (cloud resolvers rate-limit per interface); and check for dropped UDP packets (conntrack table and the known race when A and AAAA queries share a socket). Fix by: using fully qualified external names with a trailing dot or setting ndots:2 in the pod dnsConfig; deploying node-local DNS caching so most lookups never cross the network; scaling CoreDNS; adding single-request-reopen or reducing the timeout in the pod DNS options; and making HTTP clients reuse connections so they resolve far less often.
qa: E
Walk me through what happens when a laptop resolves www.example.com with empty caches.

The stub resolver in the OS sends a query to the configured recursive resolver. The resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the .com servers; a .com server refers it to example.com's authoritative servers; one of those returns the A or AAAA record. The resolver caches the referrals and the answer for their TTLs and returns the result to the laptop, which also caches it.
Follow-up: How does the resolver know where the root servers are? — They are built in: every resolver ships with a 'root hints' file listing the 13 root server names and addresses.
E
Why can't you use a CNAME at the zone apex?

A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, because it says 'this name is really that other name' for all types, and the apex must have SOA and NS records. Providers work around it with ALIAS or ANAME records, which resolve the target themselves and serve its addresses as A and AAAA records.
Follow-up: Why do people want a CNAME at the apex at all? — To point example.com at a CDN or load balancer whose IP addresses change; the apex needs the same flexibility as www.
E
What is a TTL in DNS, and what are the trade-offs of short versus long?

The TTL is how many seconds resolvers may cache a record. Short TTLs (30 to 60 s) let changes and failovers take effect quickly but mean more queries, more latency on cache misses and more dependence on your DNS provider being up. Long TTLs (hours) are cheap and keep working briefly through a DNS provider outage, but changes are slow to reach everyone.
Follow-up: What TTL would you choose for a record behind health-checked failover? — Around 30 to 60 seconds, since failover can only be as fast as caches expire.
M
How do DNS TTLs affect failover and migrations?

Resolvers and clients cache records for their TTL, so a change takes up to the old TTL to reach everyone. Lower TTLs at least one old-TTL in advance of planned changes, and remember that some clients ignore TTLs or cache addresses for their process lifetime, so keep old endpoints serving during the transition and watch their traffic drain.
Follow-up: How do you know when the old endpoint can be turned off? — When its traffic has dropped to near zero well after the TTL, not simply when the TTL has passed.
M
What does DNSSEC provide, and what does it not?

It adds signatures to records and a chain of trust from the root's key through DS records in each parent zone, so validating resolvers can verify that answers are authentic and unmodified, defending against cache poisoning and spoofing. It does not encrypt queries or responses; privacy comes from DNS over HTTPS, TLS or QUIC. And it adds operational risk: a mistake in keys or DS records makes the domain fail to resolve for validating users.

Follow-up: What happened to Slack in 2021? — During a DNSSEC rollout, a DS record cached for 24 hours by the .com zone and a Route 53 bug with wildcard records caused validating resolvers to return SERVFAIL for some users for about a day.
M
How does a CDN use DNS to send users to a nearby server?

The site's name is a CNAME to a name on the CDN's DNS. When the CDN's authoritative servers receive the query, they look at where it came from, the resolver's IP address or the client subnet passed via EDNS Client Subnet, and answer with the address of a nearby, healthy edge with a short TTL. Other CDNs return the same anycast address everywhere and let BGP routing find the nearest site.
Follow-up: What goes wrong when a user uses a distant public resolver? — Without Client Subnet, the CDN sees the resolver's location, not the user's, and may pick a far-away edge.
M
What is negative caching and how can it bite you?

When a name does not exist, the resolver caches the NXDOMAIN answer for a period taken from the zone's SOA record, so repeated lookups do not hammer authoritative servers. If a deploy script or a user queried a name before you created it, resolvers may keep answering 'does not exist' for that period after creation.
Follow-up: How do you avoid it? — Create records before anything queries them, and keep the SOA negative TTL modest, such as a few minutes.
M
Why do DNS lookups in Kubernetes often multiply, and how do you fix it?

Pods get resolv.conf with several search domains and ndots:5, so any name with fewer than five dots, like api.example.com, is first tried with each search domain appended, api.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local and so on, each for both A and AAAA, before the real name. That can mean eight or more queries per lookup, adding latency and load on CoreDNS. Fixes are fully qualified names with a trailing dot, a lower ndots in the pod's dnsConfig, and node-local DNS caches.
Follow-up: Why is ndots set so high in the first place? — So that short in-cluster names like my-svc.my-namespace resolve through the search list without callers writing the full cluster suffix.
M
Compare DNS-based load balancing with a load balancer.

DNS steering hands clients different addresses, by weight, location or health, before they connect. It works globally and costs nothing per request, but it is coarse: caching delays changes by a TTL, clients pick addresses unpredictably, and it cannot react to a server failing mid-TTL. A load balancer decides per connection or request, with live health checks, but it is a component in the path. Real systems use DNS to pick a region or edge and load balancers inside it.
Follow-up: When is plain round-robin DNS acceptable? — For internal services with retrying clients and many healthy replicas, or as a first layer in front of redundant load balancers.
M
What is a subdomain takeover?

A team deletes a cloud resource, such as a storage bucket, an app service or a CDN distribution, but forgets the CNAME that points at its provider hostname. An attacker then creates a resource with the same provider name, and your subdomain now serves their content, useful for phishing or stealing cookies scoped to your domain. Prevent it by removing DNS records as part of decommissioning and scanning for dangling CNAMEs.
Follow-up: Why are cookies part of the risk? — Cookies set for .example.com are sent to every subdomain, so a hijacked subdomain can read or set them.
H
Design the DNS setup for a critical, multi-region customer-facing service.

Use at least two independent authoritative DNS providers, or one with a strong anycast network and a tested secondary, because a DNS provider outage takes down everything behind it, as the 2016 Dyn attack showed. Put the apex and www on health-checked, latency-based records pointing at regional load balancers, with TTLs around 60 seconds. Keep NS and other stable records on long TTLs. Manage zones as code with review, monitor resolution from many locations, alert on domain and certificate expiry, and publish CAA records.

Follow-up: What is the catch with two DNS providers? — Keeping them in sync, and advanced features like health checks and geo-routing often differ between providers, so you may be limited to the common subset.
H
How does a cache poisoning attack work, and what defends against it?

An attacker makes a resolver look up a name and races the real answer with forged responses that match the query's transaction ID and port. If one is accepted, the resolver caches the attacker's address for everyone. The 2008 Kaminsky attack made this practical by querying random nonexistent subdomains to get unlimited attempts and injecting forged referrals. Defences are randomising the source port as well as the 16-bit ID, which multiplies the guessing space, DNSSEC validation, which rejects unsigned forgeries, and encrypted DNS on the client-to-resolver hop.
Follow-up: Why is a 16-bit transaction ID alone not enough? — Only 65,536 possibilities; an attacker who can send many forged replies per query attempt will eventually guess right.
H
Latency-sensitive services see occasional 5-second delays that line up with DNS lookups. What could cause it?

The glibc resolver waits 5 seconds by default before retrying a query that got no answer. So anything that drops a single DNS packet produces exactly a 5-second stall: an overloaded resolver or CoreDNS pod, rate limiting at a cloud resolver, UDP packets lost on the path, or a known Linux connection-tracking race where parallel A and AAAA queries from the same socket collide and one is dropped. Fix the loss source, run node-local caching resolvers, reduce query volume (ndots), and use resolver options like single-request-reopen or a lower timeout.
Follow-up: Why exactly 5 seconds? — It is glibc's default RES_TIMEOUT, and a lost UDP query is only retried after that timeout.
H
Your service's DNS provider is under a massive DDoS and resolvers cannot reach it. What happens to your users, and what could you have done beforehand?

Users whose resolvers still have your records cached keep working until the TTL expires; everyone else gets SERVFAIL and cannot reach you at all, even though your servers are healthy. Beforehand you could use a second authoritative provider listed in your NS records, keep longer TTLs on stable records to ride out short outages, and use a provider with large anycast capacity. During the incident, adding a secondary provider is slow because the parent zone's NS records themselves have long TTLs.
Follow-up: Why does TTL choice matter here? — A 5-minute TTL means users drop off within minutes; a multi-hour TTL keeps most users working through a short provider outage.
