t: HTTP semantics: methods, status codes, headers, caching, cookies and CORS
sum: What an HTTP message means independent of version: methods and idempotency, status codes, headers, caching and revalidation, cookies and sessions, CORS, and the production mistakes each one invites.
prereq: net2
A page load is DNS, TCP, TLS, then HTTP requests and responses; the browser checks its cache first, and proxies and CDNs sit between browser and origin.
net4
HTTP/1.1 runs over a TCP byte stream, so messages need framing such as Content-Length.
why:
By the time a request reaches your service, DNS, TCP and TLS have done their jobs, and what arrives is an HTTP message. Almost every API you build or call, every web page, every webhook and every call to an LLM provider is HTTP. The protocol looks simple, a verb, a path, some headers, a body, and that simplicity hides a lot of precise meaning that systems all along the path depend on.

Consider what goes wrong when that meaning is misunderstood. A mobile app retries a timed-out "place order" request and the customer is charged twice, because the request was a POST with no idempotency key. A CDN serves one user's account page to thousands of strangers, because the page was marked as cacheable. A deploy goes out and half the users see a broken page for a day, because the HTML was cached with a long max-age and pointed at old JavaScript. A front-end team spends a week fighting "CORS errors" that curl never shows. A load balancer returns 502s and nobody knows whether to blame the balancer or the service. Each of these is a misunderstanding of HTTP semantics, not of networking.

"Semantics" means the meaning of messages, independent of how they are carried. HTTP/1.1 sends text over TCP, HTTP/2 sends binary frames over TCP, HTTP/3 sends frames over QUIC (net8 compares them), but a GET, a 304 or a Cache-Control header means exactly the same in all three. Learn the meaning once and it applies everywhere.

This lesson covers the parts that matter in interviews and in production: the anatomy of a message, methods and the crucial ideas of safety and idempotency, status codes and what each tells a client to do, the headers you will meet most, caching and revalidation, conditional requests for safe concurrent updates, cookies and sessions, and the browser's same-origin policy and CORS. Along the way it points out the security and caching mistakes each feature invites.
primer:
A request and a response

HTTP is a request-response protocol. A client sends a request naming a resource (the thing a URL identifies, like an order or an image) and a method (what to do with it); the server sends back a response with a status code (how it went). Both can carry headers, lines of metadata, and a body. In HTTP/1.1 they are literally lines of text:

Four ideas that carry most of the meaning

Methods have promises. GET promises not to change anything (it is safe). PUT and DELETE promise that doing them twice is the same as doing them once (they are idempotent). POST promises neither. Those promises decide what browsers, proxies and client libraries may retry or cache automatically.

Status codes tell the client what to do next. 2xx: done. 3xx: look elsewhere or use your copy. 4xx: you made a mistake, do not just repeat it. 5xx: we failed, maybe try later.

Responses can be reused. A response can say "you may keep and reuse me for 60 seconds" (Cache-Control: max-age=60). Browsers and CDNs then answer from their copy without asking the server, which is the biggest performance lever on the web.

The browser keeps sites apart. A page from one site cannot read responses from another site unless that site explicitly allows it (CORS), and browsers carry small pieces of state per site (cookies), with rules about when to send them.

A worked example: one image, three visits

A browser requests /logo.png. The first time, it has nothing stored, so it sends a GET and receives 200 OK with the image, Cache-Control: max-age=3600 and ETag: "v7". It stores the image. Ten minutes later the page needs the logo again: the stored copy is only 600 seconds old, still fresh, so the browser uses it without sending anything. Two hours later the copy is stale, so the browser sends GET /logo.png with If-None-Match: "v7". The logo has not changed, so the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, and the browser reuses its copy for another hour. Three visits, one download. Section 5 of the body draws this as a flow.

The analogy, and where it breaks

HTTP is like ordering at a counter by writing slips. The slip says what you want (method and resource) and carries notes (headers: "I prefer JSON", "here is my membership card"). The clerk hands back a result with a stamp (status code) and notes of their own ("this answer is good for an hour"). Where it breaks: there are many clerks in a chain between you and the kitchen (proxies, CDNs, load balancers), and each of them reads the notes and may answer on the kitchen's behalf. HTTP's precise rules exist largely so that those intermediaries do the right thing.
body:
1. Methods, safety and idempotency

MethodMeaningSafeIdempotent
GETfetch a representation of the resourceyesyes
HEADlike GET but headers onlyyesyes
OPTIONSask what is allowed (used by CORS preflight)yesyes
PUTstore this representation at this URL (create or replace)noyes
DELETEremove the resourcenoyes
POSTprocess this body (create a child resource, run an action)nono
PATCHapply these partial changesnonot by default

A safe method is one the client does not intend to change anything. That is why browsers prefetch links with GET, crawlers follow them, and caches store their responses; it is also why an endpoint like GET /delete?id=5 is a disaster waiting for a crawler.

An idempotent method is one where sending the request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. PUT /users/7 with a full profile: repeat it and the profile is the same. DELETE /orders/9: repeat it and the order is equally gone (the second response may be 404, but the state is the same). POST /orders: repeat it and you have two orders.

Why this matters so much: networks fail in the middle. A client sends a request, the connection drops, and the client cannot know whether the server processed it. For idempotent methods the answer is easy, just retry, and HTTP clients, proxies and load balancers do so automatically. For POST, a blind retry might duplicate the action, so they do not. The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique ID for each logical operation and sends it in a header (Stripe popularised Idempotency-Key, and the IETF is standardising it). The server stores the key with the result of the first successful attempt and, if the same key arrives again, returns the stored result instead of acting again.

PATCH is not idempotent by default because a patch can be relative ("add 1 to the quantity"); a patch that sets absolute values happens to be idempotent, but clients cannot assume it.

2. Status codes and what the client should do

CodeMeaningClient should
200 OKsuccess with a bodyuse it
201 Createda new resource exists, at Locationfollow Location if needed
202 Acceptedqueued for asynchronous processingpoll or wait for a callback
204 No Contentsuccess, nothing to returndone
301 / 308moved permanently (308 keeps the method)update bookmarks; caches may store
302 / 307temporary redirect (307 keeps the method)follow this time only
304 Not Modifiedyour cached copy is still validreuse the stored body
400 Bad Requestmalformed requestfix it; do not retry as is
401 Unauthorizednot authenticatedlog in or refresh the token, then retry
403 Forbiddenauthenticated but not alloweddo not retry
404 Not Foundno such resourcedo not retry
409 Conflictclashes with current statere-read and resolve
412 Precondition Failedan If-Match condition failedre-read, merge, retry
422 Unprocessable Contentwell-formed but invalid (e.g. validation)fix the data
429 Too Many Requestsrate limitedwait (see Retry-After), back off
500 Internal Server Errorunexpected server failureretry only if idempotent
502 Bad Gatewayproxy got a bad response or connection error from upstreamretry idempotent requests
503 Service Unavailableoverloaded, no healthy backend, or maintenanceback off, honour Retry-After
504 Gateway Timeoutupstream too slow for the proxy's timeoutretry carefully; the work may have happened

Three distinctions come up in interviews. 401 versus 403: "who are you?" versus "you may not". 301/302 versus 308/307: the older pair historically allowed clients to change a POST into a GET when following the redirect; 307 and 308 guarantee the method and body are kept. 502 versus 503 versus 504: all typically generated by a proxy or load balancer rather than your code; 502 says the upstream misbehaved or the connection broke (for example the idle-timeout race in net4), 503 says there was nobody healthy to send to or the server is shedding load, and 504 says the upstream took too long. Knowing which component emitted the error is the first step in debugging it.

3. Headers you will meet constantly

Header names are case-insensitive (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them in lowercase). Grouped by job:

  • Describing the body: Content-Type (application/json; charset=utf-8), Content-Length (bytes), Content-Encoding (gzip, br).
  • Content negotiation: the client says what it can accept (Accept, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language) and the server picks a representation.
  • Identity and credentials: Authorization: Bearer <token>, Cookie, and in responses WWW-Authenticate (with 401) and Set-Cookie.
  • Routing and proxies: Host (which site, since many share an IP), X-Forwarded-For or the standard Forwarded (original client IP; trust it only when set by your own proxies, net3), X-Request-ID or traceparent for tracing.
  • Caching and conditions: Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, If-None-Match, If-Match, Vary, Age.
  • Flow control for clients: Retry-After, Location.
  • Security: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS, net2), Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and the CORS headers in section 7.

4. Caching: freshness

A cache stores responses and reuses them for later requests. There are two kinds: the browser's private cache, used by one user, and shared caches, such as CDNs and reverse proxies, used by many users. The response's Cache-Control header governs both:

  • max-age=N: the response is fresh for N seconds and may be reused without asking the server. s-maxage=N overrides it for shared caches only.
  • no-cache: may be stored, but must be revalidated with the server before every reuse. (Despite its name, it does not mean "do not cache".)
  • no-store: must not be stored anywhere. For sensitive responses.
  • private: only the browser may store it, never a shared cache. public: shared caches may store it even if it would otherwise not be cacheable (for example, a response to an authenticated request).
  • immutable: the content will never change at this URL, so do not even revalidate when the user reloads.
  • stale-while-revalidate=N: after expiry, a cache may serve the stale copy for up to N more seconds while fetching a fresh one in the background, hiding revalidation latency.

If a response has no explicit freshness information, caches may guess a heuristic lifetime, commonly 10% of the time since its Last-Modified date, which is a frequent source of "why is this cached?" surprises. Be explicit.

A cache must also know when two requests can share a response. The cache key is normally the method and the URL. If the response depends on a request header, say the server returns Brotli to clients that accept it and plain text to others, the server must list that header in Vary (Vary: Accept-Encoding) so caches keep one copy per value. Forget Vary and a CDN serves the Brotli copy to a client that cannot decode it, or the French page to everyone. Over-use Vary (for example Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent) and the cache holds thousands of near-duplicate copies with almost no hits.

5. Caching: revalidation and the 304

When a stored response becomes stale, the cache does not have to download it again. It asks the server whether its copy is still good, using a validator the server sent with the original response:

There are two validators. An ETag is an opaque version string, such as a hash of the content (ETag: "v7"); the client revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7". Last-Modified is a timestamp; the client revalidates with If-Modified-Since. If nothing changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the cache refreshes its copy's freshness. The saving is bandwidth and server work, but not the round trip.

The standard pattern for web assets combines both ideas. Build tools give static files content-hashed names (app.3f9a1.js); since a change produces a new URL, the file can be cached "forever": Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The HTML page that references them is served with no-cache and an ETag, so every visit revalidates it cheaply and picks up new asset names immediately after a deploy.

6. Conditional requests for safe updates

The same validators solve a completely different problem: two people editing the same thing. Alice and Bob both GET document 12 (ETag "v7"). Alice saves first with PUT /docs/12 and If-Match: "v7"; the version matches, so the server applies it and the ETag becomes "v8". Bob then saves with If-Match: "v7"; the current version is "v8", so the server refuses with 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting Alice's work. Bob's client re-reads, merges or asks him, and retries. This is optimistic concurrency control built into HTTP: no locks, just a check at write time. A server can insist that clients use it by answering unconditional writes with 428 Precondition Required.

7. Cookies and sessions

HTTP itself is stateless: each request stands alone. Cookies add state. A server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc123; ...attributes, the browser stores it, and on later requests to that site it sends Cookie: session=abc123. A login session is usually just a random session ID in a cookie, mapped to the user on the server, or a signed token.

The attributes are where the security lives:

  • Secure: only send over HTTPS, so it cannot be sniffed on the network.
  • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it, so a script injected by XSS (cross-site scripting) cannot steal the session.
  • SameSite=Strict | Lax | None: whether the browser attaches the cookie to requests that another site triggers. This is the main defence against CSRF (cross-site request forgery), where evil.example contains a hidden form that posts to your bank, and the browser would otherwise helpfully attach your bank cookie. Strict sends it only for requests initiated from the same site; Lax also allows top-level navigations such as following a link, but not cross-site POSTs, images or scripts; None always sends it and requires Secure. Chromium-based browsers treat cookies with no SameSite attribute as Lax.
  • Domain and Path: which hosts and paths receive it. Setting Domain=example.com sends it to every subdomain, which widens exposure; the __Host- name prefix forces a cookie to be host-only, Secure and Path=/.
  • Max-Age or Expires: lifetime; without them it is a session cookie deleted when the browser closes.

Keep cookies small: browsers limit each to about 4 KB, and every cookie for a domain is sent on every request to it, including image requests, adding bytes to every round trip.

8. The same-origin policy and CORS

An origin is the triple of scheme, host and port: https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com are different origins, as are http:// and https:// versions of the same host. The browser's same-origin policy says a script loaded by one origin may send requests to another origin but may not read the responses. Without it, any web page you visit could use your logged-in cookies to read your email from your webmail's API.

Legitimate sites often need cross-origin reads, for example a front end on app.example.com calling an API on api.example.com. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) lets the API opt in with response headers. For a simple request (GET, HEAD or POST with only basic headers and a form or plain-text content type), the browser just sends it with an Origin header, and lets the script read the response only if it carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin matching that origin. For anything else, including JSON bodies and Authorization headers, which covers most API calls, the browser first sends a preflight:

For requests with credentials (cookies or HTTP authentication), the rules tighten: the server must name the exact origin (the wildcard * is refused) and add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Servers typically check the request's Origin against an allow-list, echo it back when it matches, and add Vary: Origin so a cache does not serve one origin's CORS headers to another.

Keep in mind what CORS is and is not. It is a browser feature that relaxes the same-origin policy. It does not stop curl, a server, or an attacker's script from calling your API; it only controls whether a web page running in a user's browser may read the answer. Your API still needs authentication and authorisation.
deep:
Idempotency keys done properly

An idempotency key only works if storing the key and performing the side effect are atomic, or at least ordered carefully. The robust design: on receipt, insert the key into a table with a unique constraint and status "in progress"; if the insert fails because the key exists, return the stored response if complete, or 409 if still in progress; perform the operation in the same database transaction that records the result against the key, or, when the side effect is external (charging a card through a payment provider), pass the same key downstream so the provider deduplicates too. Keys should expire after a retention window (Stripe keeps them for at least 24 hours), and a request that reuses a key with a different body should be rejected rather than silently answered with the old result. This is the HTTP face of the distributed-systems problem that sc11 covers in depth.

Cache keys, deception and poisoning

Shared caches are a common source of serious incidents because they multiply one mistake across all users. Web cache deception exploits a mismatch between how the cache and the origin interpret a URL: a CDN rule says "cache anything ending in .css", the application routes /account/settings.css to the account page (ignoring the suffix), and the CDN stores a logged-in user's page for anyone to fetch. Cache poisoning is the reverse: an attacker finds a request header that changes the response but is not part of the cache key (an unkeyed header, such as X-Forwarded-Host used to build absolute URLs), sends a request with a malicious value, and the poisoned response is cached and served to everyone. Defences are to make the origin the single source of truth for cacheability (personalised responses marked private or no-store, and CDNs configured to respect it), never cache responses that set cookies, make routing strict about paths, and avoid using unkeyed headers to generate content.

Content negotiation versus separate URLs

HTTP lets one URL return different representations depending on Accept, Accept-Language and Accept-Encoding. Compression negotiation works well because it is universal and caches handle Vary: Accept-Encoding specially. Language and format negotiation work less well in practice: they fragment caches, make links ambiguous (which language does a shared link show?), and are invisible to users. Many APIs therefore put the version and format in the URL or a dedicated header, and sites put the language in the path, reserving negotiation for compression and image formats.

Retries across layers

A single user click may pass through a browser, a CDN, a load balancer, a service mesh sidecar and an HTTP client library, and each may retry on failure. If each retries three times, one failing request can become 35 = 243 attempts at the bottom layer, turning a small outage into a self-inflicted overload (a retry storm). The HTTP semantics give the tools to control it: only idempotent requests are retried by intermediaries, 429 and 503 carry Retry-After, and well-designed systems retry at one layer with exponential backoff and jitter, with budgets that cap retries as a fraction of traffic (sc12 covers resilience patterns).

Partial responses and HEAD

Two less glamorous features matter for large objects such as model weights, datasets and video. A Range: bytes=1000000-1999999 request asks for part of a resource, and a server that supports it answers 206 Partial Content with just those bytes. Download tools use ranges to resume interrupted transfers and to fetch one file in parallel pieces over several connections (the fix for a single connection's window limit from net4); video players use them to seek. Combined with If-Range and an ETag, a client resumes only if the file has not changed in the meantime. HEAD returns the headers of a GET without the body, so a client can check size, type and ETag before committing to a download.

Security headers as a layered defence

Beyond cookies and CORS, a handful of response headers harden browsers' handling of your pages. Content-Security-Policy restricts where scripts, styles and frames may come from, and with nonces or hashes can block injected inline scripts, the most effective XSS mitigation after output encoding. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers guessing a response's type, closing attacks where an uploaded file is interpreted as a script. Referrer-Policy limits how much of the current URL leaks to other sites. Cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP) are needed to unlock powerful features such as shared memory, because they guarantee the page cannot be mixed with other origins' data. None of these replaces correct code, but each turns a class of bugs from exploitable into harmless.
prod:
Characteristic failures

  • Duplicate side effects from retries. Mobile clients on flaky networks, load balancers retrying on connection resets, and users double-clicking all produce repeated POSTs. Symptoms: duplicate orders, double charges, duplicate emails. Fix with idempotency keys end to end.
  • Private data in shared caches. On 25 December 2015, during a denial-of-service attack, Valve changed the caching configuration of its Steam store's CDN to cope with the load; personalised store pages were cached and served to other users. Between 11:50 and 13:20 Pacific time, pages for about 34,000 users, some showing billing addresses, partial card digits, email addresses and purchase history, may have been seen by others. The lesson: cacheability must be decided by the origin per response, and emergency cache rules are exactly where these mistakes happen.
  • Stale front ends after deploys. HTML cached with a long max-age keeps referencing old bundles, or new HTML references bundles not yet uploaded to the CDN. Fix with hashed asset names, short-lived HTML and deploying assets before HTML.
  • CORS breakage. After moving an API to a new subdomain, the front end fails with CORS errors while curl works. Usually the allow-list lacks the new origin, the preflight is blocked by authentication middleware, or a credentialed request receives *. Browser DevTools' console and network tab show the preflight and the missing header.
  • Misattributed 5xx. 502 and 504 come from proxies; teams look in application logs and find nothing. Check which component generated the response (load balancer logs usually record whether the target responded) before debugging the application.
  • Cache fragmentation. A CDN hit ratio collapses after someone adds Vary: User-Agent or a per-user query parameter; origin load jumps. Watch hit ratio as a key metric.

Observability

Log method, path template (not raw path, to keep cardinality low), status code, latency, response size, cache status and request ID for every request at the edge and in services. Track rates of 4xx and 5xx separately, and break 5xx down by code and by emitting component. At the CDN, track hit ratio, origin request rate and bytes served from cache. In browsers, the Network panel shows each response's headers, whether it came from memory or disk cache, and CORS preflights. The Age response header shows how long a shared cache has held a response, and many CDNs add a cache-status header (for example cf-cache-status or x-cache) saying HIT or MISS.

A debugging order for 'the API returns the wrong thing'

First establish which component produced the response: look at server, via, age and cache-status headers, and compare with the origin's own logs. If the response came from a cache, ask why it was cacheable and what the cache key was. If it came from a proxy (a 502 or 504 with a proxy's error page), look at that proxy's logs and upstream health. Only if it came from your application does the application's code become the suspect. Reproducing with curl -v and the exact headers the client sent (cookies, Accept-Encoding, Origin) usually settles it in minutes.

Knobs

Cache-Control per response type; CDN rules for what to cache and which headers and cookies form the cache key; CORS allow-lists and preflight max-age; cookie attributes on every Set-Cookie; retry policies in clients and proxies (which methods, how many times, with what backoff); idempotency key retention; and default security headers set centrally at the edge.
myths: Cache-Control: no-cache means 'do not cache'.

no-cache means 'you may store it, but must check with the server before each reuse', usually with a cheap conditional request. The directive that forbids storing is no-store. Mixing them up either leaks sensitive pages into caches or throws away cheap revalidation.
CORS protects my API from other websites and scripts.

CORS is enforced only by browsers, and only on reading responses: it stops a malicious page from reading your API's responses in a victim's browser. curl, servers, scripts and attackers' own tools ignore it entirely. APIs still need real authentication and authorisation; CORS is a relaxation of the browser's same-origin policy, not a firewall.
401 means 'you are not allowed'.

401 Unauthorized really means unauthenticated: 'I do not know who you are; send credentials'. 403 Forbidden means 'I know who you are and you may not do this'. Returning 404 instead of 403 is sometimes done deliberately to avoid revealing that a resource exists.
POST is for creating and PUT is for updating.

The real distinction is idempotency and who picks the URL. PUT stores a representation at a URL the client names, and repeating it has the same effect, so it can create or replace. POST asks the server to process the body, often creating something at a URL the server chooses, and repeating it may do it twice.
A 5xx error should always be retried and a 4xx never.

Retry depends on idempotency and on the specific code. A 503 or 429 with Retry-After invites a retry later; a 500 from a POST that may have partly succeeded is dangerous to retry without an idempotency key. Some 4xx codes are retryable after a change (401 after refreshing a token, 409 after re-reading, 412 after fetching the new version).
Cookies marked Secure and HttpOnly are safe from cross-site attacks.

Secure keeps the cookie off plain HTTP and HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript, which limits theft by XSS. Neither stops the browser from attaching the cookie to a request that another site triggers, which is CSRF. That is the job of SameSite and of anti-CSRF tokens.
lab:
Fifteen minutes with curl and a browser. You will read raw messages, trigger status codes, watch a 304, set cookies and see CORS enforced by a browser but not by curl. On Windows PowerShell use curl.exe.

  1. Read a raw exchange. curl -v https://httpbin.org/get -o /dev/null. Look for: lines starting with > (your request line and headers) and < (the status line and response headers). Note Host, User-Agent, Accept, content-type and access-control-allow-origin.
  2. Status codes on demand. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://httpbin.org/status/503, then /status/429 and /status/404. Then curl -si 'https://httpbin.org/redirect-to?url=/get&status_code=308' | head -5. Look for: the codes and, for the redirect, a location header. Add -L to follow it.
  3. Revalidation with an ETag. curl -si https://httpbin.org/etag/v7 | head -8 shows etag: v7. Now send it back: curl -si -H 'If-None-Match: "v7"' https://httpbin.org/etag/v7 | head -3. Look for: 304 and no body: "your copy is still good". Try a different tag and you get 200 with a body.
  4. Caching headers of a real site. curl -sI https://www.wikipedia.org | grep -Ei 'cache-control|age|etag|vary|x-cache'. Then pick a static asset from any site's page source (a .js or .css file) and do the same. Look for: short or no-cache policies on HTML, long max-age or immutable on hashed assets, an age header and HIT or MISS from the CDN.
  5. Cookies. curl -si 'https://httpbin.org/cookies/set?session=abc123' | grep -i set-cookie. Then use a cookie jar: curl -s -c jar.txt -b jar.txt -L 'https://httpbin.org/cookies/set?session=abc123' followed by curl -s -b jar.txt https://httpbin.org/cookies. Look for: the server setting a cookie and curl sending it back on the next request, which is all a browser session is.
  6. CORS is a browser rule. Open https://example.com in a browser, open the DevTools console and run fetch('https://httpbin.org/get').then(r => r.json()).then(console.log): it works, because httpbin sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Now run fetch('https://www.wikipedia.org/').then(r => r.text()).then(console.log). Look for: a CORS error in the console, and in the Network tab, the request itself was sent and got a response; the browser just refused to let the page read it. Now run curl -s https://www.wikipedia.org/ | head -3: curl reads it fine. That difference is the whole point of CORS.
  7. Trigger a preflight. In the same console: fetch('https://httpbin.org/anything', {method: 'PUT', headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, body: '{}'}). Look for: in the Network tab, an OPTIONS request before the PUT, with Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers.
recap: An HTTP message is a start line, headers, a blank line and an optional body; the meaning of methods, status codes and headers is the same in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe; those plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so clients and proxies may retry them; POST and PATCH need idempotency keys to be retried safely.

Status codes form five families; the ones that matter in production are 200, 201, 204, 301/308, 302/307, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 412, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504, each implying a different response from the client.
Caching is controlled by Cache-Control (max-age, s-maxage, no-cache, no-store, private, immutable), and stale responses are revalidated with ETag or Last-Modified to get a cheap 304.
Vary tells caches which request headers change a response; getting cache keys wrong can serve one user's private page to another.
Cookies carry state such as sessions; HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes defend against script theft, network sniffing and cross-site request forgery.
The same-origin policy stops scripts reading responses from other origins; CORS headers let a server allow specific origins, with a preflight OPTIONS request for non-simple requests.
Conditional requests with If-Match give HTTP built-in optimistic concurrency control, answering 412 when someone else changed the resource first.
glossary: Cache key
What a cache uses to decide whether two requests can share a stored response: normally the method and URL, plus any headers named in Vary.
Cache-Control
The header that sets caching rules: whether a response may be stored, by whom, and for how long.
CDN (content delivery network)
A network of edge servers that cache and serve responses near users; the most important shared cache. Covered in net12.
Conditional request
A request with If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since or If-Match that the server answers differently depending on the resource's current version.
Content negotiation
The server choosing a representation (format, language, compression) based on Accept headers from the client.
Cookie
A small named value a server asks the browser to store (Set-Cookie) and send back on later requests (Cookie).
COOP / COEP
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: headers that isolate a page from other origins so it may use powerful features like shared memory.
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
A set of response headers with which a server tells browsers which other origins may read its responses.
CSP (Content-Security-Policy)
A response header telling the browser which sources of scripts, styles and other content a page may load, limiting XSS.
CSRF (cross-site request forgery)
An attack where another site makes the victim's browser send a request, with the victim's cookies, to a site where they are logged in.
ETag
An opaque version identifier for a response, used for revalidation and optimistic concurrency.
Freshness
How long a stored response may be reused without asking the server, set by max-age, s-maxage or Expires.
Header
A name-value line of metadata in a request or response, such as Content-Type: application/json.
HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)
A header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for a site (net2).
HttpOnly
A cookie attribute that hides the cookie from JavaScript.
Idempotency key
A unique client-generated value sent with a non-idempotent request so the server can recognise and ignore duplicates.
Idempotent
A method whose repeated application has the same effect on the server as applying it once.
Method
The request's verb, such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, saying what the client wants done.
Optimistic concurrency
Letting clients update without locks, but rejecting an update if the resource changed since the client read it (If-Match and 412).
Origin
The combination of scheme, host and port, e.g. https://app.example.com:443; the unit of browser isolation.
Preflight
An automatic OPTIONS request a browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request, asking the server's permission.
Range request
A request with a Range header asking for part of a resource, answered with 206 Partial Content; used for resumable downloads and video seeking.
Representation
The actual bytes returned for a resource in a given format, language and encoding.
Resource
The thing a URL identifies, such as an order or a user profile.
Retry-After
A response header telling the client how long to wait before retrying, used with 429 and 503.
Revalidation
Checking with the server whether a stale stored response is still valid, usually getting a 304 if it is.
Safe method
A method that is not meant to change server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.
Same-origin policy
The browser rule that a script from one origin may not read responses from another origin unless allowed.
SameSite
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax or None) controlling whether the cookie is sent on requests triggered by other sites.
Secure (cookie attribute)
A cookie attribute that restricts the cookie to HTTPS requests.
Shared cache
A cache used by many users, such as a CDN or reverse proxy, as opposed to the browser's private cache.
Status code
The three-digit number in a response saying how the request went, grouped into 1xx to 5xx.
URL (Uniform Resource Locator)
The address of a resource: scheme, host, optional port, path and query (net2).
Vary
A response header listing request headers that affect the response, so caches keep separate copies per value.
XSS (cross-site scripting)
Injecting script into a page so it runs in other users' browsers with the site's privileges.
drill:
Design the headers

A product catalogue site has: (1) the HTML shell of a single-page app, (2) hashed JavaScript and CSS bundles, (3) GET /api/products/42, the same for everyone and updated a few times a day, (4) GET /api/me/cart, per user, (5) POST /api/orders. Everything goes through a CDN. Give the caching (and any other) headers for each, and explain.

Answer
  1. HTML shell: Cache-Control: no-cache with an ETag. Every load revalidates cheaply (304 when unchanged) and picks up new bundle names right after a deploy. A very short s-maxage (say 60) lets the CDN absorb load if needed.
  2. Hashed bundles: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The hash in the file name changes whenever the content does, so these can be cached for a year by browsers and the CDN. Deploy them before the HTML that references them.
  3. Product API: Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600 plus an ETag. Browsers reuse it for a minute, the CDN for five minutes, and after that can serve it while refreshing in the background. When prices change, purge the CDN URL or accept up to five minutes of staleness. If it varies by language, add Vary: Accept-Language or better, put the language in the URL.
  4. Cart: Cache-Control: private, no-store (or private, no-cache if you want browser revalidation). It must never be stored by the CDN; also make sure the CDN is configured not to cache responses to requests carrying the session cookie.
  5. Orders: POST responses are not cached by default; send Cache-Control: no-store anyway. Require an Idempotency-Key header so retries after timeouts do not create duplicate orders, and return 201 Created with a Location header.

Cookies for the session: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/, ideally with a __Host- prefix. If the API is on a different origin from the page, configure CORS with an explicit allow-list, credentials allowed, and Vary: Origin.

Diagnose: the double charge

Customers occasionally get charged twice. Logs show two POST /api/payments requests with identical bodies about 30 seconds apart, both returning 200. The app uses a mobile HTTP client with automatic retries, and there is a load balancer with a 30-second timeout in front of the payments service. Explain and fix.

Answer

The payment call sometimes takes longer than 30 seconds (a slow downstream card processor). The load balancer times out and returns 504 to the client while the service keeps processing and eventually succeeds. The client, seeing a 504, retries the POST, which is not idempotent, so the service charges again. Two successful charges, two 200s in the service's logs, and one confused customer.

Fix: the client generates an idempotency key per payment attempt and reuses it on every retry; the service records the key atomically with the charge and returns the stored result for duplicates, and passes the same key to the card processor. Also: make clients retry POSTs only when they carry an idempotency key; align timeouts so the load balancer's is longer than the service's own deadline for the downstream call; and consider making long payments asynchronous (return 202 Accepted and let the client poll), so no request sits open for 30 seconds.
qa: E
Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter?

GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them has the same effect on the server as doing them once. Clients, proxies and load balancers can therefore retry them after a timeout without risk, while POST and PATCH need idempotency keys or other protection, or a retry may create a duplicate order or double charge.

Follow-up: DELETE is idempotent, but the second call returns 404. Is that a contradiction? — No: idempotency is about the effect on server state, not the response; after one or two deletes the resource is equally gone.
E
Explain the status code families and give two examples of each.

1xx are informational (100 Continue, 103 Early Hints). 2xx mean success (200 OK, 201 Created). 3xx mean go elsewhere or use your copy (301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified). 4xx mean the client did something wrong (400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found). 5xx mean the server failed (500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable).

Follow-up: Why does the distinction between 4xx and 5xx matter to monitoring? — 5xx count against your service's availability, while 4xx usually reflect client behaviour; alerting on 4xx spikes separately catches broken clients or attacks.
E
What is the difference between 401 and 403?

401 means the server does not know who you are: authentication is missing or invalid, and it should include a WWW-Authenticate header saying how to authenticate. 403 means the server knows who you are and you are not allowed to do this. A client should respond to 401 by logging in or refreshing its token, and to 403 by not retrying.
Follow-up: When might you return 404 instead of 403? — When revealing that a resource exists is itself a leak, such as another user's private document.
M
What is the difference between 502, 503 and 504?

All three usually come from a proxy or load balancer. 502 Bad Gateway means it got an invalid response or a connection error, such as a reset, from the upstream. 503 Service Unavailable means the server or proxy is overloaded, has no healthy upstreams or is in maintenance, often with Retry-After. 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream accepted the request but did not respond within the proxy's timeout.
Follow-up: What would you check first for a burst of 504s? — Upstream latency and the proxy's timeout setting; slow dependencies or a saturated backend usually push responses past the timeout.
M
What is the difference between no-cache, no-store, private and max-age=0?

no-store forbids storing the response anywhere, for sensitive data. no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation with the server before every reuse. private allows only the browser's own cache, not shared caches like CDNs. max-age=0 marks the response immediately stale, which in practice also forces revalidation, though caches may serve it stale in some error cases unless must-revalidate is added.
Follow-up: What should a logged-in account page send? — Cache-Control: private, no-store if it contains personal data, or at least private, no-cache, and never public.
M
How does revalidation with ETags work?

The server sends an ETag, a version identifier, with the response. When the cached copy becomes stale, the client sends If-None-Match with that ETag. If the resource has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the client reuses and refreshes its stored copy; otherwise it sends 200 with the new body and a new ETag. It saves bandwidth and server work, though it still costs a round trip.

Follow-up: What is a weak ETag? — One prefixed with W/, meaning semantically equivalent but not byte-identical, for example the same content compressed differently; it is fine for caching but not for range requests.
M
Why does a CORS request with cookies fail when the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *?

Credentialed CORS requests, those that include cookies or HTTP authentication, require the server to name the specific allowed origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; browsers reject the wildcard for them, otherwise any website could read authenticated responses. The server should echo the request's Origin only if it is in an allow-list, and add Vary: Origin so caches do not serve one origin's headers to another.
Follow-up: Why is echoing back any Origin dangerous? — It effectively allows every site to read authenticated responses from your API in a logged-in user's browser.
M
What triggers a CORS preflight request, and how do you reduce its cost?

A cross-origin request that is not 'simple' triggers an OPTIONS preflight: methods other than GET, HEAD or POST, custom headers such as Authorization, or a Content-Type other than form or plain text, which includes application/json. The browser waits for the preflight's approval before sending the real request, costing an extra round trip. Reduce it with Access-Control-Max-Age so browsers cache the approval, or avoid cross-origin calls by serving the API on the same origin.
Follow-up: Do preflights reach your application? — They should be answered, often by the proxy or framework middleware, without authentication, since browsers do not send credentials on preflights.
M
How do SameSite cookies defend against CSRF?

With SameSite=Strict, the browser sends the cookie only on requests initiated by the same site. With Lax, it also sends it on top-level navigations such as clicking a link, but not on cross-site POSTs, images or scripts. A forged form post from evil.example to your bank therefore arrives without the session cookie. Chromium-based browsers treat cookies without a SameSite attribute as Lax; cookies that must work cross-site need SameSite=None; Secure.

Follow-up: Is SameSite enough on its own? — It is a strong default, but sensitive state-changing endpoints should still use anti-CSRF tokens or require non-simple requests, because browser support and same-site subdomains complicate it.
M
Design the caching headers for a single-page app's HTML, its JavaScript bundles and its API.

Name bundles with a content hash (app.3f9a1.js) and serve them with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, since a change produces a new URL. Serve the HTML with no-cache (or a very short max-age) plus an ETag, so users pick up new bundle names promptly. For the API, personalised responses get private, no-store or private, no-cache; shared, non-personal data can use s-maxage for the CDN with stale-while-revalidate.
Follow-up: Why not give the HTML a long max-age too? — Users would keep loading old HTML that points at old bundles for up to that long after a deploy.
H
How would you use HTTP to prevent lost updates when two users edit the same document?

Use optimistic concurrency with conditional requests. The GET returns an ETag representing the version. The client's PUT or PATCH includes If-Match with that ETag; the server applies the change only if the current version still matches, otherwise it returns 412 Precondition Failed. The client then re-reads, merges or asks the user, and retries. Servers can require If-Match with 428 Precondition Required.
Follow-up: How is this different from an idempotency key? — An idempotency key deduplicates the same request retried; If-Match detects a different client's change in between.
H
What is web cache deception, or more generally, how can a shared cache leak private data?

A shared cache stores responses by a key, usually the URL, and trusts headers or rules to decide what is cacheable. If a personalised page is served with cacheable headers, or a CDN rule caches by file extension so that /account/profile.css returns the account page and gets cached, the next person requesting that URL receives the first user's page. Valve's Steam store leaked pages of about 34,000 users on Christmas Day 2015 when an emergency caching configuration during a DoS attack cached personalised responses.

Follow-up: What defences would you put in place? — Mark personalised responses private or no-store at the origin, make the CDN respect origin headers rather than override them by extension, and never cache responses that set cookies.
H
How do you make a POST safely retryable?

The client generates a unique idempotency key per logical operation and sends it in a header such as Idempotency-Key. The server records the key with the result of the first successful processing, atomically with the side effect, and for any later request with the same key returns the stored result instead of repeating the action. Keys expire after a retention period, and a request reusing a key with a different body is rejected.

Follow-up: What happens if a retry arrives while the first request is still in progress? — The server should detect the in-flight key, typically with a lock or unique constraint, and return a 409 or wait, not process it twice.
H
A CDN is serving gzip-compressed responses to a client that does not support gzip, or the French page to English users. What went wrong and how do you fix it?

The origin varies its response on request headers such as Accept-Encoding or Accept-Language but did not send a Vary header naming them, so the shared cache stored one variant under the URL alone and served it to everyone. Fix it by sending Vary: Accept-Encoding (most servers do this for compression) and Vary: Accept-Language where relevant, or by putting the variant in the URL such as /fr/. Avoid Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent on cacheable content because they fragment the cache into near-useless pieces.
Follow-up: Why do CDNs often normalise Accept-Encoding? — Browsers send many slightly different values; normalising to a few buckets keeps the number of cached variants small.

sum: How the three HTTP versions carry the same semantics differently: text messages and keep-alive, binary frames and multiplexed streams with HPACK, and HTTP over QUIC; head-of-line blocking at each layer, and what it all means for proxies, gRPC and load balancing.
prereq: net7
HTTP semantics (methods, status codes, headers, caching) are the same in every version; only the wire format changes.
net4
TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so one lost segment stalls everything behind it; new connections start with slow start.
net5
QUIC runs over UDP with TLS 1.3 built in, independent streams and connection migration; clients learn about HTTP/3 through Alt-Svc.
why:
In net7 you learned what an HTTP message means. This lesson is about how it is carried, and why that changed twice in a decade. The answer is a story about the modern web outgrowing its protocol.

HTTP/1.1 was standardised in 1997, when a web page was an HTML file and a few images. Today a typical page makes 50 to 100 requests for scripts, styles, fonts, images and API data, and a mobile app may fire dozens of API calls on launch. HTTP/1.1 can only have one request in flight on a connection at a time, so browsers opened about six connections per host and developers invented a whole toolkit of hacks, such as spreading assets across many hostnames and gluing images into sprite sheets, just to get more requests moving in parallel. Each extra connection paid its own TCP and TLS handshake and its own slow start (net4).

HTTP/2, published in 2015 and grown from Google's SPDY experiment, fixed that by letting many requests share one connection at the same time. Then its own limit surfaced: all those requests shared one TCP byte stream, so on lossy mobile networks a single dropped packet froze every request at once. HTTP/3, published in 2022, moved HTTP onto QUIC (net5) to remove that last bottleneck.

For an engineer this is not history trivia. The version in use changes how load balancers must be configured (a gRPC service can end up sending all its traffic to one pod), which performance hacks help or hurt, how large downloads behave through proxies, which attacks your edge must defend against, and how you debug a slow request. Interviewers ask about it because it tests whether you understand the layers underneath, and not just the API on top.

This lesson walks through each version's wire format and connection model, the three kinds of head-of-line blocking and which version fixes which, header compression, how versions are negotiated hop by hop, and the operational consequences for proxies, gRPC and security.
primer:
Same letter, different envelopes and roads

Think of an HTTP request as a letter. Its meaning, what you are asking for, is the same whichever way you send it. HTTP/1.1 sends letters one at a time down a single-lane road: the next letter cannot leave until the reply to the previous one has come back. To go faster you hire more roads (connections), each of which costs time to set up. HTTP/2 cuts every letter into numbered strips, interleaves strips from many letters on one road, and reassembles them at the other end, so dozens of letters travel at once. But the road is still a single lane that must deliver strips in exact order, so if one strip is lost, everything behind it waits. HTTP/3 gives each letter its own lane on a new kind of road (QUIC), so a lost strip only delays its own letter.

Where the analogy breaks: the "roads" are not free to build. Each new connection costs round trips for handshakes and starts slowly while TCP probes the network, which is why "just open more connections" was never a good answer.

A short history

By the late 2000s, page load times were dominated by round trips rather than bandwidth, and Google began experimenting with a replacement wire format called SPDY, deployed between Chrome and Google's servers from 2009. Its core ideas, binary framing, multiplexed streams and header compression, became HTTP/2 in 2015. Google's next experiment, running HTTP over its own UDP-based transport, became QUIC and HTTP/3, standardised in 2021 and 2022. Each step was driven by measurements of real users, which is also how you should decide whether a change helps your own traffic.

What that looks like in time

How your code sees it

Mostly, it does not. Browsers negotiate the best version automatically. HTTP client libraries do too, if enabled: Python's httpx needs http2=True, Go's standard client uses HTTP/2 automatically over TLS, and gRPC always uses HTTP/2. What your code does control is connection reuse. A client object created once and reused keeps its HTTP/2 connection open and multiplexes all calls over it; a client created per request throws that away and pays a new handshake every time, under any version.

If you remember one thing: every version sends the same HTTP messages, and each new version exists to remove a kind of waiting that the previous one imposed.
body:
1. HTTP/1.1: text, keep-alive and one request at a time

An HTTP/1.1 message is text: a request line, header lines, a blank line, then the body, exactly as drawn in net7. Because TCP is a byte stream, the receiver must know where each message ends. For bodies it uses either a Content-Length header or chunked transfer encoding, where the body is sent as a series of chunks each prefixed with its size, ending with a zero-size chunk, used when the length is not known in advance (for example, a streamed response).

HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection for every request. HTTP/1.1 made persistent connections (keep-alive) the default: after a response, the connection stays open and the next request reuses it, saving the TCP and TLS handshakes and keeping the congestion window warm. But reuse is sequential. The client sends a request, waits for the whole response, then sends the next.

HTTP/1.1 did define pipelining, sending several requests without waiting, but the responses must come back in the same order as the requests, because nothing in an HTTP/1.1 response says which request it answers. If the first response is slow (a big image, or a slow database query), all the responses queued behind it wait, even if they are ready. This is head-of-line blocking at the application level. Combined with buggy proxies, it made pipelining so unreliable that browsers never enabled it.

So browsers parallelise by opening multiple connections, about six per host. That in turn produced the HTTP/1.1 performance toolkit: domain sharding (serving assets from img1.example.com, img2.example.com to get six connections to each), sprite sheets (many small images glued into one file), concatenating all scripts into one bundle, and inlining small resources into the HTML. All of them work around the one-request-per-connection limit, and all of them have costs: more DNS lookups and handshakes, worse caching, and more bytes when only part of a bundle is needed.

A final HTTP/1.1 cost is headers. They are sent as uncompressed text on every request, and they are highly repetitive: the same cookies, user agent and accept headers, often 500 bytes to over 1 KB per request. For a page making 80 requests, that is tens of kilobytes of repeated headers on a mobile uplink.

2. HTTP/2: frames and streams

HTTP/2 keeps HTTP's meaning and changes the encoding completely. Every message is split into frames: small binary units, each with a 9-byte header that gives its length, its type and the ID of the stream it belongs to. A stream is one request/response exchange. The frame types you need to know:

  • HEADERS: opens a stream and carries the compressed request or response headers.
  • DATA: carries a piece of a body.
  • SETTINGS: each side announces its limits, such as the maximum number of concurrent streams (often 100 or more) and initial flow-control window sizes.
  • WINDOW_UPDATE: grants the peer permission to send more bytes (flow control, below).
  • RST_STREAM: cancels one stream without closing the connection, for example when the user navigates away.
  • GOAWAY: tells the peer the connection is closing and which streams were processed, for graceful shutdown.
  • PING: measures round-trip time and keeps idle connections alive.

Because every frame names its stream, frames from many streams can be interleaved on the same connection and reassembled by stream ID at the other end:

The consequences follow directly. A browser needs only one connection per origin, so one handshake and one congestion window that warms up and stays warm. Slow responses do not block fast ones. And the HTTP/1.1 hacks become counterproductive: sharding across hostnames now adds connections, handshakes and cold congestion windows, and splits the header compression context.

HTTP/2 also added flow control per stream on top of TCP's. Each stream and the whole connection have a window, 65,535 bytes by default, that the receiver enlarges with WINDOW_UPDATE frames as it consumes data. The point is fairness inside the connection: without it, one huge download could fill the receiver's buffers and starve every other stream. The side effect is a second place throughput can be capped, as the drill shows.

Two HTTP/2 features did not survive contact with reality. Prioritisation let clients describe a tree of dependencies between streams ("send the CSS before the images"), but implementations were inconsistent; it was replaced by a much simpler Priority header with an urgency level (RFC 9218), also used by HTTP/3. Server push let servers send resources before they were requested, but servers could not know what the browser already had cached; Chrome removed it in 2022, and the modern replacement is the 103 Early Hints response plus preload hints (net2).

3. Header compression: HPACK

HTTP/2 compresses headers with HPACK. Both ends keep a static table of 61 common header fields and values (such as :method: GET and accept-encoding: gzip, deflate) and a dynamic table, per connection, of headers recently sent. A header already in a table is sent as a small index number; a new one is sent literally (with Huffman coding to shrink the text) and optionally added to the dynamic table for next time. On the second request to a site, a 700-byte header block with a big cookie can shrink to a few dozen bytes. HTTP/2 also turns the request line into pseudo-headers (:method, :path, :scheme, :authority) and requires header names in lowercase.

HPACK was designed to avoid the compression side-channel attacks (such as CRIME) that hit general-purpose compression of headers: it does not let attacker-controlled data be compressed together with secrets in a way that leaks them through the output length, and sensitive values can be marked never to enter the dynamic table.

4. The remaining problem: TCP head-of-line blocking

HTTP/2's streams are independent only at the HTTP layer. Underneath, all frames of all streams travel in one TCP byte stream. If the packet carrying a DATA frame for stream 1 is lost, TCP holds back every byte after it, including complete frames for streams 3 and 5, until the retransmission arrives (net4 showed the mechanism). On a clean wired connection that happens rarely. On a mobile network with 1 to 2% loss, it happens constantly, and measurements found HTTP/2 could be slower than HTTP/1.1, whose six independent connections meant a loss stalled only one of them. There are therefore three kinds of head-of-line blocking to keep apart: HTTP/1.1's response ordering (fixed by HTTP/2), TCP's byte ordering (fixed by HTTP/3), and, within a single stream, data still arriving in order (inherent in any ordered stream).

5. HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC

HTTP/3 maps each request/response onto its own QUIC stream (net5). QUIC delivers each stream's bytes in order but treats streams independently, so a lost packet delays only the streams whose data it carried. HTTP/3's own frames are simpler than HTTP/2's because QUIC already provides streams, flow control and connection management: it mostly needs HEADERS and DATA frames per request stream, plus a control stream for settings.

Header compression had to be redesigned. HPACK's dynamic table depends on header blocks being processed in the exact order they were sent; over independent QUIC streams, a stream would have to wait for an earlier stream's table update, reintroducing head-of-line blocking. QPACK sends dynamic table updates on separate, dedicated streams and lets the encoder choose, per header block, whether to refer to entries the decoder may not have yet (and risk waiting) or to avoid them.

HTTP/3 also inherits QUIC's benefits: a combined transport and TLS handshake (one round trip, or zero with resumption), connection migration when a phone changes networks, and encrypted transport headers. And it inherits QUIC's costs: more CPU per byte, UDP that some networks block, and less passive visibility.

6. Negotiation, hop by hop

A client does not choose a version once for the whole path; each hop negotiates separately.

  • HTTP/2 over TLS is negotiated inside the TLS handshake with ALPN: the ClientHello lists h2 and http/1.1, and the server picks one in its reply, at no extra cost.
  • HTTP/2 without TLS (h2c) is not supported by browsers; it is used internally, for example by gRPC, with the client simply assuming the server speaks HTTP/2 ("prior knowledge").
  • HTTP/3 uses a different transport, so it cannot be negotiated within a TCP connection. The server advertises it with Alt-Svc: h3=":443" in a response, or with an HTTPS DNS record, and the client tries QUIC on subsequent connections, keeping TCP as a fallback.
