7. A worked comparison

Take a page that needs 60 resources from one origin, a user 80 ms away, and assume each response is small. Under HTTP/1.1 with six connections, the browser pays six TCP and TLS handshakes (in parallel, about 160 ms with TLS 1.3), then each connection fetches about ten resources one after another: roughly ten round trips, 800 ms, plus the handshakes, close to a second before everything arrives, with six congestion windows each warming up separately. Under HTTP/2 on one connection, it pays one handshake, then requests all 60 at once; responses stream back as fast as the single connection's congestion window allows, typically two or three round trips once the window has grown: a few hundred milliseconds. Now add 2% packet loss. HTTP/1.1's six connections each suffer occasional stalls, but a stall freezes only a sixth of the page. HTTP/2's single connection stalls entirely on every loss, and each loss also halves its one congestion window. That is the case where HTTP/2 can lose to HTTP/1.1 and where HTTP/3 wins clearly, since QUIC's loss affects only some streams, while its congestion control behaves like TCP's.

8. What to change when you upgrade

Turning on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 at the edge is a configuration change, but a few related changes capture the benefit. Remove domain sharding and serve assets from as few origins as practical, or at least from origins that can share a connection through coalescing. Revisit bundling: split code by route or by how often it changes, so a deploy invalidates less. Replace server push, if any, with preload and Early Hints. Check that proxies raise HTTP/2 flow-control windows and allow enough concurrent streams. Move gRPC and HTTP/2 service traffic onto layer-7 balancing. And measure real users by protocol before and after, because the effect depends on your users' networks.

This hop-by-hop independence is why most of the benefit can be captured at the edge alone: the long, lossy client-to-edge hop gets HTTP/3, while the short, clean edge-to-origin hop can use HTTP/2 or even HTTP/1.1 over pooled, warm connections without users noticing.
deep:
Long-lived connections change load balancing and deploys

With HTTP/1.1, clients open and close connections often, so even a naive L4 balancer spreads load over time. With HTTP/2 and gRPC, a client opens one connection and keeps it for hours. Three consequences follow. Load concentrates: a few heavy clients pin a few backends. Scaling out does not help immediately: new pods get no traffic until clients reconnect. And deploys are uneven: draining a pod means its clients reconnect in a burst elsewhere. The fixes are L7 proxies or service meshes that balance per request; client-side load balancing, where the gRPC client resolves all backend addresses and keeps connections to each; and servers that cap connection age or send GOAWAY periodically so clients re-spread. Kubernetes' default Service (an L4 mechanism) is the classic trap: gRPC traffic to a Deployment ends up on one pod.

Flow control as a hidden throughput cap

HTTP/2's per-stream and per-connection windows default to 65,535 bytes. A single stream can therefore have at most that much unacknowledged at the HTTP/2 layer, however large TCP's window is. At 100 ms RTT that caps a stream at about 5 Mbit/s, the same bandwidth-delay arithmetic as net4, one layer up. Browsers and good servers raise the windows immediately through SETTINGS and WINDOW_UPDATE, but proxies and internal clients with defaults can silently throttle large downloads, model-weight transfers or streaming responses. When a big transfer is slow over HTTP/2 but fine over HTTP/1.1, check the initial window settings first.

Stream-level attacks: Rapid Reset and friends

Multiplexing makes each connection far more powerful, and attackers noticed. In the Rapid Reset attack (CVE-2023-44487), which began in late August 2023 and was disclosed in October, clients opened streams with HEADERS and immediately cancelled them with RST_STREAM. Reset streams do not count against the concurrent-stream limit, so a single connection could generate an unbounded request rate while the server had already begun routing each request. Cloudflare saw peaks just above 201 million requests per second from a botnet of about 20,000 machines. Mitigations tracked the ratio of resets to completed requests per connection and closed abusive connections. In 2024 a related family of "CONTINUATION flood" bugs abused unbounded header continuation frames. The lesson for operators: protocol-level limits (streams per connection, resets per second, header sizes, connection lifetime) are as important as request-level rate limits, and edge software must be patched promptly.

Request smuggling and protocol downgrades

HTTP/1.1 has two ways to delimit a body, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked, and historically servers disagreed on what to do when both, or malformed variants, appear. If a front-end proxy and a backend disagree about where a request ends, an attacker can append a hidden second request that the backend attaches to the next user's request on the same pooled connection, leading to cache poisoning or session hijacking. HTTP/2's frames carry explicit lengths, removing the ambiguity, but edges that accept HTTP/2 and forward HTTP/1.1 must translate carefully; flaws in that translation ("H2.CL" and "H2.TE" smuggling) reintroduce the bug. Using HTTP/2 end to end, rejecting ambiguous requests and keeping parsers strict are the durable fixes.

Connection coalescing and 421

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 clients reuse a connection for another hostname if it resolves to the same IP and the connection's certificate covers that name (for example a wildcard or multi-name certificate). This saves handshakes but can surprise operators: requests for b.example.com arrive on a connection originally opened for a.example.com, perhaps at a server not configured for b. Servers answer such requests with 421 Misdirected Request, which tells the client to open a fresh connection. It shows up when certificates are shared more broadly than the routing configuration behind them.

What gRPC takes from HTTP/2

gRPC maps each call to an HTTP/2 stream: the method is the path (/package.Service/Method), messages are length-prefixed Protocol Buffers in DATA frames, and the call's final status travels in trailers, headers sent after the body, which HTTP/1.1 infrastructure rarely supports. Streaming calls are simply long-lived streams with many messages in each direction. This is why gRPC requires HTTP/2 end to end, why browsers need a translation layer (gRPC-Web), and why every HTTP/2 operational issue above, from load balancing to flow-control windows, applies directly to gRPC services.
prod:
Characteristic problems

  • gRPC hot-spotting: one pod at 90% CPU while others idle, after scaling out. Cause: long-lived HTTP/2 connections through an L4 balancer or Kubernetes Service. Fix: L7 proxy or mesh, client-side balancing, or maximum connection age on the server.
  • Slow large transfers through a proxy: fine over HTTP/1.1, capped over HTTP/2. Cause: small HTTP/2 flow-control windows. Fix: raise initial stream and connection windows.
  • Concurrency limits: requests queue on the client while the network is idle, because the server's SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS (often 100) is reached on the single connection. Clients that need more concurrency must open more connections.
  • Pages slower after enabling HTTP/2 on lossy networks: the single connection amplifies loss. HTTP/3 at the edge is the remedy for mobile-heavy audiences.
  • Legacy hacks left in place: domain sharding, huge bundles and inlined assets from the HTTP/1.1 era now hurt; audit them when upgrading.
  • Protocol attacks: Rapid Reset and CONTINUATION floods exhausted servers that had no per-connection stream abuse limits; patched software and edge protections are essential.
  • Translation bugs: request smuggling at an HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1.1 boundary, header-size limits that differ between versions, and trailers dropped by intermediaries that break gRPC status reporting.

War story: Rapid Reset, August to October 2023

Starting on 25 August 2023, Cloudflare, Google and AWS saw floods of HTTP/2 requests far larger than any before: Cloudflare recorded a peak just above 201 million requests per second, nearly three times its previous record, from only about 20,000 machines. The attackers used a legitimate protocol feature, stream cancellation, at an illegitimate rate. At Cloudflare, about 1% of requests were affected initially, with peaks around 12% during the worst waves, before new connection-level defences closed abusive connections and brought impact to effectively zero. The vendors coordinated a disclosure on 10 October 2023, and every major HTTP/2 implementation shipped patches. It is a reminder that multiplexing moves work that used to be spread over many connections onto one, and so moves the need for limits there too.

A debugging order

For a performance or error problem that might be version-related: first find out which version each hop negotiated (browser DevTools, curl -w '%{http_version}', proxy logs). Then reproduce with the version forced (--http1.1, --http2, --http3) to see whether the problem follows the version. If it does, look at the version's specific limits: flow-control windows and concurrent streams for HTTP/2, UDP reachability and CPU for HTTP/3, connection counts for HTTP/1.1.

Observability

Record the negotiated protocol per request in edge and proxy logs (most CDNs and proxies expose it, and browsers show it in DevTools' Protocol column), so you can compare latency and error rates by version. Track connections, streams per connection, resets and GOAWAYs at proxies. For gRPC, track per-pod request rate to spot pinning. curl -w '%{http_version}' shows what a single request negotiated; nghttp -v and Wireshark (with TLS keys) show individual HTTP/2 frames.

Knobs

Maximum concurrent streams; initial stream and connection window sizes; maximum header list size; idle and maximum connection age; reset-rate limits per connection; enabling HTTP/3 and the Alt-Svc lifetime; and the upstream protocol each proxy uses towards origins (HTTP/2 where the origin supports it, especially for gRPC).
myths: HTTP/2 changed how you design APIs.

HTTP/2 kept the same methods, status codes, headers and caching rules; a correct HTTP/1.1 API works unchanged over HTTP/2. What changed is the wire format and connection handling, which affects performance tuning, proxies and load balancers, not your API's meaning.
HTTP/2 always makes pages faster.

It removes the one-request-per-connection limit and compresses headers, which usually helps a lot. But all streams share one TCP connection, so on lossy networks one lost packet stalls every stream, and HTTP/2 can do worse than HTTP/1.1's six connections. HTTP/3 exists largely to fix that.
With HTTP/2, bundling and domain sharding are still best practice.

Domain sharding was a workaround for HTTP/1.1's per-host connection limit; under HTTP/2 it adds DNS lookups, handshakes and separate congestion windows, and breaks shared header compression. Giant bundles also matter less and hurt cache granularity. Moderate bundling is still sensible, because each request still has overhead.
HTTP/2 server push lets you speed up pages by sending resources before they are requested.

Push was hard to use well: servers often pushed resources the browser already had cached, wasting bandwidth. Chrome removed support in 2022 and push is effectively dead on the web. Its replacements are preload hints and the 103 Early Hints response.
An L4 load balancer spreads HTTP/2 or gRPC requests across backends.

An L4 balancer picks a backend per connection. HTTP/2 and gRPC clients open one long-lived connection and send every request over it, so all of a client's requests go to one backend. Balancing requests needs an L7 proxy that terminates HTTP/2, or client-side load balancing across several connections.
HTTP/3 replaces HTTP/2.

HTTP/3 needs UDP to get through, and some networks block it, so every HTTP/3 deployment keeps HTTP/2 over TCP as a fallback. Internally, most service-to-service traffic stays on HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 over TCP, where HTTP/3's benefits are small.
lab:
Fifteen minutes with curl, Python and a browser. You will see ALPN choose a version, watch connection reuse, compare versions and look at frames. On Windows PowerShell use curl.exe.

  1. Which version did I get? curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://www.wikipedia.org, then add --http1.1. Look for: 2 by default and 1.1 when forced. If curl -V lists HTTP3, try --http3 and see 3.
  2. Watch ALPN. curl -v https://www.wikipedia.org -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i alpn. Look for: "ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1" and "ALPN: server accepted h2": the version was agreed inside the TLS handshake.
  3. See the text protocol. curl -v --http1.1 https://www.wikipedia.org -o /dev/null shows headers exactly as sent, mixed case. With HTTP/2, curl -v shows pseudo-headers such as :method and :path and lowercase header names: the same request, different encoding.
  4. Connection reuse. curl -v --http1.1 https://httpbin.org/get https://httpbin.org/uuid -o /dev/null -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -iE 're-?using|connected to'. Look for: one "Connected to" and then a line saying the existing connection is reused: keep-alive at work. With --http2 and -Z (parallel), curl multiplexes both requests on one connection.
  5. From Python. pip install "httpx[http2]", then: 
    import httpx
with httpx.Client(http2=True) as c:
    for url in ["https://www.wikipedia.org", "https://www.google.com"]:
        r = c.get(url)
        print(url, r.http_version, r.status_code)
    Look for: HTTP/2. Note the single client object: reusing it keeps connections open, which is the habit to build for API clients.
  6. In the browser. Open DevTools' Network tab, right-click the column headers and enable Protocol and Connection ID, then load a large news site. Look for: many requests sharing one Connection ID with h2 or h3, and, on any older site still on http/1.1, about six distinct connection IDs per host.
  7. Frames, if you want to go deeper. With nghttp installed (package nghttp2-client), run nghttp -nv https://www.wikipedia.org. Look for: SETTINGS, HEADERS, DATA and WINDOW_UPDATE frames with stream IDs, exactly the vocabulary of the body.
recap: All three versions carry identical HTTP semantics; they differ in how messages are framed and in the transport underneath.
HTTP/1.1 sends text messages, keeps connections open between requests, but allows only one outstanding request per connection in practice, so browsers open about six connections per host.
HTTP/1.1 pipelining failed because responses must come back in request order, so one slow response blocks the rest: application-level head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames tagged with stream IDs and interleaves many streams on one TCP connection, compressing headers with HPACK.
HTTP/2 removes application-level head-of-line blocking but not TCP's: one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection.
HTTP/3 maps HTTP onto QUIC streams that are independent at the transport level, uses QPACK for headers, and inherits QUIC's faster handshake and connection migration.
Versions are negotiated per hop: ALPN inside TLS chooses h2 or http/1.1, Alt-Svc or HTTPS DNS records advertise h3, and each proxy can speak a different version upstream.

Long-lived multiplexed connections change operations: load balance HTTP/2 and gRPC at layer 7, tune flow-control windows, cap concurrent streams, and patch against stream-abuse attacks like Rapid Reset.
glossary: 0-RTT
Sending the first request with the handshake on a resumed QUIC or TLS 1.3 connection; replayable, so only for idempotent requests.
103 Early Hints
An informational response a server sends before the final one, listing resources to preload or preconnect.
ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation)
The TLS extension in which client and server agree on h2 or http/1.1 during the handshake.
Alt-Svc
A response header advertising that the site is also available via another protocol, such as h3 on UDP port 443.
Binary framing
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3's encoding of messages as typed, length-prefixed frames rather than text lines.
Chunked transfer encoding
HTTP/1.1's way of sending a body of unknown length as a series of size-prefixed chunks.
Connection coalescing
An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 client reusing one connection for several hostnames that share an IP address and a certificate.
CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
The public catalogue of security flaws; each gets an ID like CVE-2023-44487.
DATA frame
An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 frame carrying part of a message body.
Domain sharding
An HTTP/1.1-era trick of spreading assets over several hostnames to get more parallel connections.
Flow control window
In HTTP/2 and QUIC, how many bytes a sender may send on a stream or connection before the receiver grants more.
GOAWAY frame
The HTTP/2 frame announcing that a connection is shutting down and which streams were processed, used for graceful restarts and rebalancing.
gRPC
A remote procedure call framework using Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, with long-lived connections and streaming.
h2 / h2c / h3
ALPN names: HTTP/2 over TLS, HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP, and HTTP/3.
Head-of-line blocking
Delivery held up because an earlier item in an ordered queue is missing or slow.
HEADERS frame
An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 frame carrying a message's compressed headers and starting a stream.
HPACK
HTTP/2's header compression: a static table of common headers, a per-connection dynamic table of recent ones, and Huffman coding.
Keep-alive (persistent connection)
Reusing one TCP connection for several HTTP requests one after another; the default in HTTP/1.1.
L4 / L7 load balancer
A balancer deciding per connection using addresses and ports (L4), versus one that parses HTTP and decides per request (L7). Covered in net10.
Multiplexing
Carrying many independent request/response exchanges over one connection at the same time.
PING frame
An HTTP/2 frame that the peer must echo, used to measure RTT and keep idle connections alive.
Pipelining
Sending several HTTP/1.1 requests without waiting for responses; specified but unusable in practice because responses must return in order.
QPACK
HTTP/3's header compression, redesigned from HPACK so streams need not wait on each other.
QUIC
The UDP-based transport with independent streams and built-in TLS 1.3 that HTTP/3 runs on (net5).
Rapid Reset
A 2023 attack (CVE-2023-44487) that opened and immediately cancelled HTTP/2 streams at huge rates to exhaust servers.
Request smuggling
An attack exploiting disagreement between a proxy and a backend about where one HTTP/1.1 request ends, to hide a second request inside the first.
RST_STREAM
The HTTP/2 frame that cancels one stream without closing the connection.
Server push
An HTTP/2 feature letting a server send responses the client had not requested yet; removed from major browsers.
SETTINGS frame
The HTTP/2 frame where each side announces limits such as maximum concurrent streams and initial window size.
SPDY
Google's experimental protocol (2009) whose ideas became HTTP/2.
Stream
One request/response exchange inside an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection, identified by a stream ID.
TCP / TLS / UDP
The reliable byte-stream transport (net4), the encryption layer (net9), and the minimal datagram transport (net5).
WINDOW_UPDATE frame
An HTTP/2 frame granting the peer permission to send more bytes on a stream or the whole connection.
drill:
Diagnose it

After moving an internal gRPC service to Kubernetes with 6 replicas behind a standard ClusterIP Service, one pod runs at 95% CPU and the others at 5%. Scaling to 12 replicas changes nothing. Explain and fix.

Answer

A ClusterIP Service balances at layer 4: it picks a pod when a TCP connection is opened. gRPC clients open one long-lived HTTP/2 connection and multiplex every call over it, so all calls from a client go to the pod chosen at connect time. With few clients (or one big one), a single pod gets nearly everything, and new replicas receive no traffic because no new connections are opened.

Fixes: use a layer-7 proxy or service mesh (Envoy, Linkerd, Istio) that terminates HTTP/2 and balances each call; or use client-side load balancing, with a headless Service so DNS returns every pod IP and the gRPC client's round-robin policy keeps a connection to each; and set a maximum connection age on the server (gRPC's MAX_CONNECTION_AGE) so clients periodically reconnect and re-spread after scaling or deploys.

Estimate it

A service downloads a 2 GB file from an object store through an HTTP/2 proxy. RTT between them is 50 ms. The proxy uses HTTP/2's default initial stream window of 65,535 bytes and does not enlarge it. Roughly how long does the download take, and what is the fix?

Answer

At most one window can be in flight per round trip on the stream: 65,535 bytes / 0.05 s ≈ 1.3 MB/s, about 10 Mbit/s, no matter how fast the network or how large TCP's window. 2 GB / 1.3 MB/s ≈ 1,500 s, about 25 minutes. Over HTTP/1.1 the same path might run hundreds of times faster, limited only by TCP. The fix is to raise the HTTP/2 initial stream and connection window sizes on the proxy and client (to several megabytes, ideally near the bandwidth-delay product), or to split the download into parallel range requests on several streams.
qa: E
What is the main improvement of HTTP/2 over HTTP/1.1?

It multiplexes many concurrent request/response streams over a single connection using binary framing, removing HTTP/1.1's practical limit of one outstanding request per connection, and it compresses headers with HPACK. Browsers no longer need six connections per host, and a page's many requests share one warm TCP connection.
Follow-up: What did HTTP/1.1 already have that people forget? — Persistent connections: keep-alive lets requests reuse a connection sequentially, so the handshake cost is paid once, not per request.
E
Does moving an API from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 require changing the API?

No. Methods, paths, status codes, headers and caching semantics are identical; only the encoding on the wire and connection management change. Clients and servers negotiate the version automatically, typically with ALPN during the TLS handshake, and application code usually does not notice.
Follow-up: What might break? — Code or proxies that assume header names keep their case (HTTP/2 lowercases them), or that rely on HTTP/1.1-only features such as the Upgrade header.
E
Why did browsers open six connections per host under HTTP/1.1?

An HTTP/1.1 connection can have only one request outstanding at a time in practice, so a page with 60 resources on one connection would fetch them one round trip at a time. Opening several connections gives parallelism; browsers settled on about six per host as a compromise between speed and load on servers and networks.

Follow-up: What hacks grew from that limit? — Domain sharding across hostnames, image sprites, and concatenating scripts and styles into big bundles, all to reduce the number of requests or increase parallel connections.
M
What head-of-line blocking remains in HTTP/2, and how does HTTP/3 fix it?

HTTP/2 streams share one TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so a single lost packet stalls all streams until it is retransmitted, even streams whose data arrived intact. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, whose streams are ordered independently at the transport layer, so a loss delays only the streams whose data was in the lost packet.
Follow-up: And what head-of-line blocking did HTTP/2 remove? — The application-level kind in HTTP/1.1, where responses on one connection had to come back in request order.
M
Which HTTP/1.1-era optimisations become harmful under HTTP/2?

Domain sharding adds DNS lookups, handshakes and separate congestion windows, and defeats multiplexing and shared header compression. Aggressive concatenation and spriting matter less and hurt caching granularity, because changing one small file invalidates the whole bundle. Inlining large resources also defeats caching.

Follow-up: So should every module be a separate file? — Not quite: each request still has per-request costs in the browser and server, so moderate bundling by route or change frequency is the usual balance.
M
How are HTTP versions negotiated?

For HTTPS, the client lists the versions it supports (h2, http/1.1) in the ALPN extension of the TLS ClientHello and the server picks one in its reply, so no extra round trip is needed. HTTP/3 cannot be negotiated that way because it uses a different transport, so servers advertise it with an Alt-Svc header or an HTTPS DNS record, and the client tries QUIC on later connections, falling back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

Follow-up: What about HTTP/2 without TLS? — h2c exists, mostly used between internal services such as gRPC, with the client assuming the server speaks HTTP/2 ('prior knowledge'); browsers do not support it.
M
How does HPACK compress headers, and why does it matter?

Requests to the same site repeat nearly the same headers (cookies, user agent, accept headers), often hundreds of bytes each. HPACK keeps a static table of 61 common header fields and a dynamic table of recently sent ones, shared per connection, so a repeated header is sent as a small index, and new values are Huffman-coded. A repeated 500-byte header block can shrink to a few dozen bytes, which matters on mobile uplinks.

Follow-up: Why did HTTP/3 need QPACK instead? — HPACK assumes header blocks are processed in order; over QUIC's independent streams that would reintroduce head-of-line blocking, so QPACK sends table updates on separate streams.
M
Why is load balancing gRPC or HTTP/2 traffic tricky?

Clients keep one long-lived HTTP/2 connection per backend address and send all requests over it. An L4 balancer chooses a backend only when a connection opens, so each client's requests all land on one backend, and newly added backends receive nothing until clients reconnect. The fix is an L7 proxy or service mesh that terminates HTTP/2 and balances each request, or client-side load balancing across connections to every backend.
Follow-up: How do servers help rebalance long-lived connections? — By periodically sending GOAWAY or capping connection age, so clients reconnect and spread out.
M
What happened to HTTP/2 server push, and what replaced it?

Push let a server send resources such as CSS along with the HTML before the browser asked. In practice servers could not tell what the browser already had cached, so they often pushed redundant bytes, and gains were small and inconsistent. Chrome removed support in 2022. The replacements are preload hints in HTML and the 103 Early Hints response, which tell the browser what to fetch while leaving it in charge of its cache.
Follow-up: Why is Early Hints better than push? — The browser still decides, so cached resources are not re-sent, and hints can be sent while the application is still generating the page.
H
Explain the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset attack and how servers defend against it.

An HTTP/2 client can open a stream with a HEADERS frame and cancel it immediately with RST_STREAM. Cancelled streams do not count against the concurrent stream limit, but the server may already have started work, such as routing the request to a backend. Attackers from late August 2023 sent HEADERS and RST_STREAM pairs as fast as possible from about 20,000 machines, reaching over 200 million requests per second against Cloudflare. Defences: count resets per connection and close abusive connections, stop work quickly on cancellation, and ban offending clients.

Follow-up: Why couldn't the concurrent stream limit stop it? — The limit bounds open streams, and each stream was reset almost instantly, so the open count stayed low while the request rate was enormous.
H
What is HTTP request smuggling, and why does HTTP/2 matter to it?

HTTP/1.1 has two ways to mark a body's length, Content-Length and chunked Transfer-Encoding. If a front-end proxy and a backend disagree about which applies to an ambiguous request, the attacker can hide a second request inside the first's body; the backend treats it as the next request on the shared connection, for example prefixing another user's request. HTTP/2's binary framing gives lengths unambiguously, but many proxies accept HTTP/2 at the edge and translate to HTTP/1.1 upstream, and bugs in that downgrade reintroduce smuggling.
Follow-up: What is the most robust mitigation? — Use HTTP/2 end to end where possible, reject ambiguous requests at the edge, and keep proxies and servers on consistent, strict parsing.
H
A large file download is slow over HTTP/2 through your proxy but fast over HTTP/1.1. What would you suspect?

HTTP/2 flow control: each stream and the connection have windows that start at 65,535 bytes, and the receiver must send WINDOW_UPDATE frames to allow more. If the proxy or client keeps small windows, a single stream can only have that much in flight per round trip, capping throughput on high-latency paths regardless of TCP's window. HTTP/1.1 has no such extra layer. Raise the initial stream and connection window settings on the proxy and client.

Follow-up: Why does HTTP/2 have flow control on top of TCP's at all? — So one greedy stream cannot fill buffers and starve other streams sharing the connection; TCP's flow control only covers the connection as a whole.
H
Your edge terminates HTTP/3 and HTTP/2, and your origin speaks HTTP/1.1. Is that fine, and what should you watch?

Usually yes: the big wins of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are on the long, lossy client-to-edge hop, and edges keep warm, pooled connections to the origin. Watch for connection pool sizing to the origin (HTTP/1.1 needs many connections for concurrency), request smuggling risks at the HTTP/2-to-1.1 translation, timeouts and header size limits that differ between versions, and any features, such as gRPC or trailers, that require HTTP/2 end to end.
Follow-up: Why does gRPC need HTTP/2 all the way? — It relies on HTTP/2 trailers for status and on bidirectional streaming, which HTTP/1.1 cannot carry.
H
When would you not bother enabling HTTP/3?

For internal service-to-service traffic inside one data centre, where RTTs are sub-millisecond and loss is rare, so the handshake and head-of-line savings are tiny, while QUIC costs more CPU and needs UDP-aware load balancers and firewall rules. Also when the proxies, meshes or observability tools in the path do not support it well. It pays off on the internet-facing edge, especially for mobile and far-away users.
Follow-up: How would you prove it helped at the edge? — Compare real-user latency percentiles for h3 versus h2 traffic, segmented by network type and region, and watch fallback rates.
