sum: What TLS protects against, the cryptography underneath, the TLS 1.3 handshake, certificates and chains of trust, how CAs issue and revoke, where to terminate TLS, mutual TLS for service identity, and the certificate failures that cause outages.
prereq: net2
A cold HTTPS visit does a TCP handshake, then a TLS handshake that checks the certificate and agrees keys, then sends HTTP; SNI and ALPN travel in the ClientHello.
net4
TLS runs on top of a TCP connection, adding its own round trip before application data.
net6
DNS maps names to addresses; CAA records restrict which CAs may issue for a domain.
why:
When your laptop sends a request across a café's Wi-Fi, the packets pass through the café's router, the internet provider's equipment, and a dozen other networks before reaching the server. Any of those could be compromised, misconfigured or run by someone curious. Without protection, whoever controls one of those points can do three things: read everything, including passwords, cookies and API keys; change what you send or receive, injecting scripts into pages or altering an account number; and impersonate the server entirely, so you log in to the attacker instead.

TLS, Transport Layer Security, is the protocol that stops all three. It is the S in HTTPS, and it also secures connections to databases, message brokers, email servers, and the calls between your own microservices. It achieves this with a clever combination of cryptography and a global system of trust called PKI, the public key infrastructure, in which certificate authorities vouch for which public key belongs to which domain name.

For backend and AI engineers, TLS is more than a checkbox. Certificates expire and take systems down with them: an expired certificate inside Ericsson's software knocked out mobile data for over 30 million people in the UK and customers in ten other countries on a single day in 2018. Certificate lifetimes are being cut from over a year to 47 days by 2029, so renewal must be fully automated. Choosing where to decrypt traffic decides where plaintext exists in your system. Service meshes use mutual TLS to give every service a cryptographic identity, which is the foundation of zero-trust networking. And interviewers regularly ask you to walk through a handshake or debug a certificate error.

This lesson starts from the threat, builds the cryptographic tools one at a time in plain terms, walks through the TLS 1.3 handshake message by message, explains certificates, chains of trust and how clients validate them, covers how certificates are issued, revoked and monitored, compares places to terminate TLS, and finishes with mutual TLS. The production section is a tour of the certificate failures that cause real outages.
primer:
Three promises

TLS gives a connection three properties against anyone on the network path:

  • Confidentiality: they cannot read the data.
  • Integrity: they cannot change it without being detected.
  • Authentication: you know you are talking to the real server for that name (and, with mutual TLS, the server knows who you are).

Encryption alone is not enough. If you encrypt perfectly but to the wrong party, the attacker simply decrypts, reads and re-encrypts to the real server: a man-in-the-middle. Authentication is what makes the encryption meaningful.

The analogy: a sealed conversation with an ID check

Imagine meeting a stranger who claims to be your bank's manager. First you check their ID card, issued by a government office you trust; the card has their photo and name, and the office's seal is hard to forge. That is the certificate, issued by a certificate authority (CA) your device already trusts. But anyone could steal and show a card, so you also ask them to prove they are the person in the photo; in TLS the server proves it holds the private key matching the certificate by signing something unique to this conversation. Then the two of you agree on a secret code in a way that eavesdroppers cannot work out, even though they hear every word; that is the key exchange. From then on you talk in that code, and every sentence carries a seal that breaks if anyone alters it.

Where the analogy breaks: the "ID card" check is done by software in milliseconds, against a list of about 150 trusted root CAs built into your operating system or browser, and the "secret code" is fresh for every connection and thrown away afterwards.

The TLS 1.3 handshake, drawn

Where you meet TLS as an engineer

Most of the time TLS is invisible: your HTTP client library performs the handshake and validation for you. You meet it directly in four situations. Configuring a load balancer, CDN or ingress with certificates and choosing TLS versions. Automating certificate issuance and renewal, and being paged when it fails. Debugging a client that refuses a connection with a certificate error, which is almost always one of five causes: expired, wrong name, untrusted issuer, incomplete chain, or wrong clock. And designing how services authenticate each other, where mutual TLS is the standard answer. The body covers each.

What it costs

One extra round trip for a new connection (TLS 1.3), zero with 0-RTT resumption, a small amount of CPU for the key exchange and signature, and a few kilobytes for the certificate chain. After the handshake, encryption on modern hardware is nearly free. The old argument that HTTPS is too slow for internal traffic no longer holds; the real costs are operational: managing keys and certificates.

If you stop here, keep this model: the certificate proves the server's identity, a fresh key exchange creates the secret, and fast symmetric encryption with tamper detection protects everything after.
body:
1. The cryptographic tools, one at a time

Symmetric encryption uses one secret key for both encrypting and decrypting. It is extremely fast (modern CPUs have AES instructions and encrypt gigabytes per second per core), so it protects all the actual data. TLS 1.3 only allows authenticated encryption (AEAD) ciphers, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, which produce ciphertext plus a tag; if a single bit is altered, decryption fails. That gives integrity as well as confidentiality. The problem symmetric encryption cannot solve is how two strangers get the same secret key without anyone else learning it.

Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair: a public key that can be shared with the world and a private key kept secret. It does two jobs in TLS. Signatures: the private key signs data, and anyone with the public key can verify the signature, proving the signer holds the private key. Key exchange: two parties can arrive at a shared secret using each other's public values.

Diffie-Hellman key exchange is the key exchange TLS uses. Each side generates a fresh key pair for this connection only, sends its public part (the key share), and combines its own private part with the other's public part. Both get the same result, but an eavesdropper who sees both public parts cannot compute it. The modern form uses elliptic curves (ECDHE; the most common curve is X25519). Because these key pairs are ephemeral, created per connection and discarded, TLS gets forward secrecy: even if the server's long-term private key is stolen next year, recordings of today's traffic cannot be decrypted, because the long-term key was only ever used to sign, never to protect the session secret.

From the Diffie-Hellman result, both sides derive a set of symmetric keys (separate ones for each direction and for the handshake versus the data) with a key derivation function. That is the whole trick: asymmetric crypto to agree and authenticate, symmetric crypto to protect the traffic.

2. The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message

  1. ClientHello (plaintext): the TLS versions the client supports, its cipher suites, one or more Diffie-Hellman key shares (it guesses which group the server will choose, usually X25519, so it can send a share straight away), SNI with the hostname it wants, ALPN listing application protocols such as h2 and http/1.1 (net8), and a random value.
  2. ServerHello (plaintext): the chosen version and cipher suite and the server's own key share. Both sides can now compute the shared secret and derive handshake keys. Everything from here on is encrypted.
  3. EncryptedExtensions: remaining negotiated settings, such as the chosen ALPN protocol.
  4. Certificate: the server's certificate chain (section 3).
  5. CertificateVerify: a signature, made with the certificate's private key, over a hash of all the handshake messages so far. This proves the server holds the private key and that nobody tampered with the negotiation, because the signature covers everything both sides sent.
  6. Finished: a message authentication code over the whole transcript, confirming both sides saw the same handshake.
  7. The client validates the certificate chain and the signature, sends its own Finished, and can immediately send application data, such as the HTTP request, in the same flight.

Total cost: one round trip. If the client guessed a key-share group the server does not support, the server answers with a HelloRetryRequest and it costs a second round trip. On later connections, the server can give the client a session ticket, which lets it resume with a pre-shared key and skip the certificate exchange; with 0-RTT, the client even sends its first request in its first flight, which can be replayed, so it is only for idempotent requests (net2).

TLS 1.2, still widely supported, needed two round trips, sent the certificate in plaintext, and allowed key exchange by encrypting the secret with the server's RSA key, which has no forward secrecy. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated (RFC 8996) and should be disabled.

3. Certificates and chains of trust

An X.509 certificate is a signed data structure containing, among other things:

  • the subject public key;
  • the names it is valid for, in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension, such as api.example.com and *.example.com (a wildcard covers exactly one label: a.example.com yes, example.com and a.b.example.com no);
  • the issuer, the CA that signed it;
  • a validity period (not before and not after dates);
  • usage constraints, such as "may be used for TLS server authentication" or "is a CA";
  • the CA's signature over all of the above.

Root CAs do not sign server certificates directly: their private keys are kept offline in hardware, and they sign intermediate CA certificates, which sign the leaf certificates for servers. So the server sends a chain, and the client builds a path to a root it already trusts:

The trust store is the list of root certificates a client trusts, and there is more than one on a typical machine: the operating system's, the browser's own (Firefox ships one), Java's cacerts, Python's certifi package used by requests, Node.js's bundled list, and whatever was baked into a container image. When a certificate works in one client and not another, different trust stores are a prime suspect.

Hostname matching uses only the SAN list; the old Common Name field is ignored by modern clients. When you connect by IP address, the certificate needs an IP SAN, which public CAs rarely issue, one reason internal services should be addressed by name.

4. How certificates are issued: ACME and domain validation

A publicly trusted CA must verify that you control the domain before issuing. Almost all issuance is now automated with ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment), the protocol created for Let's Encrypt and now supported by many CAs. Your ACME client generates a key pair and asks for a certificate; the CA responds with a token and a choice of challenges:

  • HTTP-01: serve the token at http://your-domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>.
  • DNS-01: publish it in a TXT record at _acme-challenge.your-domain. Required for wildcard certificates, and works for servers not reachable from the internet.
  • TLS-ALPN-01: present it during a special TLS handshake on port 443.

The CA checks the challenge from several network locations, then issues the certificate. Tools such as certbot, cert-manager in Kubernetes, and cloud certificate managers run this loop and renew automatically.

Automation is no longer optional. Public certificate lifetimes, which were 398 days, are being cut under a 2025 CA/Browser Forum decision: to 200 days for certificates issued from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027, and 47 days from 15 March 2029. Let's Encrypt certificates have long been 90 days. Every endpoint therefore needs automated renewal and automated deployment of the renewed certificate, plus monitoring that alerts well before expiry if either fails.

5. Revocation, Certificate Transparency and CAA

If a private key leaks, the certificate should stop being trusted before it expires. Two mechanisms exist. A CRL (certificate revocation list) is a CA-published list of revoked certificates. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) lets a client ask the CA about one certificate, and OCSP stapling lets the server attach a recent signed answer to the handshake. In practice revocation is weak: browsers usually "soft-fail" (if the check does not answer, they proceed), many API clients never check, and OCSP leaked every site a user visited to the CA. Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in August 2025 and publishes CRLs only; browsers ship their own compressed revocation sets for important cases. That weakness is exactly why lifetimes are shrinking: a certificate that expires in weeks limits the damage.

Certificate Transparency (CT) attacks the problem from another angle. Every publicly trusted certificate must be recorded in public, append-only, cryptographically verifiable logs, and browsers reject certificates that lack proof of logging. So if any CA issues a certificate for your domain, legitimately or not, it becomes visible, and you can monitor the logs (for example with crt.sh) and react. A CAA DNS record (net6) lists which CAs may issue for your domain; compliant CAs must check it before issuing.

6. Reading certificate errors

Clients phrase the same few problems in different words. Mapping the message to the cause saves hours:

Message (curl/OpenSSL, Java, Python)CauseFirst check
certificate has expiredpast not-after date, or client clock wrongdates in the chain; client time
no alternative certificate subject name matches; hostname mismatchname not in SAN listSAN list vs the name used
unable to get local issuer certificate; PKIX path building failedmissing intermediate, or root not in this client's trust storechain sent by server; which trust store
self-signed certificate in certificate chainprivate or inspection CA the client does not trustissuer; corporate proxy?
handshake failure; no shared cipher; protocol versionclient and server share no version or cipherserver's minimum version and ciphers
certificate required (alert 116)server demands mTLS and client sent no certificateclient certificate configuration

The fix is almost never to disable verification (verify=False, -k, InsecureSkipVerify). That silently removes authentication and leaves the connection open to a man-in-the-middle. Point the client at the right CA bundle or fix the server instead.

7. Where to terminate TLS

"Terminating" TLS means decrypting it. Wherever that happens, a private key must be present and plaintext exists. The three common architectures:

Most internet-facing systems terminate at a CDN or load balancer and re-encrypt to backends. Passthrough is used when the application itself must see the client's certificate (some mTLS setups), or when regulations forbid decryption in shared infrastructure.

8. Mutual TLS

In ordinary TLS only the server is authenticated; clients prove who they are later, with a password or token inside the encrypted connection. In mutual TLS (mTLS), the server also sends a CertificateRequest in its handshake flight, and the client answers with its own Certificate and CertificateVerify, proving it holds the private key for a certificate the server trusts (usually one issued by a private CA). Both ends are authenticated before any application data flows.

mTLS is used where the caller is a machine rather than a person: service-to-service calls inside a platform, partner APIs between companies, and IoT device fleets. Inside Kubernetes, service meshes (such as Istio or Linkerd) automate it completely: each workload gets an identity, often a SPIFFE ID like spiffe://prod.example.com/ns/payments/sa/api derived from its namespace and service account, carried in a short-lived certificate (hours to a day) issued and rotated by the mesh's CA. The proxies beside each service perform mTLS for it, and policies then say which identities may call which services. Note the split: mTLS authenticates the caller; a separate authorisation policy decides what that caller may do.
deep:
Key management: where the private key lives

Everything in TLS rests on private keys staying private. Public CAs keep root keys in offline hardware security modules (HSMs) and bring them out only in audited ceremonies to sign intermediates. For your own services, keys live on load balancers, in cloud certificate managers (where you often cannot even export them), in Kubernetes secrets, or in secret stores such as Vault. The more places a key is copied, the larger the blast radius of one leak; wildcard certificates copied to dozens of servers are a common anti-pattern. Session ticket keys deserve the same care: TLS 1.3 servers encrypt resumption state with a ticket key, and if that key is long-lived and stolen, resumed sessions lose forward secrecy, so servers rotate ticket keys every few hours.

Post-quantum key exchange

A large enough quantum computer could break elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, and an adversary can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once such a machine exists: "harvest now, decrypt later". Since late 2024, major browsers and CDNs have enabled a hybrid key exchange, X25519 combined with ML-KEM-768, where ML-KEM is the lattice-based algorithm NIST standardised as FIPS 203 in August 2024. The shared secret combines both, so the connection is safe if either algorithm holds. The cost is size: the ML-KEM key share adds about 1.2 KB, pushing the ClientHello past a single packet, and some servers and middleboxes that assumed a one-packet ClientHello failed, the same ossification problem seen with TCP and QUIC. Post-quantum signatures for certificates are further off because they are much larger, and forging a signature matters only at connection time, not years later.

Encrypted Client Hello

Even with TLS 1.3, the ClientHello is plaintext, and its SNI field reveals which site you are visiting. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), published as RFC 9849 in 2026, lets a client encrypt an "inner" ClientHello, including the real SNI, under a public key the server's provider publishes in DNS (in the HTTPS record), while the visible "outer" ClientHello names only the provider's shared front-end. It works best on large CDNs, where one front end serves many sites, and it removes the visibility that some enterprise filters and national firewalls rely on, which is why its deployment is politically contested.

TLS inspection and why it breaks things

Many enterprises run "TLS inspection" proxies: the company installs its own root CA on employee devices, and the proxy terminates every TLS connection, inspects the plaintext, and re-encrypts to the destination with a certificate it mints on the fly, signed by that company CA. It works for browsers that trust the company root, but it breaks applications that pin certificates, tools with their own trust stores (a Python script using certifi will reject the proxy's certificates), and mTLS, since the proxy cannot present the client's private key. When a developer tool fails with certificate errors only on the office network, inspection is the first suspect, and the usual fix is pointing the tool at the corporate CA bundle.

Performance: what a handshake costs

A full handshake costs one round trip plus CPU: one ECDHE computation on each side and one signature by the server. ECDSA P-256 signatures are much cheaper for the server than RSA-2048 and produce smaller certificates, so modern deployments prefer ECDSA leaf certificates, often served alongside RSA for old clients. Short chains mean fewer bytes in the first flight, which matters because a large certificate chain can exceed TCP's initial window and cost an extra round trip. Resumption skips the certificate and signature entirely. The bulk encryption itself is rarely a bottleneck: AES-GCM with hardware support runs at many gigabytes per second per core, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 is preferred on devices without AES instructions.

Internal PKI done well

For internal services, a private CA (a cloud private CA service, Vault, cert-manager with an internal issuer, or a mesh CA built on SPIFFE/SPIRE) issues certificates that only your own clients trust. Good practice mirrors the public web: an offline or HSM-protected root, intermediates per environment or cluster, short-lived leaf certificates issued automatically, workload identities rather than IP addresses in certificates, and a tested plan for rotating the root before it expires, which means distributing the new root to every trust store long before the old one lapses.
prod:
How TLS takes systems down

  • Expired certificates. The classic self-inflicted outage: sudden, total, at a predictable minute. On 6 December 2018, an expired certificate embedded in versions of Ericsson's mobile core software shut down equipment at operators in 11 countries; in the UK alone, over 32 million O2 customers lost 4G data and texting for most of a day. Internal certificates, client certificates for mTLS and partner APIs, and certificates on appliances are the ones most often forgotten.
  • Incomplete chains. A renewed certificate deployed without its intermediate works in browsers and fails in curl, Java, Python and mobile SDKs with "unable to get local issuer certificate" or "PKIX path building failed".
  • Root and trust store changes. When Let's Encrypt's old DST Root CA X3 expired on 30 September 2021, clients with outdated trust stores or old TLS libraries (OpenSSL 1.0.2, old macOS and Android versions, embedded devices) could no longer validate sites using Let's Encrypt, even though the sites' certificates were fine. Outdated container base images and language bundles cause the same class of failure.
  • Clock skew. A device or VM with the wrong time sees valid certificates as "not yet valid" or "expired". Common after a machine sleeps for long periods or boots without network time.
  • Name mismatch. Moving a service behind a new hostname, or calling it by IP, without the name in the certificate's SAN list.
  • Hardening side effects. Disabling TLS 1.2 or old cipher suites breaks old clients and partners; test against real client traffic (your logs record negotiated versions and ciphers) before tightening.
  • mTLS rotation failures. The CA rotates its root or intermediate, but some services still trust only the old one, and calls between them fail with handshake errors.

A debugging order

When a TLS connection fails: reproduce with openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host from the failing client's network to see the chain actually served and the verify result; compare with the same command from a working network (an inspection proxy or a different load balancer may be answering); check the client's clock; identify which trust store the failing client uses; and only then look at versions and ciphers. Most incidents are resolved at the first or second step.

Observability

Inventory every certificate you depend on, public and private, including client certificates, and monitor expiry from the outside (a synthetic check that connects and reads the chain) as well as from the issuing system, because "renewed" is not the same as "deployed". Alert at 30, 14 and 7 days. Log negotiated TLS version, cipher and handshake errors at load balancers; a rise in handshake failures after a change is the fastest signal. Subscribe to Certificate Transparency monitoring for your domains to catch unexpected issuance. For debugging, openssl s_client shows exactly what a server sends; curl -v shows how a client validated it; online checkers such as SSL Labs grade public endpoints.

Knobs

Minimum TLS version (1.2 or 1.3); cipher suite and key-exchange group preferences (including hybrid post-quantum groups); certificate key type (ECDSA, optionally with RSA fallback); full chain configuration; OCSP stapling where still used; session ticket key rotation; 0-RTT acceptance; HSTS (net2); CAA records; ACME renewal timing (renew at about two-thirds of the lifetime); and, for mTLS, certificate lifetimes, trusted CA bundles and authorisation policies.
myths: The padlock means the website is trustworthy.

It means your connection is encrypted and you are talking to the holder of a certificate for that exact domain name. Phishing sites get valid certificates for their own look-alike domains in minutes. TLS authenticates the name, not the honesty of whoever owns it.
The certificate is what encrypts my data.

The certificate carries the server's public key and is used only to prove identity, by the server signing the handshake. The data is encrypted with symmetric session keys that both sides derive from an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange and throw away after the connection.
TLS hides everything about my traffic.

It hides content, paths, headers and cookies. It does not hide the IP addresses, the timing and sizes of messages, or, unless Encrypted Client Hello is used, the hostname in the SNI field. In TLS 1.2 the server's certificate was also visible; TLS 1.3 encrypts it.
Traffic inside our private network doesn't need TLS.

Attackers who get a foothold inside, misconfigured cloud networks, shared infrastructure and insider risk all make 'inside' a weak boundary. Zero-trust designs encrypt and authenticate every service-to-service call, typically with automatically managed mTLS.
Revocation means a compromised certificate stops working immediately.

Browsers mostly soft-fail revocation checks and many clients never check at all, and Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in 2025 in favour of CRLs. The practical defence is short certificate lifetimes, which is why the industry is moving to 47-day certificates by 2029.
A self-signed certificate is just as secure as a CA-issued one.

The encryption is the same, but authentication only works if clients already trust that exact certificate or its private CA. Otherwise clients either reject it or users are trained to click through warnings, which is exactly what a man-in-the-middle needs. Private CAs are the right tool for internal services.
lab:
Twenty-five minutes with openssl and curl (Linux, macOS, WSL or Git Bash on Windows). You will read a real chain, see each class of certificate error, and build a tiny private CA with working mutual TLS.

  1. Read a real chain. openssl s_client -connect www.wikipedia.org:443 -servername www.wikipedia.org -showcerts </dev/null. Look for: the "Certificate chain" list (0 s: the leaf, 1 s: the intermediate, each with i: its issuer), "Verify return code: 0 (ok)", and in newer OpenSSL versions the negotiated protocol and group. Pipe the output into openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName to see the leaf's names and dates.
  2. See each failure. Run curl -sv -o /dev/null against https://expired.badssl.com, https://wrong.host.badssl.com, https://untrusted-root.badssl.com and https://incomplete-chain.badssl.com. Look for: "certificate has expired", "no alternative certificate subject name matches", "self-signed certificate in certificate chain" and "unable to get local issuer certificate". Open the incomplete-chain one in a browser too; it may well load, which is exactly the production trap.
  3. Check TLS versions. curl -sv --tlsv1.3 --tls-max 1.3 https://www.wikipedia.org -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i 'SSL connection'. Look for: "TLSv1.3" and the cipher, such as TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.
  4. Search Certificate Transparency. Open https://crt.sh/?q=wikipedia.org. Look for: every certificate issued for the domain, with issuers and dates. This is what monitoring for mis-issuance looks at.
  5. Build a private CA and mTLS (in an empty directory; on Git Bash run export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 first): 
    openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \
  -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt -days 30 -subj "/CN=Lab CA"
openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \
  -keyout srv.key -out srv.csr -subj "/CN=localhost"
printf "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost\n" > srv.ext
openssl x509 -req -in srv.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out srv.crt -days 7 -extfile srv.ext
openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \
  -keyout cli.key -out cli.csr -subj "/CN=client-a"
openssl x509 -req -in cli.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out cli.crt -days 7
openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert srv.crt -key srv.key \
  -CAfile ca.crt -Verify 1 -www
    In a second terminal, in the same directory: (a) curl https://localhost:8443/ fails: curl does not trust your CA. (b) curl --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/ fails differently: the server requires a client certificate. (c) curl --cacert ca.crt --cert cli.crt --key cli.key https://localhost:8443/ succeeds and prints the server's status page. What it proves: trust comes from the CA file you give the client, the hostname must be in the SAN you put in srv.ext, and in mTLS the server rejects callers without a certificate from its trusted CA.
  6. Stretch. Reissue the server certificate without the -extfile line and retry (c): it fails on the hostname, because there is no SAN. Then inspect cli.crt with openssl x509 -in cli.crt -noout -text and find the subject that a service mesh would turn into an identity.
recap: TLS protects data in transit against an attacker on the network path with three properties: confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server, and optionally of the client.
Asymmetric cryptography authenticates (signatures) and agrees keys (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman); fast symmetric authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM protects the bulk data.
Ephemeral key exchange gives forward secrecy: stealing the server's long-term key later cannot decrypt recorded sessions; TLS 1.3 makes it mandatory.
The TLS 1.3 handshake takes one round trip: ClientHello with key share, SNI and ALPN; then ServerHello, the encrypted certificate, a CertificateVerify signature and Finished.
A certificate binds a public key to names in its Subject Alternative Name list and is signed by a CA; clients validate the chain up to a root in their trust store, the dates and the hostname.
Servers must send the full chain of intermediates; a missing intermediate works in some browsers but fails in API clients.
CAs verify domain control automatically through ACME; certificate lifetimes are shrinking to 200 days in 2026, 100 in 2027 and 47 in 2029, so renewal must be automated and monitored.
Certificate Transparency logs make every public certificate visible, and CAA records limit which CAs may issue; revocation via CRL or OCSP is weak in practice.
Where TLS terminates decides where plaintext exists: at the edge, re-encrypted to backends, or passed through to the application.
Mutual TLS makes the client present a certificate too, giving cryptographic workload identity for service-to-service calls, usually with short-lived certificates issued by a mesh or private CA.
glossary: 0-RTT early data
Application data sent in the first flight of a resumed TLS 1.3 connection; faster but replayable.
ACME
The protocol CAs such as Let's Encrypt use to verify domain control and issue certificates automatically.
AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data)
Encryption that also detects tampering, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305; the only kind TLS 1.3 allows.
AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305
The two AEAD ciphers TLS 1.3 uses for bulk data: AES-GCM is fastest with CPU AES instructions, ChaCha20-Poly1305 on devices without them.
ALPN
The TLS extension that negotiates the application protocol, such as h2 or http/1.1.
Asymmetric cryptography
Cryptography with a key pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key only the owner holds.
CA (certificate authority)
An organisation that verifies identity or domain control and signs certificates that clients trust.
CAA record
A DNS record listing which CAs may issue certificates for a domain.
Certificate (X.509)
A signed document binding a public key to names, with validity dates, issuer and usage constraints.
Certificate pinning
A client accepting only specific certificates or public keys for a server, beyond normal chain validation.
Certificate Transparency (CT)
Public append-only logs of issued certificates, which browsers require, so mis-issued certificates can be spotted.
CertificateVerify
The handshake message where the server (or client) signs the handshake transcript with its private key, proving it holds the key.
Chain of trust
The sequence leaf certificate, intermediate CA, root CA, each signed by the next, ending at a root the client already trusts.
Cipher suite
The set of algorithms a connection uses; in TLS 1.3 it names the AEAD cipher and hash, e.g. TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.
ClientHello / ServerHello
The first handshake messages, in which each side offers or chooses versions, algorithms and key shares.
CRL (certificate revocation list)
A CA-published list of certificates revoked before expiry.
Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE, X25519)
A key exchange that lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel; ephemeral means fresh keys per connection.
ECDSA / RSA
The two common signature algorithms for certificates; ECDSA keys and signatures are smaller and cheaper for servers than RSA.
ECH (Encrypted Client Hello)
A TLS extension (RFC 9849) that encrypts the ClientHello, including SNI, using a key published in DNS.
Forward secrecy
The property that compromising a long-term private key later does not expose previously recorded sessions.
HSM (hardware security module)
A tamper-resistant device that stores private keys and performs signing without ever revealing the key.
Intermediate CA
A CA certificate signed by a root, used to sign leaf certificates so the root key can stay offline.
KMS (key management service)
A cloud service that stores keys in HSMs and performs cryptographic operations on your behalf.
Leaf certificate
The end-entity certificate for the server (or client) itself.
ML-KEM
A post-quantum key encapsulation algorithm standardised as FIPS 203, combined with X25519 in hybrid TLS key exchange.
mTLS (mutual TLS)
TLS where the client also presents a certificate and proves its private key, so both sides are authenticated.
NIST / FIPS
The US standards institute and its Federal Information Processing Standards series, e.g. FIPS 203 for ML-KEM.
OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol)
A way to ask a CA whether one certificate is revoked; OCSP stapling lets the server attach a signed answer.
PKI (public key infrastructure)
The whole system of CAs, certificates, trust stores, issuance and revocation.
PKIX path building failed
Java's error when it cannot build a certificate chain from the server's certificate to a root in its trust store.
Private key
The secret half of a key pair; whoever holds it can sign as, or decrypt for, the certificate's identity.
Root CA
A self-signed CA certificate shipped in operating system and browser trust stores.
SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
The certificate field listing the names it is valid for; clients match the hostname against it.
Session resumption
Reusing secrets from an earlier connection (a pre-shared key or ticket) to skip the certificate exchange.
SNI (Server Name Indication)
The hostname a client puts in the ClientHello so a server hosting many sites can pick the right certificate.
SPIFFE
A standard for workload identities such as spiffe://example.org/ns/prod/sa/payments, carried in mTLS certificates.
Symmetric cryptography
Encryption where both sides use the same secret key; fast, used for bulk data.
TLS termination
The point where TLS is decrypted, such as a load balancer, proxy or the application itself.
Trust store
The set of root CA certificates a client trusts: the operating system's, the browser's, Java's cacerts or Python's certifi bundle.
WAF (web application firewall)
A layer-7 filter in front of web apps that blocks malicious requests; needs TLS terminated to see them. Covered in net14.
Wildcard certificate
A certificate for *.example.com, valid for exactly one extra label such as a.example.com, but not example.com or a.b.example.com.
drill:
Debug it

After renewing the certificate for api.example.com, browsers work fine, but a partner's Java service and curl on a Linux server fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate". The mobile app, which pins the old certificate's public key, also breaks. What happened, how do you confirm it, and how should pinning be done?

Answer
  • Missing intermediate: the server was configured with only the leaf certificate, not the full chain. Browsers often cope, because they cache intermediates or fetch them using the certificate's Authority Information Access URL; curl, Java and most API clients do not, so they cannot build a path to a trusted root.
  • Confirm: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -showcerts shows only one certificate in the chain and "verify error:num=20: unable to get local issuer certificate". Online checkers such as SSL Labs report "chain incomplete".
  • Fix: install the full chain (leaf followed by intermediates, often the fullchain.pem file from the ACME client), reload, and add a synthetic check that validates the chain with a strict client, plus expiry alerts.
  • Pinning: the app pinned the leaf key, and renewal generated a new key, so the pin no longer matches. If pinning is required, pin the public keys of the intermediate or root CA, or several keys including a pre-generated backup key that renewals will use, and ship a remotely updatable pin set with a kill switch. Many teams now avoid pinning and rely on Certificate Transparency monitoring instead.
Design it

You run 40 microservices on Kubernetes in two clusters. Security asks that every service-to-service call be encrypted and that each service can only be called by the services that need it. Outline the design.

Answer
  • Identity: give each workload an identity from its namespace and service account, expressed as a SPIFFE ID, rather than relying on IP addresses, which change constantly.
  • Certificates: a mesh or SPIRE CA per cluster, with intermediates chaining to a shared root kept in an HSM or cloud KMS, so the two clusters trust each other. Issue short-lived workload certificates (for example 24 hours) and rotate them automatically.
  • Transport: sidecar or node proxies perform mTLS on every call, in strict mode (plaintext rejected), so application code needs no changes.
  • Authorisation: policies keyed on caller identity, such as "checkout may call payments on POST /charges", default deny, managed as code with review.
  • Operations: monitor certificate issuance and expiry, handshake failures and policy denials; plan and rehearse root and intermediate rotation (trust both old and new during overlap); decide how ingress traffic is authenticated at the edge and propagated inward.
qa: E
What does TLS protect, and what doesn't it hide?

It provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication for data in transit against someone on the network path. It does not hide the IP addresses communicating, the timing and volume of traffic, or, without Encrypted Client Hello, the hostname sent in SNI. It also does nothing for data at rest or for a compromised endpoint.

Follow-up: What does integrity add beyond encryption? — Detection of tampering: without it an attacker could flip bits in ciphertext to change the plaintext predictably; AEAD ciphers make any modification fail verification.
E
Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake at a high level.

The client sends a ClientHello with supported versions and cipher suites, a Diffie-Hellman key share, SNI and ALPN. The server replies with a ServerHello containing its key share; both sides now derive handshake keys, and the rest is encrypted: the server's certificate, a CertificateVerify signature over the handshake, and Finished. The client validates the certificate and signature, sends its Finished, and application data flows, all in one round trip.
Follow-up: What happens if the client guessed the wrong key-exchange group? — The server sends a HelloRetryRequest naming a group it supports, costing one extra round trip.
E
What is a certificate, and what does a client check when it receives one?

An X.509 certificate binds a public key to names, listed in the Subject Alternative Name field, and is signed by a certificate authority. The client checks that the chain of signatures leads to a root in its trust store, that every certificate is within its validity dates, that the hostname matches a SAN entry, that the key usage allows TLS server authentication, and, where it checks at all, that the certificate is not revoked.
Follow-up: Does *.example.com cover example.com and a.b.example.com? — No; a wildcard covers exactly one label, so a.example.com only.
M
What is forward secrecy and how does TLS 1.3 achieve it?

Forward secrecy means compromising a server's long-term private key later does not allow decrypting previously recorded sessions. TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange, so each session's keys come from temporary key pairs that are discarded; the long-term key is only used to sign the handshake. Old TLS RSA key exchange encrypted the session secret with the server's long-term key, so stealing that key decrypted every recorded session.
Follow-up: Can session tickets weaken forward secrecy? — Yes: if the ticket-encryption key is long-lived and stolen, resumed sessions can be decrypted, so ticket keys must rotate frequently.
M
What is mTLS and where is it used?

Mutual TLS authenticates both sides with certificates: the server requests a client certificate, and the client sends one and signs the handshake with its private key. It is used for service-to-service identity in zero-trust networks and service meshes, for B2B and partner APIs, and for device fleets, usually with short-lived, automatically rotated certificates.
Follow-up: Does mTLS decide what a caller may do? — No, it proves who the caller is; an authorisation policy must then map that identity to permissions.
M
Browsers accept a new certificate but curl and Java clients fail with 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Why?

The server is sending only the leaf certificate, not the intermediate that signed it. Browsers often cope because they cache intermediates or fetch them using the certificate's Authority Information Access URL, but most API clients only use what the server sends plus their trust store, so they cannot build a chain to a trusted root. Configure the server with the full chain (leaf then intermediates).
Follow-up: How do you confirm it? — openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -showcerts shows how many certificates the server sends and reports the verify error.
M
How does a CA verify that you control a domain before issuing a certificate?

With ACME, the CA gives the client a token and asks it to prove control through one of three challenges: serve the token at a well-known HTTP path on the domain (HTTP-01), publish it in a DNS TXT record under _acme-challenge (DNS-01), or present it in a special TLS handshake on port 443 (TLS-ALPN-01). DNS-01 is needed for wildcard certificates and works for hosts not reachable from the internet.

Follow-up: What stops an attacker who controls the network path to the CA? — CAs validate from multiple network vantage points, so a hijack must fool several paths at once, and CAA records and CT monitoring add further checks.
M
Where should TLS be terminated in a web architecture?

Commonly at the edge or load balancer, which centralises certificates, enables layer-7 routing and a WAF, and offloads crypto. Behind it, traffic should be re-encrypted to backends if the network is not fully trusted, which is increasingly the default. TLS passthrough to the application keeps end-to-end encryption but means the balancer works at layer 4 only and cannot inspect or route by HTTP.
Follow-up: Why does it matter where plaintext exists? — Every place that decrypts is a place data can leak or be logged, and it must hold a private key worth protecting.
M
What are Certificate Transparency and CAA, and how do they help?

Certificate Transparency requires CAs to log every publicly trusted certificate in public, append-only logs, and browsers reject certificates without proof of logging, so anyone, including you, can monitor for certificates issued for your domains. CAA is a DNS record naming which CAs may issue for your domain, which compliant CAs must check before issuing. Together they make mis-issuance both harder and detectable.
Follow-up: What would you do with CT in practice? — Subscribe to a CT monitoring service for your domains and alert on any certificate you did not request.
M
Why are certificate lifetimes getting shorter, and what does that mean for operations?

Revocation does not work reliably, so the only sure way to limit damage from a compromised or mis-issued certificate is to make it expire soon. The CA/Browser Forum voted in 2025 to cut maximum lifetimes from 398 days to 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from March 2027 and 47 days from March 2029. Manual renewal becomes impossible at that pace, so issuance and deployment must be automated with ACME and every endpoint's expiry monitored.

Follow-up: What else has to be automated besides issuance? — Distributing the new certificate to every load balancer, proxy and server, reloading them without downtime, and alerting when any of that fails.
H
How does a service mesh implement mTLS and workload identity?

Each workload gets a sidecar or node proxy and an identity, often a SPIFFE ID derived from its Kubernetes namespace and service account. A mesh CA issues short-lived certificates (hours to a day) carrying that ID, delivered and rotated automatically. Proxies on both ends perform mTLS, verifying each other's certificates against the mesh CA, and then enforce authorisation policies such as 'only the checkout service may call payments'. Applications speak plain HTTP to their local proxy.

Follow-up: What happens if the mesh CA is down? — Existing certificates keep working until they expire, so short lifetimes trade blast radius for dependency on CA availability; CAs are run highly available with intermediates per cluster.
H
Explain the post-quantum transition in TLS and its operational impact.

A future quantum computer could break today's elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, so traffic recorded now could be decrypted later ('harvest now, decrypt later'). Browsers and CDNs therefore deploy hybrid key exchange, X25519 combined with ML-KEM (standardised as FIPS 203 in 2024), which stays secure if either algorithm holds. The operational catch is size: the ML-KEM key share adds over a kilobyte, so the ClientHello no longer fits in one packet, which has broken some middleboxes and servers that assumed it would.

Follow-up: Are certificates post-quantum too? — Not yet broadly; signatures are harder because post-quantum signatures and chains are much larger, and authentication only needs to resist attacks at connection time, so key exchange was prioritised.
H
What is certificate pinning, and why do many teams avoid it now?

Pinning makes a client accept only specific public keys for a server, defending against a CA mis-issuing a certificate. But pins are brittle: pinning the leaf key breaks the app whenever the key rotates, and a mistake can brick clients that cannot be updated. Browsers dropped HTTP-based pinning. If needed in a mobile app, pin CA or intermediate keys plus a pre-generated backup key, and make the pin set remotely updatable; many teams rely on CT monitoring instead.
Follow-up: How does corporate TLS inspection interact with pinning? — Inspection proxies re-sign traffic with a company CA, so pinned apps refuse the connection; enterprises must exempt them.
H
Let's Encrypt's old root expired in September 2021 and some clients broke. What happened and what is the general lesson?

Let's Encrypt's certificates chained to the DST Root CA X3 root, which expired on 30 September 2021; newer clients trusted Let's Encrypt's own ISRG Root X1 and built a valid chain to it, but older clients, such as old OpenSSL versions and devices with outdated trust stores, either did not have the new root or tried the expired path and failed. The general lesson is that trust stores are part of your dependency graph: old devices, container images and language runtimes carry their own root lists, and root changes must be tested against the oldest clients you support.

Follow-up: Where do trust stores hide in a typical backend? — The OS package (ca-certificates), Java's cacerts, Python's certifi, Node's bundled roots, and base container images, each updated on its own schedule.

t: Load balancers, reverse proxies and forward proxies
sum: Forward versus reverse proxies, L4 versus L7 load balancing, balancing algorithms and consistent hashing, health checks and draining, client identity behind proxies, timeouts, buffering and streaming, and the failure modes that make proxies a favourite source of 502s.
prereq: net1
L4 devices see addresses and ports; L7 devices read HTTP; a device can only act on what its layer shows it.
net4
TCP connections, keep-alive, idle timeouts and the reset race that turns a closed idle connection into a 502.
net7
Idempotent methods may be retried safely; 502, 503 and 504 are usually generated by proxies; X-Forwarded-For carries the client IP.
net8
HTTP/2 and gRPC multiplex many requests over one long-lived connection.
why:
A single server can only handle so much. When a service outgrows one machine, you run several copies, and suddenly you need something to decide which copy each request goes to. That something also needs to notice when a copy dies and stop sending it traffic, let you deploy new versions without dropping requests, terminate TLS in one place, and protect the servers from abusive or merely slow clients. That something is a load balancer, usually built from a reverse proxy.

Proxies sit on nearly every request you will ever serve: a CDN edge, a cloud load balancer, an ingress controller, a service-mesh sidecar, an API gateway, often several of them in a row. Because every request passes through them, their behaviour becomes your application's behaviour, whether you configured it or not. A proxy's timeout decides when a slow request becomes a 504. Its idle timeout, set against your server's, decides whether you see random 502s. Its buffering decides whether an LLM's streamed tokens appear one by one or all at the end. Its retries decide whether a timeout becomes a duplicate payment. Its health check decides whether a database hiccup takes down one server or all of them.

There is also a proxy facing the other way. A forward proxy sits between your clients and the outside world: the corporate proxy your laptop uses, or the egress proxy through which your services call third-party APIs. It controls and records what leaves your network.

This lesson builds from the idea of a proxy to the practice of load balancing: the two directions of proxying, the difference between layer-4 and layer-7 balancing, the algorithms for choosing a backend and when each wins, health checks and draining, how the real client's address survives the trip, and the timeouts, buffering and retries that account for so many production incidents. It connects directly to the system design interviews in which "put a load balancer in front" is only the start of the answer.
primer:
A proxy is a middleman that makes its own connections

A proxy receives a request from one side and makes its own request to the other side, passing the answer back. The two sides each talk only to the proxy. That position lets it inspect, change, route, cache, block or record traffic. What distinguishes the two main kinds is whom the proxy works for.

The analogy: a restaurant host

A load balancer is like the host at a busy restaurant. Guests do not walk to a table themselves; the host greets them at the door (the single public address), checks which waiters are available and not overwhelmed (health and load), and seats each party with one of them (routing). When a waiter goes on break, the host stops seating guests in their section but lets current diners finish (draining). A sophisticated host looks at each party and seats large groups with the experienced waiter (layer-7 routing on request details); a simple one just rotates through sections in order (round robin).

Where the analogy breaks: a restaurant host never makes guests wait while they go into the kitchen themselves, but a layer-7 proxy does exactly that. It opens its own separate connection to the server, so every timeout, buffer and retry it has becomes part of your request's path.

Why every service needs one

Three reasons, each worth saying in an interview. Scale: one address for clients, many servers behind it, and you add servers without clients noticing. Availability: when a server dies, the balancer stops sending it traffic, so the service survives. Change: you can deploy new versions, drain old ones and shift traffic gradually, all behind a stable address. On top of those, the reverse proxy doing the balancing is the natural place for TLS termination (net9), request routing, rate limiting, compression, caching and a web application firewall (net14), which is why it is almost always there even for a single server.

A request's path, concretely

A request to https://api.example.com/orders in a typical cloud setup: DNS returns the load balancer's address; the client's TCP and TLS handshakes complete with the balancer, not the application; the balancer reads Host and path, picks one of the healthy instances of the orders service, and forwards the request over a connection it already has open to that instance, adding X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto; the response comes back the same way. The application never sees the client's TCP connection at all.

The key questions any load balancer answers

  • At which layer does it decide? Per TCP connection using addresses and ports (L4), or per HTTP request using host, path and headers (L7).
  • How does it choose? Round robin, least busy, random pairs, or a hash that keeps related requests together.
  • How does it know a server is healthy? Probes on an interval, and watching real failures.
  • How does it change servers safely? Draining before removal, gradual ramp-up after adding.
  • What does it change about the request? Source address, headers, timeouts, buffering, retries.

The body answers them in that order.
body:
1. L4 and L7: what happens to the connection

An L4 load balancer works with TCP or UDP connections and never parses the application protocol. When a new connection arrives, it picks a backend and from then on forwards that connection's packets to it. There are three common ways to do the forwarding. In NAT mode, it rewrites the destination address to the backend's (like the DNAT in net3) and replies return through it. In a full TCP proxy mode it terminates the client's TCP connection and opens a second one to the backend, relaying bytes between them. In direct server return (DSR), it forwards the incoming packets but the backend replies straight to the client, which suits download-heavy traffic because the heavy direction bypasses the balancer. L4 is fast, cheap, works for any TCP or UDP protocol (databases, MQTT, gRPC, raw TLS), and can pass TLS through untouched. Its limit: it decides once per connection and knows nothing about requests.

An L7 load balancer is a reverse proxy that speaks HTTP. It terminates the client's connection (and usually TLS), parses each request, chooses a backend per request, and sends it over its own, separate connection from a pool it keeps to each backend:

Because the L7 proxy owns both connections, it can route by host, path or header (/api/ to one service, /static/ to another), retry a failed request on a different backend, reuse warm backend connections so backends never pay handshakes, and absorb slow clients: it reads a slow upload fully before forwarding it, so the application server's worker is busy for milliseconds rather than minutes. The costs are CPU for parsing and TLS, and the fact that it must terminate TLS to see anything.

Real deployments stack them: an anycast or DNS layer chooses a region (net12), an L4 tier spreads connections across a fleet of L7 proxies, and the L7 proxies route requests to services, which may themselves have mesh sidecars doing L7 balancing between services.

2. Choosing a backend: the algorithms

  • Round robin: each new connection or request goes to the next backend in turn. Simple and fair when requests are similar and servers identical.
  • Weighted round robin: backends get shares proportional to weights, for mixed server sizes or for sending 5% of traffic to a canary.
  • Least connections: pick the backend with the fewest open connections. Better when connections last different amounts of time.
  • Least outstanding requests: pick the backend with the fewest requests currently in progress. The right default for HTTP when request durations vary a lot.
  • Power of two choices (P2C): pick two backends at random, send to the less loaded. Explained in the deep section; the default in Envoy's least-request balancer.
  • Hashing: hash some key, such as the client IP, a user ID, a cookie or a URL, to choose the backend, so the same key always lands on the same backend. Used for caches and affinity; consistent hashing (below) keeps the mapping stable as backends change.

A worked example shows why the choice matters. Three backends, each able to process 4 requests at once. Requests arrive in a repeating pattern: one 10-second report, then two 50 ms page loads. With round robin, every third request goes to backend A, and every one of those happens to be a report, so A fills up with reports and queues, while B and C sit nearly idle serving quick pages. Least outstanding requests notices that A has 4 requests in progress and B has 0, and sends new work to B and C until A frees up. The difference in tail latency can be enormous. The same logic is why LLM inference gateways balance on queue depth: one request can take 100 ms and the next 60 seconds.

3. Consistent hashing

Suppose each backend caches data for the keys it serves. With plain hashing, backend = hash(key) mod N. Add a fourth backend, and N changes from 3 to 4: about three-quarters of all keys now map to a different backend, and every cache is suddenly cold. Consistent hashing fixes this:

Each backend is placed at many points on the ring (virtual nodes, often 100 or more per backend) so that each owns many small arcs rather than one big one, which evens out the load. Production systems add a load bound: if the chosen backend is already above, say, 125% of the average load, the key spills to the next one clockwise ("consistent hashing with bounded loads"), so a hot key cannot melt one server. Consistent hashing is used by L4 fleets to keep connections stable (Maglev), by caches and CDNs, and increasingly by LLM gateways to route requests sharing a prompt prefix to the server that already holds it.

Sticky sessions are a cruder form of affinity: the balancer sets a cookie naming the backend, or hashes the client IP, so a user keeps hitting the same server. They are sometimes necessary for legacy apps that keep sessions in memory, but they make load uneven and lose state whenever that server restarts. Prefer shared session stores or stateless tokens, and treat affinity as an optimisation.

4. Health checks

An active health check is a probe the balancer sends to each backend on an interval, such as GET /healthz expecting 200. Thresholds prevent flapping: a backend is marked unhealthy after several consecutive failures and healthy again after several successes. Put numbers on it: with AWS Application Load Balancer defaults (30-second interval, 5-second timeout, unhealthy after 2 failures, healthy after 5 successes), a crashed backend may keep receiving traffic for up to about a minute, and a recovered one waits over two minutes to return. Shorter intervals detect faster but multiply probe traffic across big fleets.

A passive health check, or outlier detection, watches real traffic instead: if a backend returns five 5xx errors in a row, or its error rate stands out from its peers, eject it for a while. Passive checks react in seconds and catch problems probes miss; the two are combined.

What the health endpoint checks is a design decision. Kubernetes distinguishes liveness (is the process alive, or should it be restarted?) from readiness (should it receive traffic right now?). A readiness check should test what this instance controls: it has finished starting, loaded its model or cache, and is not overloaded. It should not fail just because a shared dependency like the database is slow, because then every instance fails at once. Balancers anticipate that failure: when all targets are unhealthy, an AWS ALB fails open and sends traffic to all of them, and Envoy ignores health status once fewer than 50% of hosts are healthy (its panic threshold). Both bet that a total failure is more likely a bad health check than a truly dead fleet.

5. Draining and deploys

Removing a backend abruptly fails every request in progress on it. Connection draining (AWS calls it the deregistration delay, 300 seconds by default) stops new requests to the backend while letting in-flight requests finish, up to a limit. A clean shutdown sequence for an instance is: fail readiness or deregister; wait until the balancer has stopped sending new requests (at least one health-check interval, plus any propagation delay in service discovery); let in-flight requests finish; close idle keep-alive connections, or for HTTP/2 send GOAWAY; then exit. Kubernetes handles part of this with a pre-stop hook and a termination grace period, and a common bug is exiting immediately on SIGTERM before endpoints have been updated everywhere.

New instances need the opposite care. Many runtimes are slow when cold (JIT compilation, empty caches, lazy model loading), so a new instance that receives its full share immediately gives terrible latency. Balancers offer slow start: ramp a new backend's share up over a minute or two.

6. Who is the client? Addresses and schemes behind proxies

An L7 proxy opens its own connection to the backend, so the backend sees the proxy's IP address as the source. The original client's address is passed in a header. The traditional one is X-Forwarded-For: each proxy appends the address it received the request from, giving a list like X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, 198.51.100.20. The standard Forwarded header carries the same information in a structured form. X-Forwarded-Proto: https tells the backend the original request was HTTPS, so it builds correct redirect URLs and marks cookies Secure; without it, apps behind TLS-terminating proxies generate http:// links and redirect loops.

The security rule: a client can send its own X-Forwarded-For header with any value, and proxies append to it rather than replace it. So the leftmost entries are untrustworthy. The real client is the address added by your outermost trusted proxy: count trusted proxies from the right. Frameworks have a setting for this (Express's trust proxy, Django and Flask proxy-fix middleware), and getting it wrong breaks rate limiting, geolocation and audit logs, or lets attackers spoof their IP.

An L4 balancer cannot add headers, because it does not parse HTTP. It either preserves the client's source address (NAT and DSR modes can) or prepends a PROXY protocol header, a single line such as PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.7 10.0.1.5 51514 443, at the start of the TCP stream, which the backend must be configured to expect.

7. Timeouts and keep-alives across hops

Every hop in a chain like client → CDN → load balancer → proxy → application → database has its own timeouts: how long to wait to connect, how long to wait for a response, and how long to keep an idle connection open. Two rules keep them consistent.

Request timeouts should shrink as you go deeper. If the load balancer gives up after 30 seconds but the application waits 60 seconds for the database, the balancer returns 504 while the application keeps working for another 30 seconds on a response nobody will receive, and if the client retries, the work doubles. Each layer's deadline should be shorter than its caller's, ideally with the remaining deadline propagated downstream.

Idle timeouts should grow as you go deeper. A backend must keep idle keep-alive connections open longer than the proxy in front of it, so the proxy always closes them first. If the backend closes first, the proxy can send a request on a connection at the exact moment it is being closed, receive a reset, and return a 502 that never appears in the application's logs (the race from net4). AWS documents exactly this for its load balancers; the fix is typically a backend idle timeout a few seconds longer than the balancer's (60 seconds by default for an Application Load Balancer; 350 seconds for a Network Load Balancer's TCP flows).

Long-running work, such as report exports or batch inference, should not hold an HTTP request open past these limits at all: accept the job, return 202 Accepted with a job ID, and let the client poll or receive a callback.

8. Buffering, limits and streaming

Reverse proxies usually buffer: they read the whole upstream response (up to some size) as fast as the backend can send it, freeing the backend's worker, then feed it to the client at the client's pace. They also read request bodies before forwarding. That protects application servers from slow clients, including deliberate slowloris attacks that trickle bytes to hold connections open. But buffering breaks streaming. A server-sent events endpoint or an LLM API streaming tokens will appear frozen, then dump everything at the end, because the proxy is holding the stream. The fix is to disable buffering for those routes (in nginx, proxy_buffering off or the X-Accel-Buffering: no response header), avoid response compression that waits for large blocks, and raise idle timeouts or send periodic heartbeat comments, since a model may think for tens of seconds before the first token.

Proxies also enforce limits that surface as mysterious errors: nginx rejects request bodies over 1 MB by default with a 413 error (client_max_body_size), and header size limits produce 400 or 431 errors when cookies grow too big.

9. Forward proxies in production

Forward proxies are not only a corporate IT thing. Many production platforms route all outbound traffic from services through an egress proxy. It enforces an allow-list of external destinations, which limits where stolen credentials or a compromised service can send data. It gives partners a small set of stable source IPs to allow-list. It centralises outbound credentials and TLS settings for third-party APIs. And it defends against SSRF (server-side request forgery), where an attacker tricks a service into fetching an internal URL such as the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254. For HTTPS destinations, clients use the CONNECT method to ask the proxy for a tunnel; TLS then runs end to end through it, so the proxy sees the destination host and port but not the content, unless it performs TLS inspection (net9).
deep:
Why power of two choices works

With many load balancers, each tracking only the requests it sent, "least connections" has a herding problem: every balancer sees the same backend as currently least loaded and sends its next request there, so that backend is flooded, then all switch to the next. Pure random choice avoids herding but occasionally piles requests onto an unlucky backend; with n backends the busiest one's excess load grows roughly like log n / log log n. Mitzenmacher's analysis showed that sampling just two random backends and picking the less loaded drops that to about log log n, an exponential improvement, while needing only local, slightly stale information. It is cheap, robust to staleness and works with any load signal (outstanding requests, latency, queue depth), which is why Envoy, Linkerd and many L4 fleets use it.

Keeping the load balancer itself available

A load balancer is itself a single point of failure unless it is a fleet. Large L4 fleets announce the same virtual IP from many machines using BGP; routers spread packets across them with ECMP (net3), and a machine that fails simply stops announcing. The catch: after the fleet changes, packets of an existing connection may hash to a different balancer machine, which must forward them to the same backend as before. Google's Maglev solves this with a consistent hashing scheme designed for minimal disruption plus a local connection-tracking table; GitHub's GLB Director uses a stateless two-tier design so any director can forward any packet correctly. For smaller setups, pairs of balancers share a floating IP with a protocol like VRRP, or you use a managed cloud balancer that hides all of this.

Retries, budgets and hedging at the proxy

Proxies are an attractive place to retry because they see failures first and can pick a different backend. They are also where retry storms start. When backends are overloaded, each failed request retried twice triples the offered load, exactly when capacity is lowest; with retries at the client, the gateway and the mesh, attempts multiply. Good proxy retry policy: retry only idempotent requests or ones with idempotency keys (net7); retry only on failures that mean "never processed" (connection refused, reset before response, 503 from a draining instance), not on timeouts of heavy work; use one or two attempts with jittered backoff; and enforce a retry budget such as "retries may add at most 20% to traffic", after which failures pass through. A related technique, hedging, sends a second copy of a slow idempotent request to another backend after, say, the p95 latency, and takes whichever answers first, trading a little extra load for much better tail latency.

Zone awareness and the cost of crossing zones

Cloud regions have several availability zones, and traffic between zones adds latency (typically under 2 ms) and usually costs money per gigabyte. A balancer that spreads every request evenly across all zones sends two-thirds of traffic cross-zone in a three-zone setup. Zone-aware routing prefers backends in the caller's zone while enough healthy capacity exists there, spilling over only when needed. The trade-off is resilience and balance: if one zone has fewer healthy backends, strict locality overloads them. Most meshes implement a middle ground that keeps traffic local unless the local zone falls below a capacity threshold.

Load balancing without a balancer: client-side and DNS

A central balancer is not the only design. In client-side load balancing, each client gets the list of backend addresses from service discovery (DNS returning all instances, or a registry) and chooses itself, with its own health tracking. gRPC supports this natively, and it removes a hop and a bottleneck, at the cost of logic in every client and slower reaction to changes. At the other extreme, DNS-based balancing (net6) spreads clients across regions or data centres with coarse, cached decisions. Large systems use all three: DNS or anycast to pick a region, a central L4 and L7 tier at the edge, and client-side or mesh balancing between internal services.

Dynamic configuration and its risks

Modern proxies are configured by control planes rather than static files: Envoy receives routes, clusters and endpoints through its xDS APIs, and Kubernetes ingress controllers regenerate configuration as services change. That enables instant endpoint updates and gradual traffic shifts, but it also means a bad configuration reaches every proxy within seconds. Proxy and CDN configuration pushes are a leading cause of large outages (the Fastly incident in net2 was triggered by a customer configuration change). The defences are the same as for code: validation before push, staged rollout to a fraction of proxies, automatic rollback on error-rate increases, and the ability to fall back to last known good configuration.
