t: Network security: segmentation, firewalls, DDoS and zero trust
sum: Defence in depth for networked systems: threat models, firewalls and cloud security groups, segmentation and least privilege, egress control and SSRF, WAFs, DDoS by layer and rate limiting, and the move from perimeter security to zero trust.
prereq: net3
VPCs, public and private subnets, route tables, NAT gateways and network ACLs; stateful devices track connections.
net9
TLS encrypts and authenticates connections; mTLS gives workloads cryptographic identities.
net10
Reverse proxies terminate connections, route by request, rate-limit and hide backends; forward proxies control egress.
net12
CDNs absorb traffic with anycast and run WAFs at the edge; origins must accept only CDN traffic.
why:
Every earlier lesson in this track described how to make traffic flow. This one is about stopping the traffic that should not. The two goals pull against each other: every open port, route, peering link and API is a convenience for your systems and an opportunity for an attacker. Network security is the discipline of keeping the first while shrinking the second.

The stakes are concrete. In 2019 an attacker tricked a misconfigured firewall at Capital One into fetching credentials from the cloud's internal metadata service and used them to copy data on more than 100 million people. Databases left reachable from the internet are found by automated scanners within minutes of being exposed. Denial-of-service attacks now peak in the tens of terabits per second, far more than any single company's links could carry. And security controls themselves can cause outages: a single bad firewall rule at Cloudflare in 2019 consumed nearly all the CPU serving HTTP traffic across its network and dropped about 80% of its traffic for 27 minutes.

For backend, platform and AI engineers, network security shows up in design reviews and interviews as a set of recurring questions. Which subnets should this service live in? Who can reach the database, and how is that expressed? How do engineers get into production? What stops a compromised service from sending data anywhere? What happens when someone floods the login endpoint? What does "zero trust" actually mean, beyond the marketing? Each has a principled answer.

This lesson starts from threat modelling and the idea of defence in depth, then works through the controls layer by layer: firewalls and cloud security groups, segmentation and least privilege, administrative access, egress control and server-side request forgery, web application firewalls, denial-of-service attacks and rate limiting, and finally the shift from perimeter security to zero trust. The production section covers how these fail and how teams keep secure designs secure as systems change.
primer:
Start with a threat model

Security decisions only make sense against a threat model: what are you protecting (customer data, credentials, availability), from whom (opportunistic internet scanners, targeted criminals, a malicious insider, a compromised dependency), and by which paths could they get in? You will never block everything, so the goal is to make the likely attacks hard, make the damage of a successful one small, and make attacks visible.

A useful default assumption is assume breach: design as if some component will be compromised, and ask how far an attacker could go from there. That question, "what is the blast radius?", drives most of the controls in this lesson.

The analogy: a well-run office building, and where it fails

A traditional office protects itself with a perimeter: a front door with a guard, and once you are inside with a badge, you can walk into most rooms. That is perimeter security, and it has a known failure: anyone who gets past the door, by tailgating or with a stolen badge, can wander everywhere. A better-run building also locks the server room, the finance office and the records room separately, checks badges at each, logs who entered, and gives each person access only to the rooms they need. That is defence in depth and least privilege. The most modern version, zero trust, stops treating "inside the building" as meaningful at all: every door checks who you are, whether your device is healthy and whether you should be there right now.

Where the analogy breaks: in networks, attackers can try millions of doors per second from anywhere in the world, automatically, so defaults matter far more than in a building: anything left open will be found.

Three kinds of attacker you plan for

It helps to name the adversaries, because they behave differently. Opportunistic scanners sweep the entire IPv4 internet continuously looking for open ports, default passwords and known vulnerabilities; they find anything exposed within minutes and are defeated mostly by not exposing things. Targeted attackers study your organisation, phish your staff and chain small weaknesses together; they are slowed by defence in depth and caught by detection. Denial-of-service attackers do not want in at all; they want you offline, and are handled by capacity, filtering and design. A fourth, increasingly important category is compromised dependencies: a library or vendor you trust that turns malicious, which is why egress control and least privilege matter even for code you did not write.

The layers

The rest of the lesson works from the outside in, with one theme throughout: express access by identity (which service, which person) wherever possible, rather than by IP address, because identities are stable and meaningful while addresses change constantly in cloud and container environments.
body:
1. Firewalls: stateless and stateful

A firewall allows or blocks traffic according to rules about source and destination addresses, ports and protocol. The important distinction is state. A stateless firewall judges every packet on its own. To let a server make an outbound HTTPS call, it needs a rule allowing packets out to port 443 and a rule allowing the replies back in, which arrive at the client's ephemeral port (1024 to 65535), so stateless rules end up broader than intended. A stateful firewall tracks connections: once it has allowed an outbound connection, it automatically allows that connection's replies and nothing else. Almost all modern firewalls, including cloud security groups, are stateful; network ACLs are the main stateless exception.

Two principles govern rule design. Default deny: block everything, then allow what is needed, rather than allowing everything and blocking known-bad. And least privilege: each allowed path should be as narrow as possible in source, destination and port.

2. Cloud building blocks

In a cloud VPC (net3), the controls map onto these ideas:

  • Public subnets have a route to the internet gateway. Only components that must be reached from the internet belong there: load balancers, NAT gateways, perhaps a CDN-facing proxy.
  • Private subnets hold application servers and databases. They have no inbound route from the internet at all; outbound traffic goes through a NAT gateway (or nowhere).
  • Security groups are stateful, allow-only firewalls attached to each instance or network interface. Their most useful feature is that a rule can reference another security group instead of an IP range: "the database security group allows port 5432 from the app security group". Any instance in the app group can connect, however many there are and whatever their addresses, and nothing else can.
  • Network ACLs are stateless, ordered allow and deny rules on whole subnets. Because they are stateless, allowing outbound calls requires allowing inbound replies on ephemeral ports. Teams use them as a coarse second layer, for example to deny a known-bad address range across a subnet.
  • Private connectivity: VPC endpoints (or PrivateLink) let workloads reach cloud services such as object storage, or a partner's service, without crossing the internet; peering and transit gateways connect VPCs privately.

3. Segmentation and least privilege

Segmentation means dividing systems into zones with only the necessary paths between them, so that one compromise does not grant access to everything (limiting lateral movement). Common boundaries: production separate from staging and development (ideally separate accounts, not just subnets), tiers separated (edge, application, data), and sensitive systems such as payments or personal data isolated further. Within Kubernetes, pods can talk to any other pod by default; a NetworkPolicy in each namespace that denies everything by default, followed by specific allows selected by pod labels ("pods labelled app=api may receive from pods labelled app=frontend on port 8080"), brings the same discipline inside the cluster. Policies only work if the cluster's network plugin enforces them, such as Calico or Cilium.

The trend is toward microsegmentation by identity rather than by subnet: rules that say "the checkout service may call the payments service" enforced by security-group references, NetworkPolicy labels, or a service mesh's mTLS identities (net9). Identity-based rules keep working as workloads move and scale, where IP-based rules rot.

4. Administrative access

How engineers reach production is one of the most attacked paths. The anti-patterns are SSH or database ports open to 0.0.0.0/0 (scanned and attacked within minutes), IP allow-lists for offices or home connections (brittle, and they authenticate a location, not a person), and shared keys or passwords (no accountability, impossible to revoke for one person). Modern practice: no inbound administrative ports at all. Engineers authenticate with single sign-on and multi-factor authentication to a session manager (such as AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or Google's Identity-Aware Proxy for TCP) that opens an audited session to a specific instance, or port-forwards to a database, using the engineer's own identity and short-lived credentials. Access to production data can require just-in-time approval, and every session is logged.

A useful test for any access path is to ask three questions: who can use it (a named person, a service identity, or anyone who can reach an address), how that is verified (strong authentication or network location), and whether its use is recorded. Paths that fail all three, such as a shared key to an open port, are the ones attackers find first.

5. Egress control and SSRF

Teams guard inbound traffic carefully and often leave outbound wide open. Yet most attacks need to reach out: malware downloading tools or contacting its command server, stolen data being sent away (exfiltration), or a server being tricked into making requests. Egress control restricts which destinations workloads may reach: an egress proxy or firewall with an allow-list of required external domains (net10), DNS filtering, and private endpoints for cloud services so that most traffic never needs the internet.

SSRF (server-side request forgery) is the network attack most specific to cloud applications. Any feature that fetches a URL supplied by a user, such as a webhook, an image importer, a "fetch this link preview" or an LLM tool that browses, can be pointed at internal addresses. The most valuable target is the cloud instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which hands out temporary credentials for the instance's role to anything on the instance that asks. That is how the Capital One breach worked in 2019: an attacker abused a misconfigured web application firewall to make requests to the metadata service, obtained credentials for its role, which could read far more storage buckets than it needed, and copied the data. Defences, in layers: validate and restrict outbound URLs in code (resolve the hostname and reject private, loopback and link-local addresses, and re-check after redirects); route user-directed fetches through an egress proxy that enforces the same rules; enforce IMDSv2, which requires a session token obtained with a PUT request carrying a special header, something a simple SSRF cannot do; and give every role the least privilege it needs, so stolen credentials are worth little.

6. Web application firewalls

A WAF is a layer-7 filter, usually at the CDN or load balancer, that inspects HTTP requests. It applies managed rule sets that detect common attack patterns, such as SQL injection strings and script injection, often organised around the OWASP Top 10 list of common web vulnerabilities; custom rules (block this path, require this header); rate limits; and bot management. Its strengths are speed and central control: when a new vulnerability is announced, a WAF rule can block exploitation across all applications within minutes, a virtual patch while code is fixed. Its limits are equally important: attackers find encodings and variants that rules miss, rules produce false positives that block real users, business-logic abuse (such as scraping prices or trying stolen passwords slowly) looks like normal traffic, and a WAF is software on the request path that can fail or be misconfigured, as both the Capital One breach and Cloudflare's 2019 outage show. New rules should run in count-only mode first and be rolled out in stages.

7. Denial of service, by layer

A DDoS attack tries to make a service unavailable by overwhelming some resource. Attacks fall into three families, each needing a different defence:

TypeWhat it exhaustsExamplesDefence
Volumetric (L3/L4)link bandwidthUDP floods, reflection and amplification via DNS, NTP, memcached (net5)networks bigger than the attack: anycast CDNs, cloud shields, scrubbing centres
Protocolstate tables, CPU of middleboxes and serversSYN floods, connection floods, fragment attacks, HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (net8)SYN cookies, connection limits, stateless edge filtering, patched software
Application (L7)application CPU, database, downstream APIsfloods of search, login or checkout requests; slowlorisrate limits, caching, bot detection and challenges, cheap or authenticated expensive endpoints

Volumetric attacks have grown enormously: Cloudflare reported successive records through 2025, ending with a 31.4 Tbps attack lasting just 35 seconds. No company's own internet links can absorb that; the only defence is a provider whose anycast network spreads the attack across hundreds of locations and filters it there (net12), with an origin that cannot be reached any other way. Application-layer attacks are the opposite: modest bandwidth, requests that look legitimate, aimed at your most expensive operations. They are defended in your own design: rate limiting, commonly with a token bucket per client or key (a bucket holds up to B tokens, refills at R per second, and each request spends one, so short bursts are allowed but the average is capped); caching so repeated requests are cheap; requiring authentication or a challenge for expensive endpoints; and autoscaling with limits, so an attack costs money but does not melt shared dependencies such as the database.

8. Encryption in transit, inside the network too

Older designs encrypted traffic from users to the edge and left internal traffic in plaintext, on the theory that the internal network was trusted. That assumption fails in shared cloud networks, where you do not control the physical path, and in any breach, where an attacker inside can read internal traffic, including credentials and tokens. The modern default is to encrypt everything: TLS to load balancers and re-encryption to backends (net9), TLS to databases and caches, and mTLS between services, usually automated by a service mesh so application teams do not manage certificates by hand. Encryption also carries identity, which is what makes the next idea possible.

9. From perimeter to zero trust

The traditional model trusts the internal network: anything on the corporate LAN or VPN is inside, and internal apps often accept any request from an internal address. That fails badly when an attacker gets one foothold, a phished laptop or a vulnerable server, because the inside is flat and trusting. Google's BeyondCorp work, published from 2014, described the alternative that became known as zero trust, later formalised by NIST in SP 800-207.

In practice zero trust means: staff reach internal applications through identity-aware proxies with single sign-on, multi-factor authentication and device posture checks, rather than a VPN that grants broad network access; services authenticate each other with mTLS and short-lived certificates and enforce authorisation policies per call (net9); credentials are short-lived and scoped; and every access is logged and evaluated continuously. Firewalls and segmentation remain, but as noise reduction and blast-radius limits, not as the thing that grants trust. VPNs still have roles, such as site-to-site links between networks.
deep:
Identity beats addresses

IP-based rules were natural when servers had fixed addresses for years. In clouds and Kubernetes, addresses are assigned and reassigned every few minutes, the same address may belong to a different workload tomorrow, and NAT hides the true source (net3). Rules written as IP ranges therefore drift towards being either too broad (a whole /16 allowed "to be safe") or broken. The durable alternatives all attach policy to identity: security-group references and tags in the cloud, pod labels and service accounts in Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, SPIFFE identities in mTLS certificates for a service mesh, and IAM roles for access to managed services. A senior design review question is always "what identity is this rule really about?"

Egress as a control point

Egress control is one of the highest-value, least-implemented controls. A default-deny egress posture, where each service declares the external domains it needs and everything else is blocked and logged, defeats a large class of attacks at once: malware cannot fetch payloads or reach its command server, exfiltration must go through a monitored path, and SSRF cannot reach arbitrary destinations. The implementation challenges are operational: domains resolve to changing IPs (so rules need an egress proxy or DNS-aware firewall, not IP lists), dependencies change, and developers need a fast, self-service way to request new destinations. DNS query logs are a cheap first step even before enforcement, because unusual lookups are an early indicator of compromise and of DNS-based exfiltration (net6).

Detection: assume the controls will fail

Preventive controls reduce risk; they never remove it. Mature teams therefore invest in detection: VPC flow logs to see which connections were accepted and rejected (a burst of rejected connections from inside is often an attacker scanning), DNS logs, load balancer and WAF logs, cloud control-plane audit logs (who changed a security group, who created an access key), and managed threat detection services that correlate these. What matters is triage: alerts routed to someone who can act, with runbooks, and regular exercises. The combination of "reduce blast radius" and "see it quickly" is what keeps a compromise small.

Policy as code

Most network exposures are self-inflicted: a temporary rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 that nobody removed, a storage bucket made public for a demo, a peering link added without review. Managing network configuration as infrastructure as code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests) makes every change reviewable, and policy as code tools (such as Open Policy Agent rules, cloud configuration rules or scanners in CI) automatically reject changes that violate standards, such as admin ports open to the world, databases in public subnets, or security groups without owners. Continuous scanning of the running environment catches drift from changes made outside the pipeline.

DDoS readiness as an engineering practice

DDoS resilience is decided before the attack. Know what your provider absorbs automatically and what needs configuration; make sure the origin cannot be reached except through the protected edge (net12); identify your most expensive endpoints and give them tighter rate limits, caching or authentication; prepare switches you can flip under attack, such as a stricter challenge mode, turning off costly features, or serving a static page; and practise them. Application-layer attacks often cause collateral damage through shared dependencies, so isolating the database and critical paths from expensive, attackable features matters as much as edge filtering.

Shared responsibility in the cloud

Cloud providers secure the physical network, the hypervisors and the managed services' internals; customers secure what they configure: which ports are open, which subnets are public, who holds which role, whether data is encrypted and which destinations workloads can reach. Nearly every well-known cloud breach has been on the customer side of that line, through misconfiguration rather than a provider flaw. That is why configuration review, policy as code and least-privilege roles carry so much weight in cloud security, and why "the cloud provider handles security" is a dangerous misunderstanding.

Security controls as availability risks

Firewalls, WAFs and proxies are inline on every request, so they are also availability risks. Cloudflare's July 2019 incident is the textbook case: a WAF rule with a regular expression prone to catastrophic backtracking was deployed globally at once and drove CPU on HTTP-serving machines to nearly 100%, causing about 80% traffic loss for 27 minutes; recovery was slowed because the team's internal tools also depended on the affected systems. The fixes Cloudflare described apply broadly: regular-expression engines with linear-time guarantees, per-rule CPU budgets, performance tests in CI, staged rollouts even for urgent security changes with the ability to accelerate them deliberately, and kill switches that work when everything else is broken.
prod:
Characteristic failures

  • Exposed management ports and databases: a security group with 0.0.0.0/0 on 22, 3389, 5432 or 6379, found by scanners within minutes. Detect with configuration scanning; prevent with policy as code.
  • Flat internal networks: a single compromised host can reach everything, turning a small incident into a breach. Segment by tier and sensitivity, default-deny inside clusters.
  • SSRF to metadata and internal services: URL-fetching features reaching 169.254.169.254 or internal admin endpoints. Enforce IMDSv2, validate destinations, route through an egress proxy.
  • Over-privileged roles: network controls hold, but a stolen credential can read everything. Least privilege for every role limits the value of any credential.
  • Origin bypass: attackers find the origin's address and go around the CDN's DDoS and WAF protections. Allow only CDN traffic at the origin.
  • Controls that break availability: a WAF rule blocking legitimate traffic or consuming CPU, a NetworkPolicy change that cuts a critical path, a firewall change that drops health checks. Stage and monitor security changes like any deploy.
  • Security groups nobody understands: hundreds of rules with no owners or descriptions; nobody dares remove any. Tag rules with owners and reasons, and review periodically.

War story: Capital One, 2019

An attacker exploited a server-side request forgery weakness in a misconfigured ModSecurity web application firewall running on an EC2 instance in Capital One's AWS environment. The firewall could be made to send requests to the instance metadata service, which returned temporary credentials for the IAM role attached to the instance. That role was allowed to list and read the contents of a large number of S3 buckets. The attacker used the credentials to download data from credit card applications affecting more than 100 million people in the US and around 6 million in Canada. Every layer contributed: an SSRF-able component, a metadata service that answered simple GET requests (AWS introduced IMDSv2 later that year), a role with far more privilege than a firewall needed, and no egress or anomaly control that stopped bulk downloads. It is the canonical example of why defence in depth, least privilege and egress control all matter.

A response checklist when you suspect a compromise

Contain first: isolate the affected instances by swapping their security groups for a quarantine group rather than deleting them, so evidence survives; revoke and rotate the credentials they could access; and block known attacker destinations at egress. Then investigate with flow logs, DNS logs and audit logs to find where the attacker went and what they touched, and only then rebuild from known-good images. Rehearsing this before an incident, including who is allowed to make which changes, is what makes the first hour calm instead of chaotic.

Observability

Flow logs (accepted and rejected), DNS query logs, WAF logs with rule hits, rate-limit counters, load balancer logs, and cloud audit logs of configuration changes. Dashboards of top rejected sources, unusual egress destinations and spikes in 4xx or 429 responses surface attacks and misconfigurations. Regular external scans of your own public address ranges show what the internet can see.

Knobs

Security group and NetworkPolicy rules; network ACLs; egress allow-lists and proxy rules; IMDSv2 enforcement and hop limit; WAF managed rule sets, custom rules and their modes (count or block); rate limits per endpoint and key; DDoS protection levels and challenge modes; session manager and identity-aware proxy policies; and the policy-as-code rules that gate every infrastructure change.
myths: Our servers are in a private network, so they are safe.

A private network stops unsolicited inbound connections from the internet, nothing more. Attackers get in through what you do expose (a web app with an injection bug, a phished laptop on the VPN, a compromised dependency) and then move sideways through a flat internal network. Segmentation, identity-based access and least privilege limit what one foothold can reach.
A WAF protects the application from vulnerabilities.

A WAF blocks known attack patterns and buys time, but attackers routinely find encodings and variants it misses, and it knows nothing about your business logic. The Capital One breach started by abusing a misconfigured WAF itself. Fix vulnerabilities in the code; treat the WAF as a filter and an emergency patch point.
Blocking inbound traffic is enough; outbound can be open.

Most attacks need outbound connections: malware calling home, stolen data leaving, SSRF reaching internal or third-party endpoints. Egress control, such as allow-lists, egress proxies and DNS filtering, is what stops a compromised service from sending data anywhere it likes.
DDoS protection is just about having more bandwidth.

Volumetric floods are absorbed by very large networks, but application-layer attacks use modest bandwidth and valid-looking requests aimed at expensive endpoints like search or login. Those need rate limits, caching, bot detection, challenges and making expensive work cheap or authenticated.
Zero trust means buying a zero-trust product.

Zero trust is an architecture principle: network location grants no trust, and every request is authenticated and authorised by identity, device and context. Products help implement parts of it, but it is achieved through identity-aware access for people, mTLS and authorisation policies for services, short-lived credentials and least privilege.
Security groups and network ACLs are interchangeable.

Security groups are stateful, attached to network interfaces and allow-only, so return traffic is automatic and rules can reference other groups. Network ACLs are stateless, apply to whole subnets and evaluate ordered allow and deny rules, so return traffic on ephemeral ports must be allowed explicitly. They are complementary layers.
lab:
Twenty minutes. You will audit what your own machine exposes, implement and flood a token-bucket rate limiter, and read a default-deny Kubernetes policy.

  1. What am I exposing? List listening sockets: ss -tlnp (Linux/WSL), lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P (macOS) or netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING (Windows). Look for: which services listen on 0.0.0.0 or [::] (all interfaces, reachable from your network) versus 127.0.0.1 (this machine only). Anything on all interfaces that you do not need is attack surface. If you have nmap, nmap -sT -p 1-10000 127.0.0.1 shows the same from the outside view.
  2. A token bucket. Save as bucket.py and run it: 
    import time
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, burst):
        self.rate, self.burst = rate, burst          # tokens/second, bucket size
        self.tokens, self.last = burst, time.monotonic()
    def allow(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

b = TokenBucket(rate=5, burst=10)          # 5 requests/s on average, bursts of 10
t0 = time.monotonic(); allowed = denied = 0
while time.monotonic() - t0 < 3:           # an attacker firing as fast as possible
    if b.allow(): allowed += 1
    else: denied += 1
print(f"allowed {allowed}, denied (would be 429) {denied}")
    Look for: about 25 allowed in 3 seconds (the 10-token burst plus 5 per second) and a huge number denied. Change burst to 1 and see bursts disappear; this is the trade-off between tolerating legitimate spikes and stopping floods. Real gateways keep one bucket per key or client, often in Redis so all instances share it.
  3. Read a real policy. This Kubernetes NetworkPolicy set denies all traffic in a namespace, then allows the frontend to call the API on one port: 
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: {}                 # every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]  # no rules listed = nothing allowed
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: frontend-to-api, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  ingress:
  - from: [ { podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: frontend } } } ]
    ports: [ { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 } ]
    Look for: rules expressed with labels, not IP addresses, and the consequence of denying egress too: the API pods now cannot even reach DNS or the database until you add egress rules for them. If you have a local cluster with an enforcing network plugin (for example kind with Calico), apply them and test with kubectl exec and curl.
  4. Check security headers. curl -sI https://github.com | grep -iE 'strict-transport|content-security|x-frame|x-content-type'. Look for: the HSTS, CSP and related headers from net7, which are the browser-side layer of defence in depth.
  5. If you use AWS: on an EC2 instance, curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ works only if IMDSv1 is allowed. With IMDSv2 enforced, you must first get a token: TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60') then pass -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN". What it proves: a simple SSRF that can only make GET requests cannot perform the PUT step.
recap: Network security starts from a threat model: what you protect, from whom, and how they could get in, and assumes some defence will eventually fail.
Defence in depth layers controls at the edge, the network boundary, each workload, service identity, the application and the data, so one failure does not expose everything.
Firewalls filter by addresses, ports and protocol; stateful firewalls and cloud security groups track connections so replies are allowed automatically, while network ACLs are stateless.
Segmentation splits systems into zones with only the necessary paths between them, preferably expressed by identity (security-group references, service identities) rather than IP ranges.
Administrative access should use identity-aware session managers or proxies with individual credentials and audit logs, not SSH or database ports open to the internet.
Egress control and protection of the cloud metadata endpoint (IMDSv2) limit exfiltration and server-side request forgery.
A WAF filters known attack patterns at layer 7 and is a mitigation layer, not a replacement for fixing application bugs.

DDoS attacks come as volumetric floods, protocol attacks and application-layer floods, each needing different defences: large anycast networks, SYN cookies and connection limits, and rate limiting, caching and bot management.
Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location: every request is authenticated and authorised using user, device and workload identity over encrypted connections.
Visibility, through flow logs, DNS logs and alerting, and policy as code are what keep a secure design secure as it changes.
glossary: Allow-list (deny by default)
Permitting only explicitly listed traffic and blocking everything else.
Bastion host
A hardened server exposed for administrators to log in through into a private network; increasingly replaced by session managers.
Blast radius
How much damage one compromised component can cause; segmentation and least privilege shrink it.
Bot management
Detecting and handling automated traffic, for example with behavioural signals, fingerprints and challenges.
CSP (Content-Security-Policy)
A response header restricting which scripts and resources a page may load, limiting cross-site scripting (net7).
DDoS (distributed denial of service)
Overwhelming a service with traffic from many sources so legitimate users cannot use it.
Defence in depth
Layering independent security controls so that the failure of one does not expose the system.
Egress control
Restricting which destinations workloads may connect to outbound.
Exfiltration
An attacker moving stolen data out of your environment.
Firewall
A device or software that allows or blocks traffic based on rules about addresses, ports, protocols and connection state.
Flow logs
Records of accepted and rejected network connections (addresses, ports, bytes), such as AWS VPC Flow Logs.
IAM (identity and access management)
The system that defines identities and what each may do, such as AWS IAM roles and policies.
Identity-aware proxy
A proxy that authenticates users and checks device and policy before forwarding requests to internal apps, replacing broad VPN access.
IMDS / IMDSv2
The cloud instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which hands out instance credentials; version 2 requires a session token obtained with a PUT request, defeating simple SSRF.
Lateral movement
An attacker who has compromised one system using it to reach others inside the network.
Least privilege
Giving each person, service and network path only the access it needs and nothing more.
Microsegmentation
Fine-grained segmentation down to individual workloads or services, often enforced by identity rather than subnet.
Network ACL
A stateless, ordered set of allow and deny rules applied to all traffic entering or leaving a subnet.
NetworkPolicy (Kubernetes)
A Kubernetes resource specifying which pods may talk to which, enforced by the cluster's network plugin.
OWASP Top 10
A widely used list of the most common web application security risks, published by the OWASP foundation.
Perimeter security
The model of trusting everything inside the network boundary and defending the boundary.
Policy as code
Expressing security rules in code checked automatically, such as blocking 0.0.0.0/0 on admin ports in infrastructure reviews.
Rate limiting
Capping how many requests a client, key or IP may make in a time window, often with a token bucket.
Reflection / amplification
Attacks that bounce spoofed requests off third-party servers whose larger replies hit the victim (net5).
Scrubbing centre
A facility that receives a victim's traffic during an attack, filters out attack packets and forwards the clean traffic.
Security group
A cloud provider's stateful, allow-only firewall attached to instances or network interfaces, able to reference other groups.
Session manager
A service that gives authenticated, audited shell or port-forwarding access to instances without open inbound ports, such as AWS SSM Session Manager.
Shared responsibility model
The split in cloud security between what the provider secures (infrastructure) and what the customer secures (configuration, identities, data).
SSM (AWS Systems Manager)
The AWS service whose Session Manager gives audited shell access to instances without open inbound ports.
SSRF (server-side request forgery)
Tricking a server into making requests of the attacker's choosing, often to internal addresses or the metadata service.
Stateful vs stateless firewall
A stateful firewall tracks connections and allows replies automatically; a stateless one judges each packet on its own.
SYN flood
An attack sending many connection openings without completing them, to exhaust a server's queue of half-open connections (net4).
Threat model
A structured description of what you protect, who might attack it, how, and which defences address each path.
Token bucket
A rate-limiting algorithm where a bucket refills at a steady rate and each request spends a token, allowing short bursts up to the bucket size.
VPN (virtual private network)
An encrypted tunnel that places a device or network onto another network; in perimeter models it grants broad internal access.
WAF (web application firewall)
A layer-7 filter that inspects HTTP requests for attack patterns such as SQL injection and applies custom rules and rate limits.
Zero trust
A security model in which no request is trusted because of its network location; each is authenticated and authorised by identity and context.
drill:
Review the design

A startup's AWS setup: all EC2 instances, including PostgreSQL, sit in public subnets with public IPs; the database security group allows 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 "because the office IP changes"; SSH (22) is open to the world; developers connect with a shared SSH key; the app calls external APIs directly. Redesign it and prioritise the fixes.

Answer
  1. Immediately: remove 5432 and 22 from 0.0.0.0/0; an internet-exposed database is scanned within minutes. Rotate the database credentials and the shared SSH key; check logs for unauthorised access.
  2. Network layout: a VPC with public subnets containing only the load balancer and NAT gateways; application instances and the database in private subnets without public IPs (ideally a managed database). The database security group allows 5432 only from the application's security group.
  3. Admin access: no SSH from the internet; use SSM Session Manager (no open ports, IAM-authenticated, audited) with individual identities; database access for developers through a session manager port-forward or an identity-aware proxy, not IP allow-lists.
  4. Egress: outbound traffic via the NAT gateway, restricted where practical (egress proxy or firewall allow-list of partner APIs); VPC endpoints for S3 and other AWS services; IMDSv2 enforced.
  5. Edge: CDN and WAF in front of the load balancer with rate limiting on login and expensive endpoints, and the load balancer accepting traffic only from the CDN.
  6. Visibility and governance: flow logs, CloudTrail and threat-detection alerting, and everything in infrastructure as code with policy checks so review catches the next "temporary" open port.
Design it

Your product adds an AI agent that can fetch arbitrary web pages the user mentions and summarise them. What network risks does this create, and how do you contain them?

Answer
  • Risk: a built-in SSRF engine. A user (or a prompt injected into a fetched page) can ask the agent to fetch http://169.254.169.254/, internal admin panels, databases' HTTP interfaces or other tenants' services, and the summary leaks the response.
  • Isolation: run the fetcher as a separate service in its own subnet or sandbox with no route to internal networks, no instance role credentials (or IMDS disabled or IMDSv2 with hop limit 1), and no access to other services.
  • Egress path: all fetches go through an egress proxy that resolves hostnames itself and blocks private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges, re-checks after every redirect, and limits ports, response sizes and timeouts.
  • Abuse limits: rate limits per user, caching of fetched pages, and blocking of known-bad destinations, so the feature cannot be used to attack third parties at scale.
  • Output handling: treat fetched content as untrusted data, not instructions, and log what was fetched for audit.
qa: E
What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL?

A security group is stateful and attached to instances or network interfaces, with allow rules only, so return traffic is automatically permitted and rules can reference other security groups. A network ACL is stateless and applies to a whole subnet, with ordered allow and deny rules, so return traffic on ephemeral ports must be allowed explicitly. Security groups are the primary control; ACLs are a coarse extra layer.

Follow-up: Why does a missing ACL rule for ephemeral ports break outbound calls? — The reply packets come back to a random high port, and a stateless ACL drops them unless ports 1024 to 65535 are allowed inbound.
E
What is defence in depth? Give an example for a web application.

Layering independent controls so one failure does not expose the system. For a web app: a CDN with DDoS protection and WAF at the edge; a load balancer as the only public entry; application servers in private subnets with security groups allowing only the load balancer; a database reachable only from the application's security group; mTLS and authorisation between services; input validation in code; encryption of data at rest; and flow logs and alerting throughout.
Follow-up: Which layer matters most? — None alone; the point is that an attacker must defeat several, and each layer catches mistakes in the others.
E
Why should databases and SSH never be open to 0.0.0.0/0?

The whole internet is scanned continuously, and new exposed database or SSH ports are found and attacked with credential stuffing, known exploits and brute force within minutes. Keep databases in private subnets reachable only from application security groups, and replace internet-facing SSH with session managers or identity-aware proxies that need no open inbound port and give per-person, audited access.

Follow-up: The office IP changes, so someone opened the port to everyone. What is the better fix? — Access through an identity-aware proxy or session manager, which authenticates people rather than IP addresses.
M
What does zero trust mean in practice?

Network location grants no trust: every request is authenticated and authorised using user and workload identity, device posture and policy, over encrypted connections, with least privilege and short-lived credentials. In practice staff reach internal apps through identity-aware proxies with single sign-on and device checks rather than a VPN that grants broad network access, and services call each other over mTLS with authorisation policies based on service identity.
Follow-up: Does zero trust mean no firewalls? — No, segmentation still reduces exposure and noise; it just stops being the thing that grants trust.
M
How do you defend against application-layer DDoS attacks?

Rate limit per client, key and endpoint; cache responses so repeated requests are cheap; use bot detection and challenges for suspicious traffic; apply WAF rules for obvious patterns; protect or require authentication for expensive endpoints like search, login and exports; autoscale within limits; and put the application behind a CDN or edge network that can absorb and filter traffic before it reaches the origin.

Follow-up: Why is rate limiting by IP alone weak? — Attackers spread requests over many IPs (botnets, residential proxies), and many legitimate users share IPs behind NAT, so combine IP with keys, sessions and behavioural signals.
M
What is SSRF, and how did it contribute to the Capital One breach?

Server-side request forgery tricks a server into making a request of the attacker's choosing, for example fetching http://169.254.169.254/, the cloud metadata endpoint, which returns temporary credentials for the instance's role. In 2019, an attacker abused a misconfigured web application firewall at Capital One to do exactly that, obtained credentials for an over-privileged IAM role, and copied data on over 100 million people from S3. Defences are validating and restricting outbound requests, IMDSv2, least-privilege roles and egress controls.

Follow-up: How does IMDSv2 help? — It requires a session token obtained with a PUT request carrying a special header, which simple SSRF through a GET-based fetch cannot do, and the token's hop limit stops it being relayed.
M
How would you segment a Kubernetes cluster's network?

Start with a default-deny NetworkPolicy in each namespace, then allow only the required flows, such as the frontend pods to the API pods on port 8080 and the API to the database, selected by labels rather than IPs. Separate environments into different clusters or at least namespaces with policies, restrict egress to known destinations, and add a service mesh with mTLS and authorisation policies for identity-based rules at layer 7.
Follow-up: What is needed for NetworkPolicies to do anything? — A network plugin that enforces them, such as Calico or Cilium; without one, policies are accepted but silently ignored.
M
What is a WAF good for, and what are its limits?

It inspects HTTP requests at the edge and blocks known attack patterns such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, enforces custom rules and rate limits, and can be updated within minutes as a virtual patch when a new vulnerability appears. Its limits: attackers find encodings and variants it misses, it causes false positives that block real users, it knows nothing about business logic abuse, and a misconfigured WAF can itself become an attack path.

Follow-up: How do you roll out new WAF rules safely? — In count or log-only mode first, measure what they would block, then enforce, and deploy in stages because a bad rule can break or slow everything.
M
Explain the three kinds of DDoS attack and how each is mitigated.

Volumetric attacks flood links with raw traffic, often reflected and amplified UDP, and are absorbed only by networks bigger than the attack, such as anycast CDNs and scrubbing centres. Protocol attacks exhaust state in servers or middleboxes, such as SYN floods, and are mitigated with SYN cookies, connection limits and stateless filtering at the edge. Application-layer attacks send valid-looking requests to expensive endpoints and need rate limiting, caching, bot detection and challenges.
Follow-up: How big do volumetric attacks get now? — Cloudflare reported records climbing through 2025 to 31.4 Tbps for a 35-second attack, far beyond any single organisation's own links.
M
Why is egress control important, and how do you implement it?

Because most attacks need to send data out or reach out: malware calling its command server, data being exfiltrated, SSRF reaching arbitrary hosts. Route outbound traffic through NAT gateways and an egress proxy or firewall with an allow-list of required destinations, use DNS filtering, use private endpoints for cloud services so that traffic never needs the internet, and alert on unusual outbound flows in flow logs.
Follow-up: What is the practical difficulty? — Maintaining the allow-list as services add dependencies; teams make it self-service with review, so it does not become a blocker that everyone bypasses.
H
Design network access for engineers to reach production systems securely.

No inbound SSH or database ports from the internet. Engineers authenticate with single sign-on and multi-factor authentication to an identity-aware proxy or a cloud session manager that grants time-limited, audited access to specific hosts or databases, ideally approved just in time for incidents. Access is logged and sessions recorded; credentials are short-lived and individual, never shared keys. Break-glass accounts exist, are alarmed and reviewed.
Follow-up: Why not a VPN? — A VPN typically puts the laptop on the network with broad reach, so one compromised laptop can scan and move laterally; per-application access limits the blast radius.
H
A WAF rule deployment took down a large CDN. How can a security control cause an outage, and how do you prevent it?

Security controls run inline on every request, so a bug in them is a global availability problem. In July 2019, Cloudflare deployed a WAF rule containing a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking; it pushed CPU on the machines serving HTTP to nearly 100% worldwide and caused about 80% traffic loss for 27 minutes. Prevention: engines that guarantee linear-time regular expressions, CPU budgets per rule, performance tests in CI, staged rollouts with automatic rollback, and a fast kill switch for the control.

Follow-up: What does it say about the trade-off between security speed and reliability? — Emergency security rules must deploy fast, so the deployment path needs guardrails that make fast also safe, rather than skipping stages.
H
Compare perimeter security with zero trust using a concrete attack.

A phishing email compromises an engineer's laptop. Under a perimeter model with a flat VPN, the laptop is 'inside', so the attacker can scan the internal network, reach admin panels that trust internal IPs, and pivot to databases. Under zero trust, each internal app requires the user's identity, a healthy managed device and policy approval on every request; services accept only authenticated service identities; so the stolen session gives access only to what that user is allowed, from that device, and anomalous access is flagged.
Follow-up: What remains hard in zero trust? — Legacy systems that cannot do modern authentication, keeping policies precise as systems change, and the operational weight of identity infrastructure.
H
How would you implement rate limiting for a public API across many gateway instances?

Use a token bucket or sliding window per key (API key, user or IP), with limits per endpoint class. With many gateway instances, either keep counters in a shared low-latency store such as Redis with atomic operations, accepting a network hop, or approximate with local buckets that each get a share of the limit, plus periodic synchronisation. Return 429 with Retry-After, keep separate stricter limits for login and expensive operations, and apply coarse limits at the CDN edge first so floods never reach the gateways.

Follow-up: Why a token bucket rather than a fixed window? — Fixed windows allow double bursts at window boundaries; a token bucket allows controlled bursts up to its size while enforcing the average rate.

sum: A systematic method for network problems: scoping, layer-by-layer checks, splitting latency into phases, the performance maths of RTT, bandwidth-delay product, loss and MTU, the toolkit from dig to tcpdump and eBPF, and debugging inside containers and Kubernetes.
prereq: net1
Debug bottom-up by layer; 'refused' means something answered with a reset, 'timed out' means nothing answered.
net2
A request's time splits into DNS, TCP, TLS, server time and transfer; each handshake costs a round trip.
net4
Throughput is limited to window divided by RTT; loss shrinks the congestion window; TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT and retransmissions show up in ss.
net6
Stub resolvers retry lost queries after a 5-second timeout; Kubernetes ndots multiplies lookups.
net10
Proxies generate 502, 503 and 504 and have their own timeouts, retries and logs.
why:
Sooner or later every engineer gets the message: "the service is slow", "it times out sometimes", "it works from my laptop but not from production", "the upload hangs at 99%". Network problems are frustrating because the symptom appears far from the cause, and because many components are involved: resolvers, load balancers, proxies, NATs, firewalls, TLS, the kernel's TCP stack, connection pools, and the application. It is tempting to guess, restart things, or blame "the network". Engineers who are good at this do something different: they narrow the problem down systematically, with measurements, until only one explanation fits.

This final lesson of the track pulls everything together into that skill. You already know the pieces: how DNS resolves (net6), how TCP behaves under loss and distance (net4), how TLS fails (net9), how proxies generate 502s and 504s (net10), how NAT and firewalls drop idle or unexpected traffic (net3, net14), and how pools and event loops behave (net13). Debugging is the art of asking the right question in the right order, choosing the tool that answers it, and knowing what a healthy answer looks like.

The second half is performance: the small amount of arithmetic that explains most network speed problems. Why a download between continents crawls on a fast link. Why 1% packet loss matters so much. Why a request that is fast in one region is slow in another. Why a VPN makes large requests hang while small ones work. These are standard interview questions, and each has a numerical answer.

This lesson covers a debugging method, how to split latency into phases, the performance fundamentals of RTT, bandwidth-delay product, loss and MTU, the command-line toolkit organised by the question each tool answers, how to debug inside containers and Kubernetes, and how to approach the hardest case: intermittent failures.
primer:
The method in one line

Scope it, then go layer by layer from the client's point of view, comparing a working case with a failing one, and measure instead of guessing. Everything else in this lesson is detail on that sentence.

The analogy: a doctor's diagnosis

A good doctor does not start by prescribing. They take a history (when did it start, what changed, who else is affected), examine systematically from the most basic vital signs upward, run the test that best separates the likely causes, and compare against what "normal" looks like. Network debugging is the same: scoping is the history, the layer-by-layer checks are the examination, a packet capture is the blood test, and baselines are "normal". Where the analogy breaks: you can usually reproduce a network problem on demand and test a hypothesis in seconds, so you should, rather than reasoning at length.

The decision path

Three habits that save hours

Reproduce from the right place. A request from your laptop takes a different path, resolver and set of firewall rules from a request made inside a production pod. Get a shell where the failing client runs, or as close to it as possible, before drawing conclusions.

Change one thing at a time, and write it down. Under pressure it is tempting to restart services, flush caches and tweak timeouts all at once. If the problem then disappears, you have learned nothing and it will return. Keep a running log of what you checked, what you saw and what you changed, with timestamps; it becomes the incident timeline for free.

Prefer tests that split the hypotheses in half. "Does it fail with the VPN off?" or "does it fail against a pod IP instead of the Service name?" each rule out half of the possible causes in one step. A good debugger is always asking which single test would eliminate the most explanations.

Before any tool: scope

Five questions narrow most problems before a single command runs. Who is affected: one user, one region, one client version, everyone? What exactly fails: every request, some requests, only large ones, only new connections? Since when, to the minute? What changed around then: deploys, configuration, DNS, certificates, firewall rules, provider incidents? And from where can you reproduce it? A problem that affects only one availability zone, starting at 14:02, right after a security-group change, has usually solved itself before you open a terminal.

Scoping also tells you who to involve and how urgent it is: a problem for one user on hotel Wi-Fi is a support ticket; a problem for every user in one region since a change ten minutes ago is an incident with an obvious first action, rolling that change back.

Then compare: a request that works against one that fails, a healthy host against a sick one, today against yesterday's baseline. Differences are evidence; similarities rule things out.
body:
1. Step by step with the right tool

Each step of the decision path has a tool that answers exactly its question, and a way of reading the answer.

Name resolution. dig +short api.example.com shows what the resolver returns; dig @8.8.8.8 api.example.com compares another resolver; dig +trace walks the delegation from the root (net6). But programs do not use dig; they use the system's resolver library, which also reads /etc/hosts and applies search domains. getent hosts api.example.com on Linux follows the same path most programs do, so when dig and the application disagree, getent usually explains why.

Reachability of the port. nc -vz host 443 (or Test-NetConnection host -Port 443 in PowerShell) attempts a TCP connection and reports success, "connection refused" or a timeout. Recall net1's distinction: refused means a host answered with a reset, so check whether the service is running and what address it is bound to (ss -ltnp on the server); timed out means nothing answered, so look at security groups, network ACLs, routes and whether the address is right. Flow logs show whether a firewall rejected the connection.

TLS. openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host shows the certificate chain the server actually sends, its dates and names, the negotiated protocol and the verification result (net9). Always pass -servername, or you may test the wrong certificate on a server that hosts several.

HTTP. curl -v https://host/path shows the request, the status line and the response headers. The first question for any 5xx is which component generated it: the server and via headers, the error page's style and the proxy's logs usually tell you whether a CDN, load balancer or the application answered (net10).

The wire. When the tools above disagree or the symptom is ambiguous, capture packets. sudo tcpdump -i any -nn host 10.0.1.5 and port 5432 -w cap.pcap records the conversation with one database, and Wireshark decodes it, flagging retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, zero windows and resets automatically. Captures answer the questions nothing else can: did the SYN arrive? Did the server answer? Who sent the reset? Did data stop in one direction?

2. Where does the time go?

For slowness, the most productive first step is splitting a request into phases. curl reports cumulative times at each milestone:

curl -s -o /dev/null https://api.example.com/v1/items -w \
 'dns %{time_namelookup}  tcp %{time_connect}  tls %{time_appconnect}  ttfb %{time_starttransfer}  total %{time_total}\n'

Subtract consecutive values to get each phase: TCP handshake = tcp − dns, TLS handshake = tls − tcp, server time plus one round trip = ttfb − tls, transfer = total − ttfb. Browsers show the same phases in DevTools' timing tab, and real-user monitoring collects them from every visitor (net2).

Interpreting the phases uses what you know about round trips. The TCP handshake phase should be about one RTT to the server; TLS 1.3 about one more. If they are each 200 ms, the user is far away or the path is poor, and the fix is proximity (a CDN edge or a nearer region) or fewer handshakes (connection reuse). If handshakes are small but time to first byte is large, the server or something behind it is slow: now switch to application tracing and logs. If DNS is large, look at resolvers; exactly five seconds means a lost query and a retry. If transfer dominates, the response is large relative to throughput, which the next sections explain.

3. Latency and bandwidth are different things

Latency is how long a bit takes to get there and back (RTT); bandwidth is how many bits per second the path can carry. They are independent: a satellite link can have high bandwidth and terrible latency; a local connection can have low latency and modest bandwidth. Small requests, such as API calls and page loads, are dominated by latency, because they consist of a few round trips each carrying little data. Large transfers are dominated by throughput, but only after TCP has ramped up, and throughput depends on latency too, as the next section shows. The practical rule: to make small things faster, remove round trips or shorten them; to make big things faster, make sure enough data is in flight.

A few reference numbers help intuition: within one data centre or availability zone, RTTs are well under a millisecond; between zones in a region, about 1 to 2 ms; across a continent, 30 to 80 ms; between continents, 100 to 300 ms. Light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so there is a hard floor on every long-distance RTT (net1).

4. The bandwidth-delay product

TCP can only have one window of unacknowledged data in flight per round trip (net4), so a single connection's throughput is at most window ÷ RTT. The bandwidth-delay product (BDP), bandwidth × RTT, is the window needed to keep a path full. Worked examples:

PathBandwidthRTTBDP (window needed)Throughput with a 64 KB window
Same zone10 Gbit/s0.2 ms250 KBabout 2.6 Gbit/s
Across a continent1 Gbit/s60 ms7.5 MBabout 8.7 Mbit/s
Singapore to Frankfurt1 Gbit/s160 ms20 MBabout 3.3 Mbit/s

Modern Linux grows windows automatically (window scaling plus buffer autotuning) up to limits set by net.ipv4.tcp_rmem and tcp_wmem, so a healthy connection on a clean path reaches much higher throughput than the last column. When it does not, the window is being capped: window scaling disabled or stripped by a middlebox, buffer maximums too small, or an application that sets SO_RCVBUF explicitly, which switches off autotuning. ss -ti on a live connection shows the numbers: rtt, cwnd, rcv_space, the window scale factors (wscale) and the delivery rate.

5. Loss and its cost

On long paths, loss is usually the limit, not windows. Every loss makes TCP's congestion control reduce its sending window (net4), and a lost final segment may wait for a retransmission timeout of at least 200 ms on Linux. The Mathis approximation says a loss-based TCP connection achieves roughly MSS ÷ (RTT × √loss). On a 100 ms path, 1% loss gives about 1,460 × 8 ÷ (0.1 × 0.1) ≈ 1.2 Mbit/s, and 0.01% loss about 12 Mbit/s: a hundredfold drop in loss gives only a tenfold rise in throughput, and both are far below a gigabit. For short requests the same losses show up as tail latency: a request that normally takes 20 ms sometimes takes 220 ms or more.

Where to see loss: retransmission counters (nstat -az TcpRetransSegs, ss -ti showing retrans), Wireshark's retransmission flags, and mtr for loss along a path. Where it comes from in practice: congested links, overflowing queues in middleboxes or on hosts, cloud per-instance packet-rate limits, and full connection-tracking tables. Its opposite, bufferbloat, is equally real: oversized buffers that avoid loss by queueing, so latency climbs to hundreds of milliseconds under load while loss stays near zero.

6. MTU problems

Every link has a maximum packet size, its MTU: 1,500 bytes on standard Ethernet, up to 9,001 bytes (jumbo frames) inside an AWS VPC, but traffic through an internet gateway, a VPN or between regions without a transit gateway is limited to 1,500. Tunnels, VPNs and overlay networks add headers, so the usable MTU inside them is smaller (VXLAN adds 50 bytes, net1). When a packet is too big for a link and marked "don't fragment", the router drops it and should send back an ICMP "fragmentation needed" (IPv6: "packet too big") message, so the sender can shrink its packets: that is Path MTU Discovery. If a firewall blocks those ICMP messages, the sender never learns, and full-size packets vanish: a PMTU black hole. The signature is unmistakable once you know it: connections open, small requests work, but large responses, uploads or TLS handshakes with big certificate chains hang and eventually time out.

To test by hand, ping with the don't-fragment flag and a payload that makes a 1,500-byte packet (1,472 bytes of data plus 20 bytes of IP header plus 8 of ICMP): ping -M do -s 1472 host on Linux, ping -D -s 1472 host on macOS, ping -f -l 1472 host on Windows. If that fails with "message too long" or silence while smaller sizes succeed, reduce the size until it works; that is the path MTU. Fixes: allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (and ICMPv6 type 2) through firewalls, clamp the TCP MSS on the tunnel so both ends send smaller segments, or lower the interface MTU.

7. The toolkit, organised by question

QuestionToolHealthy looks like
What does the name resolve to?dig, getent hostsexpected address, sensible TTL, fast query time
Is the port open?nc -vz, Test-NetConnection"succeeded" quickly
What is listening here?ss -ltnpservice on the right address and port
Is TLS right?openssl s_client"Verify return code: 0", correct names and dates
What does HTTP say, and how long did each phase take?curl -v, curl -wexpected status; phases consistent with RTT
What is the path, and where is loss?mtr, tracerouteloss 0% at the destination
How are my connections doing?ss -tan, ss -ti, nstatfew retransmissions, no CLOSE_WAIT growth
How fast can this path go?iperf3close to link speed within a zone
What exactly was exchanged?tcpdump, Wiresharkhandshakes complete, no resets or repeated retransmissions

Reading mtr needs care: routers answer its probes with low priority and rate limits, so a middle hop may show 30% "loss" while forwarding your traffic perfectly. Only loss that begins at some hop and continues all the way to the destination is real.

8. Debugging inside containers and Kubernetes

Every container and pod has its own network namespace: its own interfaces, routing table, DNS configuration and, in Kubernetes, its own NetworkPolicies. So "it works from my laptop" and even "it works from the node" say little about what the pod sees. Debug from inside: kubectl exec -it pod -- sh if the image has tools, or attach an ephemeral debug container with a toolbox image, such as kubectl debug -it pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app, which shares the pod's network namespace. From there, check DNS against the cluster resolver (watch for ndots expansion, net6), curl the Service name and then a pod IP directly (if the IP works and the name does not, look at the Service's selector and kubectl get endpoints), and test whether a NetworkPolicy blocks the path. Kubernetes adds its own failure modes: Services with no ready endpoints, readiness probes failing, kube-proxy or eBPF data-plane rules out of sync, and connection-tracking races.
deep:
Intermittent problems: correlate, then capture

The hardest network problems affect a small fraction of requests. The approach that works is statistical before it is technical: slice failures by every dimension you have, such as backend instance, availability zone, client host or version, time of day, request size, connection age, protocol version and source network, and look for the dimension where failures concentrate. Common fingerprints: one bad instance behind a load balancer (failures concentrate on one target), one zone with a faulty path (failures by zone), requests above a size threshold (MTU), connections idle longer than a NAT or balancer timeout (failures on first use after quiet periods, net3, net10), overloaded DNS (exact five-second delays), pool connections that died (errors on first query after a failover), and ECMP hashing onto a bad link, which looks random per request but is consistent per connection 4-tuple, so a retry on a new connection succeeds (net3). Only after narrowing does a packet capture become efficient, taken on both sides of the suspect hop.

The USE method for network resources

Brendan Gregg's USE method is a checklist: for every resource, check utilisation (how busy), saturation (how much work is queued) and errors. Applied to networking: interface utilisation against bandwidth and packet-rate limits (cloud instances have both, and small-packet workloads hit packets per second first); saturation as queue lengths, socket backlogs, drops and TCP retransmissions; errors as interface errors, conntrack "table full" messages, ICMP unreachables and resets. Doing this for NICs, NAT gateways, load balancers, conntrack tables, file descriptors and connection pools turns "the network is slow" into a short list of saturated resources.

eBPF observability

eBPF lets small verified programs run inside the Linux kernel at events such as TCP state changes, retransmissions, packet drops and socket calls, aggregating results cheaply. The bcc tools collection includes tcpretrans (every retransmission, with addresses and state), tcplife (every connection's duration and bytes, with process names), tcpconnect and tcpaccept, and tools that report the kernel's drop reasons. In Kubernetes, network plugins built on eBPF, such as Cilium with Hubble, show per-flow visibility including which policy dropped a packet. These answer many questions that previously needed full captures, with overhead low enough for production, and they attribute traffic to processes and pods rather than just addresses.

Connection tracking and cloud limits

Stateful components everywhere keep per-connection state: Linux's conntrack table (used by NAT, Docker and Kubernetes kube-proxy in iptables mode), cloud security groups, NAT gateways and load balancers. All have limits. When Linux's table fills, the kernel logs "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet" and new connections fail silently; cloud providers impose per-instance limits on tracked connections and packets per second, surfacing as allowance-exceeded metrics rather than errors. High connection churn, long timeouts for idle flows and UDP-heavy workloads fill these tables. Mitigations are raising limits, shortening timeouts for short-lived flows, reducing churn with connection reuse, and, for specific high-volume flows, disabling tracking where the design allows.

Baselines turn debugging into comparison

Most debugging time is spent establishing what "normal" is. Teams that record baselines, such as RTT distributions between zones and regions, throughput per instance type, typical retransmission rates, DNS resolution times and per-phase request latency percentiles, answer "is this abnormal?" in seconds. Synthetic probes that continuously measure key paths (client regions to edge, edge to origin, service to database) provide both the baseline and early warning. Baselines also feed capacity and placement decisions: knowing that a cross-region round trip is 70 ms tells you immediately that a chatty service calling a database in another region will be slow.

Reproducing network conditions on purpose

Many network bugs only appear under conditions that developers never see locally: 150 ms of latency, 2% loss, a 1,400-byte MTU, a connection dropped mid-request. Linux's tc netem can add delay, jitter, loss, duplication and reordering to any interface; browser DevTools can throttle latency and bandwidth; and fault-injection features in proxies and service meshes can add delays or abort a percentage of requests between services. Testing timeouts, retries and streaming code against these conditions before production is far cheaper than discovering their behaviour during an incident, and the lab uses exactly this technique.

Latency is a distribution

Averages hide the problems users feel. A page that makes 50 requests will almost certainly include at least one request at the p98 of your latency distribution, so tail latency is the user experience. Network effects concentrate in the tail: retransmission timeouts, DNS retries, cold connections paying handshakes, queueing behind large responses, and garbage collection pauses on either end. Measure and alert on p95 and p99 per phase, compare tails across hosts and zones, and treat a rising tail with a flat average as an early sign of loss or saturation.
prod:
Classic problems and their fingerprints

SymptomLikely causeConfirm with

"Cannot assign requested address"ephemeral port exhaustionTIME_WAIT counts per destination
