Worked incident: the upload that stalls at 99%

Users behind a new corporate VPN report that uploading files larger than about 1 MB to an internal service stalls near completion and times out, while browsing works. Scoping shows it affects only VPN users and only large uploads, starting the day the VPN was rolled out. The decision path passes steps 1 to 4 (names resolve, ports open, TLS works, small requests return 200). A capture on the client shows the TCP connection established, data flowing, then repeated retransmissions of 1,448-byte segments with no acknowledgements; a capture on the server shows none of those segments arriving. ping -M do -s 1472 through the VPN fails and -s 1400 succeeds: the tunnel's MTU is smaller than 1,500, and a firewall blocks the ICMP messages that would tell the client. Enabling MSS clamping on the VPN gateway fixes it within minutes. Total investigation time was short because the method went straight from scope ("large, VPN-only, since rollout") to the MTU hypothesis to a decisive test.

Worked incident: the slow region

After launching in Asia, users there see page loads three times slower than in the US. Real-user timings split by phase show DNS normal, TCP and TLS phases around 200 ms each, and time to first byte around 400 ms: the handshakes and requests are travelling to the US origin. The CDN had been configured only for static assets, so HTML and API calls went direct. Routing HTML and API traffic through the CDN (terminating TLS at Asian edges and forwarding over warm connections) and caching public API responses briefly cut the handshake phases to about 10 ms and time to first byte to about 220 ms (net12). The measurement took minutes; the diagnosis followed directly from the phase breakdown.

Knobs you will reach for

Timeouts (connect, read and idle) at every hop; keep-alive and connection reuse; socket buffer maximums and congestion control on long-haul senders; MTU and MSS clamping on tunnels; ICMP rules that allow Path MTU Discovery; conntrack limits and timeouts; resolver settings and node-local DNS caches; and synthetic probes and baselines that make "is this normal?" answerable.
myths: If ping works, the network is fine.

Ping tests ICMP reachability and round-trip time to one address. The TCP port can still be blocked, TLS can fail, large packets can be dropped by an MTU black hole, and the application can be slow. Conversely, many hosts block ICMP, so a failed ping proves little.
Loss shown at a middle hop in mtr means that router is dropping my traffic.

Routers answer the ICMP probes mtr sends with low priority and rate limits, so a hop can show loss while forwarding your traffic perfectly. Only loss that continues through every later hop to the destination indicates real loss on your path.
A faster link will fix slow transfers.

Long-distance transfers are usually limited by window size and round-trip time, or by packet loss, not by link speed. A single TCP connection with a 64 KB window across 160 ms gets about 3 Mbit/s on any link. Measure throughput against the bandwidth-delay product before buying bandwidth.
The network team can see the problem; application teams don't need packet captures.

Many network-looking problems live at the endpoints: a full accept queue, a pool of dead connections, a resolver timeout, a proxy's idle timeout. A capture taken on the client and the server, where the application runs, is often the only way to see which side stopped talking.
Intermittent failures are random and can't be debugged.

Intermittent problems nearly always correlate with something: one backend instance, one availability zone, one client version, a time of day, request size, or connection age. Slicing errors by those dimensions usually turns 'random' into 'always on host 7' or 'always after 350 seconds idle'.
Latency averages tell you how users experience the service.

Averages hide the slow tail where timeouts, retransmissions and queueing live. Users making many requests per page almost always hit the tail. Track p95, p99 and maximums, and break latency into phases so you know which part is slow.
lab:
Twenty-five minutes on Linux or WSL (some steps also work on macOS). You will add artificial latency and loss to your own machine and watch throughput, timings and TCP internals respond, then find a path MTU. Clean up with the commands given.

  1. Baseline. Install iperf3. In one terminal run iperf3 -s; in another, iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 5. Look for: tens of Gbit/s on loopback: no distance, no loss.
  2. Add distance. sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem delay 50ms (100 ms RTT, since both directions cross loopback). Run ping -c 3 127.0.0.1 to confirm about 100 ms, then iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 10. Look for: throughput ramping up over the first seconds (slow start) and settling far below the baseline. Now cap the window: iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 10 -w 64K. Look for: a few Mbit/s, in the region of 64 KB ÷ 0.1 s ≈ 5 Mbit/s (Linux adjusts requested buffer sizes, so expect roughly 5 to 10): the bandwidth-delay product limit, as the table predicts.
  3. Add loss. sudo tc qdisc change dev lo root netem delay 50ms loss 1% and run iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 10 again. Look for: a large further drop, and in the iperf3 output the Retr column counting retransmissions. While it runs, ss -ti dst 127.0.0.1 shows cwnd staying small and retrans climbing.
  4. Timings under distance. Still with the delay, start python3 -m http.server 8000 and run curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8000/ -w 'tcp %{time_connect} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n'. Look for: about 0.1 s to connect (one RTT) and about 0.2 s to first byte (one more RTT for the request): phases are multiples of RTT.
  5. Clean up: sudo tc qdisc del dev lo root. Rerun ping to confirm the delay is gone.
  6. Find your path MTU. ping -M do -s 1472 -c 2 8.8.8.8 (macOS: ping -D -s 1472 -c 2 8.8.8.8; Windows: ping -f -l 1472 8.8.8.8). Look for: replies if your path carries 1,500-byte packets. If you are on a VPN, try again with it on: you will probably need a smaller size such as 1,400, and "message too long" or silence at 1,472 shows the tunnel's overhead.
  7. Read a path. mtr -rwc 20 1.1.1.1 (install mtr). Look for: the destination's loss column (should be 0%), and any middle hops showing loss that does not continue to later hops: ICMP rate limiting, not real loss.
  8. Capture a timeout. sudo tcpdump -i any -nn host 10.255.255.1 in one terminal and curl --connect-timeout 20 http://10.255.255.1/ in another. Look for: the same SYN sent again and again with no reply: at one-second intervals at first on recent kernels, then with doubling gaps (older kernels double from the start: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s). That retry pattern is the signature of a silently dropped connection.
recap: Start every network investigation by scoping: who is affected, what exactly fails, since when, and what changed.
Work layer by layer from the client's point of view: name resolution, reachability of the port, TLS, then HTTP, and the first failing layer is where to look.
Compare a working case with a failing one; the difference between them is usually the answer.
Split slow requests into phases (DNS, connect, TLS, time to first byte, transfer) with curl -w or browser timings, and investigate the dominant phase.
Round-trip time sets the cost of every handshake and request; the bandwidth-delay product sets how large a window must be to fill a path.
Packet loss shrinks TCP's congestion window, so small loss rates on long paths cut throughput dramatically and inflate tail latency.
Mismatched MTUs with blocked ICMP create black holes where small exchanges work but large transfers hang; ping with the don't-fragment flag finds the limit.
The toolkit maps to questions: dig for names, nc for ports, openssl s_client for TLS, curl for HTTP and timings, mtr for paths, ss for socket states, tcpdump and Wireshark for the truth on the wire.
In containers and Kubernetes, debug from inside the workload's network namespace, because its DNS, routes and policies differ from your laptop's.
Intermittent problems are solved by correlation: slice failures by host, zone, client, time, size and connection age.
glossary: Bandwidth
The rate at which a link can carry data, e.g. 1 Gbit/s.
BDP (bandwidth-delay product)
Bandwidth times round-trip time: the amount of data that must be in flight to keep a path full.
Bufferbloat
Excessively large router buffers that turn congestion into long queueing delays instead of timely loss signals.
conntrack
Linux's connection-tracking table used by NAT and stateful firewalls; when full, new connections are dropped.
curl -w
curl's write-out option that prints timing and status variables for a request, such as time_connect and time_starttransfer.
eBPF
A Linux technology for running small, safe programs inside the kernel, used by low-overhead tracing tools such as tcpretrans and by network plugins such as Cilium.
ECMP (equal-cost multipath)
Spreading flows over several equal paths by hashing their addresses and ports, so one bad link affects only some connections (net3).
Ephemeral debug container
A temporary container attached to a running pod to run diagnostic tools in the pod's namespaces (kubectl debug).
Fault injection
Deliberately introducing delays, errors or dropped connections to test how a system behaves under failure.
ICMP
The IP control protocol used by ping, traceroute and Path MTU Discovery messages (net1).
iperf3
A tool that measures achievable throughput between two hosts.
Jitter
Variation in latency between packets or requests.
Latency
The time for data to travel, often measured as round-trip time.
MSS clamping
A router rewriting the maximum segment size in TCP handshakes so both ends send packets small enough for a tunnel.
mtr
A tool combining ping and traceroute that shows loss and latency per hop continuously.
MTU (maximum transmission unit)
The largest packet a link carries without fragmentation, 1,500 bytes on standard Ethernet.
Network namespace
A Linux mechanism giving a process its own network interfaces, routes and firewall rules; each container or pod has one.
Packet capture (pcap)
A recording of packets seen on an interface, taken with tcpdump or Wireshark and saved in pcap format.
Percentile (p95, p99)
The value below which that percentage of measurements fall; p99 latency is exceeded by only 1% of requests.
PMTU black hole
A path where oversized packets are dropped and the ICMP messages that would report it are blocked, so large transfers hang.
PMTUD (Path MTU Discovery)
How a sender learns the smallest MTU on a path, using ICMP 'fragmentation needed' or 'packet too big' messages.
Retransmission
TCP resending a segment it believes was lost; a rising retransmission rate signals loss on the path.
RTT (round-trip time)
The time for a packet to reach the destination and a reply to return.
ss
The Linux socket statistics tool, showing connections, states, queues and per-connection TCP internals.
tc netem
A Linux traffic-control module that adds delay, loss, duplication and reordering to an interface for testing.
tcpdump
A command-line packet capture tool with filters by host, port and protocol.
Throughput
The rate of useful data actually delivered, which may be far below bandwidth.
traceroute
A tool that reveals the routers on a path by sending packets with increasing TTL (net1).
TTFB (time to first byte)
The time from sending a request to receiving the first byte of the response; includes one RTT plus server processing.
USE method
Brendan Gregg's checklist: for every resource, check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors.
Wireshark
A graphical packet analyser that decodes protocols and flags TCP problems such as retransmissions and zero windows.
drill:
Diagnose from the data

A client in Singapore downloads large files from a server in Frankfurt (RTT 160 ms) over a 1 Gbps path, but gets only about 3 Mbps. ss -ti shows no retransmissions and a receive window stuck around 64 KB. Separately, after a VPN was introduced, some HTTPS requests to an internal service hang forever while others work; small API responses succeed, large ones never finish. Explain both and the fixes.

Answer

Download: throughput ≤ window ÷ RTT = 64 KB ÷ 0.16 s ≈ 400 KB/s ≈ 3.3 Mbps, exactly what is observed. The BDP is 1 Gbps × 0.16 s = 20 MB, so the window must be about 300 times larger. With no loss, the cause is a window cap: window scaling disabled (often by a middlebox stripping the option) or small socket buffers (the net.ipv4.tcp_rmem maximum, or the application setting SO_RCVBUF explicitly, which disables autotuning). Fix: enable window scaling, raise buffer maximums, let autotuning work; otherwise use parallel streams.

VPN hangs: a classic PMTU black hole. The VPN encapsulation reduces the effective MTU below 1,500; small packets fit, but full-size packets carrying large responses (or big TLS certificate chains) exceed it and are dropped. Path MTU Discovery would fix it, but the ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages are blocked, so the sender never learns and keeps retransmitting the same large packets. Confirm with ping -M do -s 1472 host failing versus smaller sizes succeeding, and tcpdump showing repeated retransmissions of full-sized segments. Fix: allow ICMP type 3 code 4, enable TCP MSS clamping on the VPN gateway, or lower the interface MTU.

Triage it

At 14:05 an on-call engineer sees p99 latency for the checkout API jump from 300 ms to 5.3 s, while p50 is unchanged and error rates are flat. Nothing was deployed. Where do you look first, and why?

Answer

A tail jump to almost exactly 5 seconds above normal, with a flat median and no errors, is the fingerprint of occasional lost DNS queries being retried after the resolver's 5-second timeout (net6). First, split the slow requests' time by phase (tracing spans or client DNS timing): if DNS dominates the slow ones, check the resolver (CoreDNS or the VPC resolver) for saturation, drops or rate limiting starting at 14:05, and check whether traffic or query volume rose (ndots expansion multiplies it). If DNS is normal, the next candidates for a clean +5 s are client retry timers with a 5-second timeout, or connection attempts to a dead backend that time out and retry elsewhere; slicing the slow requests by backend instance and zone distinguishes those. Mitigate with node-local DNS caching, lower ndots, fully qualified names, and connection reuse so fewer lookups happen at all.
qa: E
What is the bandwidth-delay product and why does it matter?

Bandwidth multiplied by round-trip time: the amount of data that must be in flight to keep a path full. If the TCP window or socket buffers are smaller, throughput is capped at window divided by RTT, so long high-bandwidth paths need large windows. For 1 Gbit/s at 100 ms that is 12.5 MB, far beyond the 64 KB a window without scaling allows.

Follow-up: How do you get a transfer to fill such a path? — Enable window scaling and raise socket buffer maximums so autotuning can grow, use several parallel streams, and consider BBR if loss is present.
E
A service is unreachable. Walk through your first five checks.

Does the name resolve to the expected address from the client (dig)? Can the client reach the port, and is the failure refused or a timeout (nc -vz)? If it connects, does TLS complete with a valid certificate for the name (openssl s_client)? If TLS works, what does HTTP return, including status and headers (curl -v)? And what changed recently: deploys, DNS, firewall rules, certificates?
Follow-up: Why check from the client rather than your laptop? — The client may use a different resolver, network, routes and firewall rules, so only its view reproduces the problem.
E
How do you tell whether a slow request is slow because of the network or the server?

Split its time into phases with curl -w or browser timing: DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, time to first byte and transfer. If connect and TLS are each about one RTT and small, but time to first byte is large, the server is slow. If connect and TLS are large, the path is long or lossy. If DNS is large, look at resolvers.
Follow-up: What does a DNS time of almost exactly 5 seconds suggest? — A lost DNS query retried after the stub resolver's default 5-second timeout.
M
What is a PMTU black hole?

When a path has a smaller MTU than the sender assumes, for example through a VPN or overlay network, oversized packets are dropped, and the ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages that should tell the sender are blocked by a firewall. Small exchanges work but large transfers hang, and TLS handshakes with large certificate chains may stall. Allowing that ICMP type, clamping TCP MSS on the tunnel, or lowering the MTU fixes it.

Follow-up: How do you find the path MTU by hand? — ping with the don't-fragment flag and decreasing sizes (ping -M do -s 1472 on Linux) until it succeeds; 1472 bytes of data plus 28 bytes of headers equals 1500.
M
How do you break down where the time goes in a slow HTTPS request?

Use curl's timing variables: time_namelookup for DNS, time_connect for the TCP handshake, time_appconnect for TLS, time_starttransfer for time to first byte and time_total. They are cumulative, so subtract consecutive values to get each phase, then investigate the dominant one. Browsers show the same phases in DevTools and to real-user monitoring through the Resource Timing API.

Follow-up: What would a large gap between time_appconnect and time_starttransfer mean? — The server, or something behind it, took a long time to produce the first byte: application processing, a slow database, or a proxy queue.
M
How do you read mtr output without being misled?

Each row is a router on the path, with loss and latency for probes sent to it. Routers deprioritise and rate-limit the ICMP replies mtr relies on, so a middle hop can show loss or high latency that does not affect traffic passing through it. Only loss or latency that starts at some hop and persists through all later hops, including the destination, indicates a real problem on the path from that point.
Follow-up: Why is mtr better than a single traceroute? — It runs continuously, so it shows loss rates and latency variation over time rather than one snapshot.
M
When would you take a packet capture, and where?

When logs and metrics cannot tell which side stopped talking or what exactly was exchanged: connection timeouts, resets, hangs, TLS failures, or suspected loss. Capture on both ends if possible, filtered to the relevant host and port, and compare: if the server's capture shows the SYN arriving but no SYN-ACK leaving, the server is at fault; if SYN-ACKs leave but never reach the client, the return path is. Save to a pcap file and analyse in Wireshark.

Follow-up: What do you do when traffic is TLS-encrypted? — Timing, sizes, handshakes, resets and retransmissions are still visible; for content, log TLS keys with SSLKEYLOGFILE on a test client so Wireshark can decrypt.
M
How does packet loss affect TCP performance, in numbers?

Each loss makes TCP shrink its congestion window, and a lost final segment may cost a retransmission timeout of at least 200 ms on Linux. The Mathis approximation puts throughput at about MSS divided by RTT times the square root of the loss rate, so on a 100 ms path, 1% loss limits a classic TCP connection to roughly 1 to 1.5 Mbit/s regardless of link speed. For short requests, the effect shows up as tail latency rather than throughput.

Follow-up: Where does loss usually come from in cloud environments? — Congested links or middleboxes, instance or NAT packet-rate limits, full conntrack tables, and overflowing queues on the receiving host.
M
How do you debug networking from inside a Kubernetes pod?

Run tools in the pod's own network namespace, since its DNS configuration, routes and policies differ from the node's and your laptop's. Use kubectl exec if the image has tools, or kubectl debug to attach an ephemeral container with a toolbox image such as netshoot. From there run dig against the cluster DNS, curl the service name and the pod IPs directly, check NetworkPolicies, and compare with the same checks from another pod.

Follow-up: The service name fails but the pod IP works. What next? — Check the Service's selector and endpoints (kubectl get endpoints), since a Service with no matching ready pods has nothing to route to.
M
What would you check if a Linux host starts dropping new connections under load while CPU is fine?

The accept queue (ss -ltn shows Recv-Q near Send-Q, and ListenOverflows counters rise) if the application is slow to accept; the conntrack table, if the kernel log says 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet'; ephemeral port exhaustion for outbound connections (many TIME_WAIT sockets, 'Cannot assign requested address'); file descriptor limits ('Too many open files'); and cloud per-instance packet-rate or connection-tracking limits.

Follow-up: How do you fix a full conntrack table? — Raise nf_conntrack_max and memory, shorten timeouts for short-lived flows, and reduce connection churn with keep-alive; for very high-rate services, avoid tracking where possible.
H
A transfer from Singapore to Frankfurt runs at 3 Mbit/s on a 1 Gbit/s path with no retransmissions. Diagnose it.

With no loss, the congestion window is not the limit, so the receive window is. Throughput is at most window divided by RTT: at 160 ms RTT, 3.3 Mbit/s corresponds to a window of about 64 KB, the maximum without window scaling. The BDP is 1 Gbit/s times 0.16 s, 20 MB. Likely causes are window scaling disabled or stripped by a middlebox, small socket buffer maximums, or the application setting SO_RCVBUF explicitly, which disables autotuning. Confirm with ss -ti (rcv_space, snd_wnd, wscale) and fix the window.
Follow-up: If fixing the window is impossible, what then? — Use several parallel connections, each with its own window, as many transfer tools do.
H
Some requests to a service fail intermittently with timeouts, about 1% of them. How do you approach it?

Correlate before guessing. Slice failures by backend instance, availability zone, client host, time, request size, connection age and protocol. A single bad instance behind a load balancer, one zone with a faulty network path, requests above a size (MTU), connections idle longer than a NAT or balancer timeout, DNS lookups hitting an overloaded resolver, or a pool handing out dead connections each leave a distinct fingerprint. Once narrowed, capture packets on both sides of the failing path.

Follow-up: What if failures correlate with nothing? — Look lower: ECMP means some flows hash onto a bad link, which appears random per connection but is consistent per 4-tuple; retrying on a new connection succeeding is a strong hint.
H
How would you establish a performance baseline for a service's network, and why?

Measure, per path that matters (client to edge, edge to origin, zone to zone, region to region, service to database), the normal RTT distribution, throughput per connection and per instance, retransmission rate, DNS resolution time and connection establishment time, and record typical p50, p95 and p99 per phase. Keep them on dashboards. During an incident, the question 'is this abnormal?' then has an answer in seconds, and capacity planning uses real numbers rather than assumptions.
Follow-up: Which baseline is most often missing? — Cross-zone and cross-region latency and throughput, which shape database placement and replication decisions.
H
What does eBPF add to network debugging in production?

eBPF lets small, verified programs run inside the kernel at events such as TCP state changes, retransmissions and packet drops, and aggregate results cheaply. Tools like tcpretrans, tcplife and tcpconnect from the bcc collection show every retransmission, connection lifetime or new connection with process names, with little overhead, and Kubernetes network plugins such as Cilium expose per-flow visibility and drop reasons. That answers questions that previously needed full packet captures.
Follow-up: Why is 'drop reason' so valuable? — It says whether a packet died on a policy, a full queue, conntrack or a routing miss, turning a vague 'packets are lost' into a specific fix.
